The CBN shall not handle cases that fall within these categories: a) Time barred complaints; and b) Cases before the courts or cases already ruled upon by the courts of law (except where directed by the court through an order). | The bank shall: 1. |  | 25 | Requirement to Display Corporate Names on Websites, Portals, Applications, and Other Online Business Platforms |  | FPR/PRD/CIR/INT/001/003 | The Central Bank of Nigeria has observed with concern that some licensed entities that operate transaction websites/portals or online applications do not conspicuously display their corporate names to facilitate recognition by the public. This practice portends risk to consumers of such products and services, including potential negative perception of the products or services, misleading consumers and difficulty to seek redress when the need arises.  In view of the above and to engender trust and confidence in the use of such products and services, all licensed financial institutions are hereby required to:  1. Conspicuously display their corporate names on all their websites, portals and online applications.  2. Include ‘Licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria’ beside or under their names. | The bank shall: 1. Clearly display the institution’s corporate name on all websites, portals, and mobile/web applications. 2. Add the phrase “Licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria” next to or directly beneath the corporate name on each platform. | - Non-compliance could lead to regulatory sanctions or penalties. - Loss of consumer trust and difficulty in brand recognition. - Exposure to reputational damage and potential legal issues when consumers cannot trace or verify the provider. | Medium | High | - Corporate Communications- Digital Channels Unit / Product Owners- IT & Web Development Team- Compliance Department | - Periodic compliance check of all online platforms. - Pre-launch compliance checklist for new digital products or portals. - Regular IT audits to verify compliance with naming display rules. - Branding guidelines updated to enforce proper name usage. | Low | Low |
|  | 26 | Consumer Protection Regulation | 3 | FAIR TREATMENT OF CONSUMERS |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  | 3.1 | GENERAL PROVISIONS | Institutions shall comply with the following provisions to ensure fair treatment of consumers:  3.1.1 Treat consumers equitably without bias at all stages of the relationship. 3.1.2 Give consumers who meet the minimum legal and non – discriminatory eligibility requirements, equal access to basic services without regard to their social status, physical ability, marital status, gender, age, religion, tribe or ideology. 3.1.3 Consider the needs of the financially excluded, including the vulnerable groups such as low-income consumers, women, seniors, physically challenged and the non-literate in the development and implementation of their business models, strategies and processes. | Banks must:  1. Treat all consumers fairly and without discrimination at every stage of their interaction.  2. Provide equal access to basic services for all eligible consumers, regardless of status or identity.  3. Design and implement services that also consider the needs of vulnerable and financially excluded groups (e.g., low-income earners, women, elderly, physically challenged, and non-literate individuals). | Failure to uphold fairness and non-discrimination may result in reputational damage, customer complaints, regulatory penalties, and loss of consumer trust. | Medium | High | Chief Customer Experience Officer, Head of Retail/Consumer Banking, Compliance Officer, CSR/Financial Inclusion Officer | - Develop inclusive service policies and procedures. - Train staff on equitable treatment and non-discrimination. - Provide alternative access channels for vulnerable groups (e.g., USSD, local language support). - Monitor and report consumer complaints and resolution trends. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | 3.2 | EQUITY | It shall be the duty of Institutions to treat consumers equitably always. Therefore, Institutions shall:  3.2.1 Treat consumers with courtesy and respect and shall not engage in practices such as threats, intimidation, use of abusive or offensive language, humiliation, misrepresentation, deception or unfair inducements. 3.2.2 Apply lending fees on disbursed amounts only in respect of term loans, except for fees which are normally applicable on undisbursed portions. 3.2.3 Apply non-credit related fees/charges on an account only to the extent of the balance in the account, and defer the outstanding fees/charges until the account is funded and the customer notified of the deferred fees/charges. 3.2.4 Promptly oblige consumers’ request for account closure or to switch providers, without unreasonable closing/switching barriers. 3.2.5 Ensure that variations to contracts including interest rate, fees or charges are only made if expressly provided for in the contract and shall notify consumer of any such variation. 3.2.6 Respond to customers’ enquiries/requests within five (5) working days of receiving the enquiries/requests. 3.2.7 Communicate a decision (acceptance or decline) on applications for waivers, extensions, and other concessions to a customer within ten (10) working days, otherwise the application shall be deemed to have been granted. 3.2.8 Not act in a manner that is inconsistent with the terms and conditions of their contracts with their customers. 3.2.9 Not seek repayment or withhold, in part or in full, customer’s funds to secure repayment before the due date, except with the written authorization of the customer. 3.2.10 Not charge early liquidation fees for consumer and SME loans with variable interest rate. | The bank must:  1. Treat all customers with respect and avoid threats, deception, or unfair practices.  2. Only charge lending fees on actual loan amounts disbursed (unless otherwise specified).  3. Only apply non-credit fees up to the available balance and defer the rest, with clear customer notification.  4. Allow customers to close accounts or switch providers easily, without delays or hurdles.  5. Notify customers of any contract changes only if stated in the contract and with proper notice.  6. Respond to all customer enquiries/requests within 5 working days.  7. Communicate decisions on waivers/concessions within 10 working days, or such requests are considered granted.  8. Honor all contract terms and avoid acting contrary to agreements with customers.  9. Do not withhold customer funds or demand early repayment unless authorized in writing.  10. Do not charge early liquidation fees on variable interest loans to consumers and SMEs. | Failure to comply may result in regulatory sanctions, customer complaints, reputational damage, financial penalties, and increased litigation risk. | High | High | - Head, Retail Banking - Customer Experience Manager - Legal & Compliance Officer - Product & Loan Operations - Collections Team | - Staff training on ethical customer interaction.  - Automated fee application rules.  - Account closure and switching procedures.  - Contract template review and approval process. - Complaint handling and escalation workflow.  - CRM system tracking timelines for all enquiries and waiver decisions. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | 4 | DISCLOSURE AND TRANSPARENCY |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  | 4.1 | GENERAL PROVISIONS | To promote transparency and enhance disclosure practices, Institutions shall comply with the following provisions:  4.1.1. Ensure that documents provided or made available to consumers shall: a. Be written in clear, legible and simple English language and in a minimum font size of 10. b. Be provided in a durable form for future reference. c. State the name, contact details of the Institution and the consumer. d. Contain a statement that the Institution is regulated by the Central Bank of Nigeria. e. Not be misleading or deceptive.  4.1.2. Put procedures in place to ensure that an oral explanation of the document is provided to the consumer in a language that he or she understands if: a. the consumer requests; or b. it is reasonably obvious that the consumer is illiterate or visually impaired or, for any other reason, cannot understand the document.  4.1.3. Conspicuously display in their banking halls and publish on their websites and internet banking platforms, accurate and up to date information on all their products and services. Such information shall include: a. prime and maximum lending rates; b. deposit rates; and c. exchange rates of foreign currencies.  4.1.4. Disclose to the consumer in writing, all Terms and Conditions of a transaction agreement. 4.1.5. Ensure that the disclaimer “Terms and Conditions Apply” or any other phrase conveying a similar meaning shall only be used if the terms and conditions have been explained and disclosed in the contract or in other medium accessible by the customer. The Institution shall at all times, draw the consumer’s attention to such disclosure. 4.1.6. Clearly explain technical terms used in documents to the consumer to aid understanding. 4.1.7. Agree with consumers on the communication channel(s) to be used for all correspondences and include the channel(s) in all contract documents. 4.1.8. Ensure that their websites and other information dissemination channels are functional and regularly updated with the current features of products and services offered. 4.1.9. Comply with the rates, fees, charges, or prices published or disclosed at the engagement points. 4.1.10. Inform consumers of applicable and indicative foreign exchange rates through customer engagement points and advise consumers to always check the rates before consummating foreign exchange transactions. 4.1.11. Bear all costs associated with disclosures to customers required by the Regulations, except for deposits and withdrawals by or on behalf of the customer. | The bank must: 1. Use clear, simple English (minimum font size 10) in customer-facing documents, and ensure documents are durable and personalized (with names, contacts, CBN disclosure, etc.). 2. Provide oral explanations for documents when requested or needed (e.g., for illiterate or visually impaired customers). 3. Clearly display on all platforms: up-to-date lending, deposit, and FX rates. 4. Disclose all transaction terms and conditions clearly in writing.5. Only use "Terms and Conditions Apply" if the T&Cs are explained and accessible.6. Explain all technical terms to consumers. 7. Agree on a communication channel with the customer and include it in the contract. 8. Ensure all dissemination platforms (website, mobile app, etc.) are functional and current. 9. Honour the rates and charges displayed at the point of engagement. 10. Inform customers of applicable FX rates at the point of transaction. 11. Bear the cost of disclosures required by law. | Non-compliance may result in poor customer experience, regulatory penalties, loss of trust, reputational damage, legal actions, and customer attrition. | High | High | - Head, Customer Experience - Legal & Compliance Department - Retail/Commercial Banking Heads - Corporate Communications - Product & Digital Banking Teams | - Disclosure templates approved by Legal and Compliance.  - Website and banking app update protocols.  - Periodic review of posted rates.  - Document accessibility processes.  - Standard operating procedure (SOP) for KYC and communication preference documentation.  - Internal audit checks on displayed and applied rates. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | 4.2 | ADVERTISEMENT | Institutions shall comply with the following disclosures for all advertisements and promotional materials:  4.2.1 The content of advertisements shall be factual and unambiguous, expressed in clear and simple language and shall not be offensive, misleading, deceptive, injurious, or exaggerate the benefits of the products or services being advertised. 4.2.2 The overall impression of advertisements shall not emphasize benefits of a product or service while de-emphasizing its associated risks. 4.2.3 Disclose their contact details in any advertisement or promotional material. 4.2.4 Clearly disclose details of the cost of a product or services, including all fees and other associated charges. 4.2.5 Fully disclose the nature and value of benefits, where an advertisement refers to, or is linked to other value adding benefits. 4.2.6 Not make references to unaudited financial statements. 4.2.7 Not mention names of competitors or make comparisons in their advertisements. 4.2.8 Unsolicited advertisements through emails, text messages, voice calls and other channels sent by or on behalf of a Institution shall be at no cost to the consumer and shall contain an opt-out provision for future advertisements. 4.2.9 Notify the Director, Consumer Protection Department of the CBN prior to the commencement of advertisement of product or service by submitting a description of the content of the advertisement. | The bank must: 1. Ensure advertisements are factual, clear, and not misleading. 2. Avoid exaggerating benefits or hiding product/service risks. 3. Display contact details in all adverts. 4. Disclose full cost of products/services, including fees and charges. 5. Clearly state the value and nature of any benefits tied to a product. 6. Not reference unaudited financials. 7. Avoid mentioning competitors or making comparisons. 8. Be free to recipients and must include an opt-out option from unsolicited ads via email/SMS/calls. 9. Notify CBN before launching any product/service advertisement with content details. | - Non-compliance may result in regulatory sanctions or fines. - Could lead to consumer mistrust and reputational damage. - Legal liabilities due to deceptive advertising or omitted cost disclosures. - May be accused of anti-competitive practices if competitors are referenced. - Failure to notify CBN could cause regulatory breaches. | High | High | - Marketing & Corporate Communications Department- Compliance Department- Legal Department- Product/Service Owners- Contact Centre Team | - Implement advertisement approval workflows involving Legal and Compliance. - Maintain advertising policy and checklist in line with regulatory expectations. - Establish review committee to vet content before publication. - Use standard templates to ensure inclusion of contact and cost details. - Opt-out system enabled and tested on all unsolicited communication channels. - Maintain a record of CBN notifications and approvals. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | 4.3 | PRE-CONTRACT DISCLOSURES | Institutions shall comply with the following requirements prior to the execution of any contract with consumers:  4.3.1 Disclose all terms and conditions of a product or service on offer, as well as the features, risks, benefits, fees and other associated charges. 4.3.2 Disclose in contracts, the possibility of variations in interest rates or foreign exchange due to changes in market conditions. 4.3.3 Disclose similar products and services within the Institution, to enable consumers make comparisons and informed choices. 4.3.4 Provide the consumer, a Key Facts Statement (KFS) in the format attached as Annexure A stating a summary of key information on consumer loans. 4.3.5 Allow consumers a minimum of two (2) days from date of receipt, to review draft contract before execution except where the customer waives this in writing. 4.3.6 Give a consumer a cooling-off period of three (3) working days after the signing of a credit contract within which the consumer may cancel the contract without having to pay any penalty or charges. However, the consumer may choose to waive the option by notifying the bank in writing. | The bank must: 1. Disclose all terms, conditions, features, risks, benefits, fees, and charges of the product or service before contract execution. 2. Clearly state in the contract if interest rates or FX rates may vary due to market conditions. 3. Provide information on similar products and services to help customers make comparisons. 4. Issue a Key Facts Statement (KFS) in the required format for consumer loans. 5. Give consumers at least 2 days to review draft contracts before signing, unless waived in writing. 6. Allow a 3-working-day cooling-off period post-signing for contract cancellation without penalties, unless waived by the consumer in writing. | - Regulatory non-compliance penalties. - Consumer complaints or litigation for lack of disclosure or coercion. - Reputational risk due to perceived lack of transparency. - Breach of consumer protection laws leading to enforcement actions. | High | High | - Legal Department- Product Managers- Compliance Department- Retail/Consumer Banking Unit- Credit/Risk Department | - Standardized product disclosure templates (including the KFS). - Mandatory pre-contract disclosure checklist. - Internal review of draft contracts by Legal and Compliance. - Staff training on disclosure obligations. - Automated systems to flag contracts not meeting the 2-day review or cooling-off rule. | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | 4.4 | CONTRACTUAL DISCLOSURES | Institutions shall comply with the following requirements during the lifecycle of any contract with consumers:  4.4.1 Notify consumers of any transaction on their account immediately it is made. At a minimum, the notification shall include date, amount, payer, transaction reference, channel and the cleared account balance. 4.4.2 Ensure that descriptions in account statements are clear. At a minimum, it shall include, transaction reference, payer transaction channel, location and account balance. 4.4.3 Ensure that, at a minimum, credit contracts contain the following information: a. Key features and risks; b. Tenor of the contract; c. The nature, amount and method of calculation of any interest, fee or charge and when it is payable; d. The applicable Annual Percentage Rate (APR) to be calculated using the formula stated in Annexure B1 and B2; e. Notice of possible variations in interest rates, and how the consumer will be informed of changes; and f. Information on how to lodge a complaint to the Institution and escalate complaint to the CBN where necessary.  4.4.4 Provide consumer with monthly statements (or confirmation/investment advice as the case may be) for all products and account types, including loan accounts, special accounts and other related accounts at no cost. 4.4.5 Provide account balances to consumers on request. 4.4.6 Give prior notice of variation in interest rates to customers. At a minimum, the notice shall state: a. The reason for the variation; b. The commencement date; c. The revised repayment schedule (where necessary); and d. The alternatives available such as concession, restructuring, re-negotiation, opt-out or termination of the contract.  4.4.7 Ensure that variations in interest shall only be implemented after requisite notification to consumers: 10 working days (DMB) and 5 working days for other Institutions. | The bank must: 1. Send instant alerts to customers for every transaction, showing date, amount, payer, channel, reference, and new balance. 2. Make sure account statements are clear and include transaction reference, payer, channel, location, and balance. 3. Ensure credit contracts show key features, risks, tenor, interest/fees/charges (with calculations), APR (as per formula), rate variation process, and complaint channels. 4. Provide monthly statements (or confirmation/advice) for all account and product types (loans, investments, etc.) free of charge. 5. Provide account balances when requested by customers. 6. Before changing interest rates, give prior notice stating: reason, start date, revised schedule, and customer options (restructure, renegotiate, exit, etc.). 7. Delay interest changes until 10 working days’ notice for DMBs or 5 working days for others has been given. | Failure to comply can lead to customer complaints, regulatory sanctions, disputes over unfair charges or changes in terms, reputational damage, and class-action lawsuits. | High | High | - Legal and Compliance Unit - Retail/Commercial Lending Teams - Core Banking Product Managers - Customer Experience/Operations - IT/Alert Notification & Statement Delivery Team | - Automated transaction alert system.  - Template-based contract documents reviewed by Legal.  - System-generated monthly statements.  - SMS/email balance inquiry processes.  - Interest variation approval workflows with customer notification embedded. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | 4.5 | For deposit products | a. minimum balance requirement and other limit on account balances or transactions where applicable; b. monthly maintenance fee, any applicable tenor for a term deposit and any penalty for terminating a term deposit early; c. savings withdrawal options; and d. any reason(s) and timeline within which the account could become inactive or dormant. | The bank must disclose the following clearly to customers when offering deposit products: a. The minimum balance required, and any limits on how much can be held or transacted. b. The monthly maintenance fees, the duration (tenor) of term deposits, and penalties for early termination. c. How and when customers can withdraw from savings accounts. d. The reasons and timeframes that would lead to an account becoming inactive or dormant. | If these requirements are not met, customers may feel misled, resulting in disputes, regulatory penalties from the CBN, customer churn, and reputational damage. | Medium | High | - Retail Banking Products Team - Compliance & Legal Department - Customer Service/Branch Ops - Marketing & Communications - IT (Digital Banking/Account Setup) | - Product disclosure templates and brochures.  - Account opening forms include fee and limit breakdowns.  - Dormancy notification process in place.  - Maintenance fee schedules published online and in branches. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | 4.6 | DISCLOSURE ON DEFAULT OF CREDIT REPAYMENT | a. Institutions that are DMBs shall notify consumers within 3 days from the first day of default, through the agreed medium that a default charge would be applied on the account after 7 days from the date the obligation becomes due. c. Default charge shall be disclosed in customers’ statements of account separately from the interest charge. | The bank must: a. Notify consumers within 3 days of the first default that default charges will apply after 7 days of overdue payment. c. Disclose default charges separately from interest in account statements. | - Regulatory breaches and potential CBN sanctions for non-compliance. - Customer distrust and disputes due to unclear or delayed notification. - Reputational risk from customer complaints or legal action regarding improper disclosure or penalty application. | High | High | - Credit Risk Management- Collections & Recovery Unit- Legal and Compliance Department- Customer Service/Experience Department- IT/Software Team (Loan Management System) | - Embed notification triggers in loan management system. - Automated alerts (SMS, email, in-app) to notify customers as required. - Standard operating procedures (SOPs) for collections to ensure timelines are met. - Ensure statement templates separate default charges from interest. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | 5 | RESPONSIBLE BUSINESS CONDUCT |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  | 5.1 | GENERAL PROVISIONS | To promote good business practices, Institutions shall comply with the following provisions:  5.1.1 Conduct their business in a responsible, professional and ethical manner. 5.1.2 Train their staff to promote competence, efficiency and professionalism in the discharge of their duties. 5.1.3 Provide clear information about products and services, features, terms and conditions and the applicable fees and charges. 5.1.4 Provide and inform consumers of the channels to make enquiries and complaints. 5.1.5 Notify customers of circumstances or situations that may affect the terms of their contracts or relationships. 5.1.6 Display all applicable fees for electronic payment services with the option to accept or decline before a transaction is consummated. This should include a notice that third-party charges may apply. 5.1.7 Not impose any product, service or channel on consumers. 5.1.8 Not charge fees for issuance and renewal of products or services which have not been requested by the customer. 5.1.9 Not compel consumers to buy a product or service as a condition for the purchase of another product or service unless where the products or services are directly dependent. | The bank shall: 1. Conduct all business dealings professionally, ethically, and responsibly. 2. Train staff to uphold competence and professionalism. 3. Provide clear, accurate product/service information, including terms, conditions, and fees. 4. Inform customers about available complaint/enquiry channels. 5. Notify customers of any change that affects their contracts. 6. Display all e-payment fees and allow customer consent before transactions. 7. Not force products/services on consumers. 8. Not charge for unrequested products. 9. Not compel bundling of products unless they're interdependent. | - Risk of CBN sanctions and legal penalties for failure to comply. - Potential customer dissatisfaction, complaints, and churn. - Reputational damage due to unethical or misleading practices. - Risk of class-action lawsuits or regulator intervention from bundled/forced product offerings. | High | High | - Legal and Compliance Department- Product Management Team- Customer Experience/Service Department- Marketing and Sales Team- IT/Business Process Automation Team | - Develop a Consumer Protection Compliance Policy. - Ensure product/service literature is standardized and approved before publication. - Implement staff training and compliance onboarding. - Automate fee display and consent features in digital channels. - Maintain and publicize a complaints resolution framework. - Regular reviews of bundled offerings and customer opt-in records. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | 5.2 | RESPONSIBLE LENDING | To ensure that the capability of consumers to repay credits are professionally assessed, Institutions shall comply with the following requirements:  5.2.1 Include in credit risk assessment procedures, the type and circumstances for which a credit will be suitable as well as clear lines of authority for approving the product. 5.2.2 Before granting credit to consumers, assess their capability to repay in a sustainable manner taking into consideration their financial circumstances. 5.2.3 Ascertain the credit history of consumers from the Credit Risk Management System, Credit Bureau and other sources of credit reference before advancing credits. 5.2.4 Have a policy to deal with consumers who are in financial difficulty. 5.2.5 Monitor loan performance and upon early detection of repayment difficulties engage the customer to discuss alternative repayment options. 5.2.6 Not compel consumers to buy products or services, such as insurance or valuation from a particular third-party provider as a pre-condition for the grant of a credit facility, but can provide the option to choose from at least three (3) providers or any number as may be prescribed by CBN from time to time. 5.2.7 Ensure that guarantors confirm in writing that they have read and understood their commitments, potential implications and the maximum amount they are guaranteeing, and have either: a. sought and obtained independent professional advice before executing the guarantee; or b. declared that they do not need independent advice. 5.2.8 Provide periodic update to Guarantors on the loan performance to enable them to assess the likelihood of being called upon to discharge their commitments. 5.2.9 Issue Letter of Discharge at no cost to customers within 5 business days after liquidation of their loans, and where the loan is guaranteed, the guarantor shall also be notified accordingly. 5.2.10 Notify customers where their loan requests are declined. The reason(s) for decline shall be provided upon request. | The bank shall: 1. Include credit suitability criteria and approval authority in credit risk procedures. 2. Assess a consumer's ability to repay before granting credit, considering their financial situation. 3. Check consumer credit history from CRMS, credit bureaus, or other sources before loan approval. 4. Maintain policies for dealing with consumers in financial difficulty. 5. Monitor loans and engage struggling customers early to find repayment solutions. 6. Not force customers to use specific service providers (e.g., insurance); offer at least 3 options. 7. Ensure guarantors provide written confirmation of understanding and advice status. 8. Send guarantors periodic updates on loan performance. 9. Issue free Loan Discharge Letters within 5 business days post-loan repayment and notify guarantors. 10. Inform customers of declined loan applications and provide reasons upon request. | - Regulatory sanctions for non-compliance with responsible lending principles. - Increased loan defaults due to poor credit assessment. - Reputational damage and customer complaints due to unfair practices or lack of transparency. - Legal liability from guarantors or consumers who were not properly informed. - Potential CBN penalties for compelling use of third-party services. | High | High | - Credit Risk Management Unit- Loan Approval Officers- Legal and Compliance Department- Customer Service/Experience- Loan Monitoring/Collections Team | - Incorporate responsible lending checks into credit policy and procedures. - Embed income and affordability checks in loan application systems. - Set automated CRMS and credit bureau validation before approval. - Develop SOPs for handling financial difficulty cases. - Train staff on third-party product disclosure rules. - Require written declarations and advice confirmations from guarantors. - Automate alerts for periodic loan performance updates to guarantors. - Automate discharge letter issuance within 5 business days. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | 5.3 | SALES PROMOTION | To ensure that advertisements and promotional materials on products and services are clear and not misleading, Institutions shall:  5.3.1 Provide information that would aid consumers’ decisions. 5.3.2 Carry out marketing of products and services in an ethical and professional manner. 5.3.3 Ensure that sales and marketing staff are properly trained and competent to perform their functions. The staff should be knowledgeable in key features, risks and critical terms of product offering. 5.3.4 Establish a process to periodically check and monitor the competence and conduct of sales and marketing staff. 5.3.5 The remuneration of marketing/sales staff shall not be solely based on sales volume/target but must give consideration to the interests and circumstances of the customers. 5.3.6 Provide consumers with the option to opt out from receiving marketing materials. | The bank shall: 1. Ensure all product/service ads and promotions are clear and not misleading. 2. Disclose adequate information to help customers make informed decisions. 3. Conduct marketing activities in a professional and ethical manner. 4. Ensure marketing/sales staff are well-trained and competent on key product features, risks, and terms. 5. Establish a system to regularly assess staff conduct and competence. 6. Sales staff remuneration must not be solely based on targets – it must reflect customer welfare. 7. Allow customers to opt-out of marketing messages. | - Regulatory sanctions for misleading advertising or unethical marketing practices. - Reputational damage and loss of customer trust. - Legal claims from mis-sold products or deceptive marketing. - Customer churn due to aggressive or unethical sales tactics. - Poorly trained staff may lead to non-compliance and increased complaints. | High | High | - Head of Marketing- Head of Compliance- Head of Human Resources- Sales and Product Teams- Customer Experience/Service Team | - Implement a compliance review process for all advertisements and promotions. - Develop and deliver regular training for all marketing and sales staff. - Enforce a code of ethics for marketing and sales. - Conduct regular performance assessments and competency reviews of staff. - Design a balanced scorecard for sales incentives that includes customer satisfaction. - Include opt-out options clearly in all promotional messages (SMS, emails, etc.). | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | 5.4 | DATA PROTECTION AND PRIVACY | To ensure data protection and privacy of consumers, Institutions shall:  5.4.1 Protect the privacy and confidentiality of consumer information and assets against unauthorized access, and be accountable for acts or omissions in respect thereof. 5.4.2 Obtain the written consent of consumers to collect and process their personal data for specific purpose and provide them with the option to withdraw the consent at any time. 5.4.3 Not transfer personal data of consumers to a third party without their express consent, except in compliance with a legal obligation. 5.4.4 Inform consumers whenever their data is exchanged with an authorized third party, stating details of the exchange. 5.4.5 Review data processing and privacy procedures to ensure that the purpose(s) for which initial consent was granted remained valid. 5.4.6 Keep accurate and updated data of consumers always. | The bank must: 5.4.1 Ensure customer information is secure, confidential, and protected from unauthorized access, and be accountable for any misuse or exposure. 5.4.2 Get written consent from customers before collecting or processing their personal data, and give them the option to withdraw it anytime. 5.4.3 Do not share personal data with third parties unless the customer explicitly agrees or there’s a legal requirement. 5.4.4 Always notify customers when their data is shared with any authorized third party, including who received it and why. 5.4.5 Regularly review data processing practices to ensure they still align with the customer’s original consent. 5.4.6 Keep customer records accurate and current at all times. | Data breaches, unauthorized disclosures, or failure to get proper consent can lead to heavy fines (NDPA/NDPR/CBN), loss of customer trust, reputational damage, and litigation. | High | High | - Data Protection Officer (DPO)- IT Security- Compliance & Legal- Customer Service- Operations- Digital Channels / CRM Team | - Data Protection & Privacy Policy (aligned with NDPA/NDPR). - Consent forms embedded in digital/onboarding journeys. - Encryption, firewalls, and access control protocols. - Periodic internal audits on data access logs. - Customer communication protocols and records. - Data quality and KYC validation processes. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | 6 | COMPLAINTS HANDLING & REDRESS |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  | 6.1 | GENERAL PROVISIONS | The resolution of disputes shall be the responsibility of Institutions. Consumer complaints shall first be lodged with Institutions for timely resolution and redress. Institutions shall:  6.1.1 Develop documented processes on Complaints Handling that will guarantee fairness, transparency, responsiveness and independence of the complaint handling mechanism. 6.1.2 Allocate adequate resources for complaints handling/redress and the processes manned by skilled and well-trained members of staff. 6.1.3 At all customer engagement points, disclose channels and contact details for lodging complaints, timeframe for resolution, and options for escalation. Where it is not practicable to comply with this, refer customers to where the information required could be obtained. | The bank: 6.1.1 They have a clear, written policy on how customer complaints will be handled. The policy must ensure fairness, openness, quick response times, and independence. 6.1.2 Adequate resources (budget, personnel, technology) are provided to handle complaints, and the team is made up of well-trained professionals. 6.1.3 At all customer service points (physical branches, digital platforms, ATMs, mobile apps), information must be made available on:– How to make a complaint– Contact details– Timeframe for resolution– How customers can escalate unresolved issuesIf not feasible in a location, direct the customer to where this information can be obtained. | Poor complaints handling could lead to regulatory sanctions, reputational damage, erosion of customer trust, and increased litigation or escalations to the CBN Consumer Protection Department. | Medium | High | - Customer Service / Customer Experience Team- Compliance Team- Branch Managers- Contact Center Managers- IT / Digital Channels Team | - Complaint Management Policy (documented and approved). - Dedicated complaints handling unit with escalation matrix. - CRM system for tracking and resolving complaints. - Complaint channels published on websites, mobile apps, branches. - Periodic staff training on dispute resolution protocols. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | 6.2 | COMPLAINTS MANAGEMENT CHANNELS | Institutions shall provide multiple dedicated channels to receive and handle consumer complaints including verbal complaints. The channels may include letters, e-mails, telephone lines, social media and digital software platforms. |  |  |  | 6.3 | INTERNAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION | Institutions shall establish Internal Dispute Resolution (IDR) structures and processes for the effective management of consumer complaints. The IDR mechanism shall satisfy the following requirements:  6.3.1 Be under the oversight of the Executive Compliance Officer or an equivalent. 6.3.2 Upon receipt of a complaint, communicate to the consumer within 24 hours, an acknowledgment containing: a. a unique identification or tracking number, b. contact details of the complaints desk, c. expected resolution timeline, d. escalation options; and e. an assurance that the complaint is being addressed.  6.3.3 Use the unique identification or tracking number in all correspondence with the complainant. 6.3.4 Designate a unit for complaints handling independent of other products or business functions taking into consideration, the nature and complexity of their business. 6.3.5 Staff responsible for handling complaints shall be required to declare any conflict of interest that may affect their objectivity in handling a complaint. 6.3.6 Resolve complaints received within the time specified in the Timelines for Complaints Resolution by Institutions in Annexure D. 6.3.7 Refund identified excess charges, non-payment or under-payment of interest on deposits, unauthorized debits, etc. along with interest as provided in the extant Monetary, Credit, Foreign Trade and Exchange Policy Guidelines or any regulation issued by the CBN. 6.3.8 Issue a letter of apology to the complainant where the above applies. 6.3.9 Reconstruct customers' accounts to establish excess charges on overdrawn accounts, and pay interest on the identified excess charges after reconstruction, in accordance with extant CBN Regulations. 6.3.10 Remit established refunds and interest thereon to the complainants' accounts within the prescribed Timelines for Complaints Resolution by Institutions contained in Annexure D. 6.3.11 Send a Summary Resolution Communication (SRC) for resolved complaints, to the complainant by the next business day conveying: a. the basis for the decision(s); b. the right of appeal available to the complainant for a second level review by the Institution; and c. the right of escalation to the CBN, or other Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) avenues where the complainant is not satisfied with decisions arrived at.  6.3.12 A complaint shall be considered as resolved where the complainant has indicated acceptance of the resolution in writing to the Institution within 30 days after the receipt of the SRC, otherwise the complaint shall be deemed resolved and closed in the records of the Institution. 6.3.13 Where a complainant is dissatisfied with a decision communicated by a Institution, the complainant shall, within 30 days from the date of the receipt of the SRC, request in writing for a 2nd level review. 6.3.14 Upon receipt of a request for 2nd level review, the Institution shall review, resolve and communicate decision(s) within the Timelines for Complaints Resolution by Institutions as contained in Annexure D for second level review. 6.3.15 Identify recurring complaint types, identify their root cause(s), implement remedial measures, and generate a Root Cause Analysis Report (RCAR). 6.3.16 Prepare quarterly RCAR and submit to the Central Bank of Nigeria on or before 14th day of January, April, July and October respectively. 6.3.17 The RCAR shall contain the frequency of occurrence, identified root cause(s) and the remedial actions implemented. 6.3.18 Report complaints statistics in annual reports and the abridged Financial Statement in line with the approved format or any other format as may be prescribed by the CBN from time to time. 6.3.19 Institutions may outsource complaints handling functions subject to CBN approval. | The bank shall: 1. Establish an Internal Dispute Resolution (IDR) structure and process. 2. Place the IDR under the oversight of the Executive Compliance Officer or equivalent. 3. Upon receiving a complaint, send an acknowledgment within 24 hours that includes:  a. A unique tracking number for the complaint.  b. Contact details of the officer responsible for handling the complaint. | - Regulatory sanctions for failing to acknowledge or resolve complaints within timelines. - Reputational damage due to poor complaint management. - Increase in customer attrition and public distrust if complaints are not promptly or transparently handled. - Risk of legal action from dissatisfied customers. - Operational disruptions caused by poorly managed complaints. | High | High | - Executive Compliance Officer- Customer Experience/Service Team- Head of Operations- IT/Complaint Management System Administrator | - Develop and maintain a formal IDR policy. - Automate complaint logging and tracking system with timestamped acknowledgment. - Assign dedicated complaint handling officers with SLAs. - Implement workflow alerts to ensure timely escalation and response. - Regular training for staff on customer complaint handling. - Set up a central complaint database for monitoring resolution timelines. | Medium | Medium |

|  |  |  | 1.6 | Other Risk Management Control Functions | All SFIs shall ensure the effectiveness of their cybersecurity governance by reviewing their processes and controls annually. In this regard, these risk management control functions shall have the following responsibilities:  1.6.1. Risk Management i. The Risk Management function, internal or outsourced, shall independently and proactively evaluate all cybersecurity risks. This should be executed using appropriate tools and methodologies for risk identification, analysis and control. The assessment report shall be presented to Senior Management monthly and the Board Risk Management Committee quarterly. ii. Senior Management shall ensure that staff or external risk management professionals engaged to evaluate the institution’s cybersecurity posture possess the requisite qualifications and experience.  1.6.2. Audit i. The Audit function shall be independent and the scope of cybersecurity audits shall be clearly defined. ii. The SFI’s cybersecurity programme shall be reviewed by the Audit function, internal or external, to determine the effectiveness of the controls put in place and ascertain if they are adequate for the institution’s risk exposure. iii. Senior Management shall ensure that internal or outsourced audit staff engaged to review the institution’s cybersecurity posture, possess requisite qualifications and experience.  1.6.3. Compliance The Compliance function of SFIs shall periodically review the cybersecurity programmes and processes to ensure adherence to relevant CBN directives and extant regulations. | The bank must: 1. Review cybersecurity governance processes and controls at least annually. 2. Assign a Risk Management function (internal or external) to independently and proactively assess all cybersecurity risks using suitable tools and methodologies. 3. Present risk assessment reports to Senior Management monthly and to the Board Risk Management Committee quarterly. 4. Ensure Risk Management staff or external professionals have appropriate qualifications and experience. 5. Maintain an independent Audit function with a clearly defined scope for cybersecurity reviews. 6. Conduct cybersecurity audits to evaluate the effectiveness and adequacy of implemented controls. 7. Ensure Audit personnel (internal or external) possess the requisite qualifications and experience. 8. Assign the Compliance function to periodically review cybersecurity programmes for compliance with CBN directives and applicable regulations. | - Weakness or absence of risk, audit, or compliance oversight may lead to unidentified cybersecurity threats, ineffective governance, non-compliance with regulations, and security breaches. | - High | - High | - Head of Risk Management - Head of Internal Audit - Chief Compliance Officer - Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) - Board Risk Management Committee - Senior Management | - Implement formal and structured risk assessment tools and methodologies. - Submit monthly reports to Senior Management and quarterly to the Board Risk Committee. - Conduct periodic independent cybersecurity audits. - Verify qualifications of all audit, risk, and compliance staff or consultants. - Maintain clearly defined cybersecurity audit scope and periodic compliance reviews. | - Medium | - Medium |
|  |  |  | 2.1 (2.1.1, 2.1.2 & 2.1.4) | The Risk Management System | 2.1.1. Risk Identification SFIs shall identify associated threats and vulnerabilities to the confidentiality, integrity and availability of their information assets to determine their cyber risk exposure.  2.1.2. Risk assessment SFIs are required to evaluate risks to their operations, probability of occurrence, impact of risk crystallisation, and security controls to mitigate identified risks. This process should be carried out annually and whenever major changes occur within the institution such as an acquisition, merger or when new technology is deployed to handle key business processes. The outcome of this process should be documented in a Cybersecurity Risk Control Self-Assessment. An independent Audit function shall be responsible for ensuring that the methodology used in risk assessment is reviewed periodically.  2.1.4. Risk mitigation/Risk treatment SFIs should implement risk mitigation and control measures consistent with the criticality of information assets. Risk treatment options such as risk reduction, acceptance, avoidance, transfer and management of residual risk should be selected based on the outcome of the risk assessment. Risk acceptance criteria should be as defined and approved by the Board. In cases where the SFI chooses to transfer risk, a detailed risk assessment for outsourcing or cyber risk insurance should be documented. | The bank must: 1. Identify all threats and vulnerabilities that may affect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of their information assets (2.1.1). 2. Assess risks to operations, evaluate likelihood and potential impact, and review current security controls (2.1.2). 3. Conduct these assessments annually and during major changes like acquisitions, mergers, or implementation of new technologies. 4. Document the result of each assessment in a Cybersecurity Risk Control Self-Assessment. 5. Ensure the Audit function periodically reviews the risk assessment methodology for adequacy (2.1.2). 6. Apply risk mitigation and control measures based on the criticality of affected assets (2.1.4). 7. Choose and document appropriate risk treatment options—such as risk reduction, acceptance, avoidance, or transfer. 8. Define and get Board approval for risk acceptance criteria (2.1.4). 9. For risk transfers (e.g., outsourcing or insurance), conduct and document a detailed risk assessment (2.1.4). | - Failure to properly identify, assess, and treat cyber risks may lead to data breaches, financial losses, regulatory penalties, and reputational damage. | - High | - High | - Chief Risk Officer (CRO) - Chief Compliance Officer (CCO) - Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) - Head of Internal Audit - Board Risk Management Committee | - Maintain a risk register identifying threats and vulnerabilities. - Perform and document Cybersecurity Risk Control Self-Assessments. - Ensure annual and change-triggered risk assessments. - Establish Board-approved risk acceptance criteria. - Maintain audit-reviewed risk assessment methodology. - Maintain documentation for risk treatment decisions (e.g., acceptance, transfer). | - Medium | - Medium |
|  |  |  | 2.2 (ii & iv) | Vulnerability Identification | ii. SFIs shall ensure the conduct of yearly vulnerability assessments and threat analysis to detect and evaluate risk to its information assets and determine the appropriateness of security controls to mitigate identified risk. iv. SFIs shall ensure that internal vulnerability scans are carried out quarterly. | The bank must:  1. Conduct annual vulnerability assessments and threat analysis to identify and evaluate risks to its information assets and ensure the right security controls are in place. 2. Perform internal vulnerability scans every quarter to proactively identify system weaknesses. | Not identifying or addressing vulnerabilities could lead to data breaches, cyberattacks, unauthorized access, financial loss, and regulatory penalties. | High | High | CISO / Head, IT Risk & Governance | - Maintain a yearly calendar for third-party-led vulnerability assessments. - Automate internal scans with up-to-date scanning tools. - Document vulnerabilities, assign remediation tasks, and track closure. - Store scan results and remediation logs for audit purposes. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | 2.3 (i-iv, vii & viii) | Third party risk management | i. SFIs shall implement a third-party risk management framework to assess and mitigate the risks associated with such relationships. The third-party risk management framework should include processes for vendor selection, due diligence, contract negotiations, ongoing monitoring and incident response. ii. Third-party cybersecurity awareness programme shall be conducted at least annually to inform stakeholders about their roles and responsibilities around cybersecurity. iii. Contracts with third parties shall be used to implement appropriate measures designed to meet the objectives of the SFI’s cybersecurity programme. iv. Third parties shall be routinely assessed using audits, test results, or other forms of evaluations to confirm that contractual obligations are fulfilled. vii. Business continuity response and recovery planning and testing shall be conducted with third-party providers. viii. SFIs shall implement Insurance cover for various insurable technology risks to mitigate financial losses. | The bank must  1. Implement a Third-Party Risk Management (TPRM) Framework covering vendor selection, due diligence, contract terms, monitoring, and incident response. 2. Conduct annual cybersecurity awareness programs for third-party stakeholders. 3. Ensure contracts with vendors reflect cybersecurity expectations aligned with internal policies. 4. Perform regular evaluations or audits to verify vendor compliance with contractual and cybersecurity obligations. 7. Include third-party vendors in business continuity and recovery testing. 8. Obtain insurance cover for insurable technology-related risks to reduce financial exposure. | Weak vendor management may expose the bank to cybersecurity breaches, non-compliance fines, data leaks, service disruption, and reputational damage due to third-party failures. | High | High | - Head, Procurement - Head, IT Risk & Information Security - Legal & Compliance Unit | - Implement formal TPRM framework with documented procedures. - Enforce due diligence checklists and third-party risk ratings. - Maintain central register of all contracts and SLAs. - Schedule periodic vendor performance reviews and audits. - Conduct annual cybersecurity training for critical third parties. - Include business continuity clauses in vendor agreements. - Review insurance policies annually for adequacy. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | 2.4 | Cybersecurity Maturity Assessment | An SFI shall conduct annual evaluation using the CBN Cybersecurity Self-Assessment tool (CSAT) to determine its maturity level.  2.4.1. Determining the Current Cybersecurity Profile (current state) To determine its current state, an SFI shall carry out the following: i. Identify its Inherent Cyber risks. ii. Assess existing Cybersecurity mitigants.  2.4.2. Establishing a Target Cybersecurity Profile (desired state) An SFI shall determine its desired state of cybersecurity maturity. The information security function shall ensure that a roadmap towards achieving the target cybersecurity profile is included in the SFI’s corporate strategy. | The bank must:  1. Conduct a yearly self-assessment using the CBN Cybersecurity Self-Assessment Tool (CSAT). 2. Identify their inherent cybersecurity risks and assess existing cybersecurity controls (to determine current state). 3. Define their target cybersecurity maturity level (desired state). 4. Develop a roadmap, aligned with corporate strategy, to close gaps between current and target maturity levels. | Without a clear understanding of cybersecurity maturity and gaps, the bank may leave critical risks unaddressed, resulting in exposure to cyber threats and possible regulatory sanctions. | High | High | Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) / Cybersecurity Lead | - Use of the CBN Cybersecurity Self-Assessment Tool (CSAT) - Periodic internal cybersecurity audits - Management review of cyber maturity reports - Integration of cyber roadmap into corporate strategy | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | 3 (3.1-3.4 & 3.7) | Enhancing Cybersecurity Resilience | Cyber resilience is the SFI’s ability to prevent, withstand and recover from cyber incidents. SFIs are required to establish procedures to enhance their cyber resilience. This will ultimately strengthen the financial industry’s cybersecurity posture. The following are the minimum controls that an SFI shall put in place to ensure the confidentiality, integrity and availability of critical information assets among others. 3.1 Know Your Environment An SFI shall proactively familiarise itself with its business environment and identify its critical assets. To ensure effective security measures, an SFI shall establish mechanisms for maintaining up-to-date inventory of authorised software, hardware as well as internal and external network connections. Additionally, an SFI shall identify and document its data, assets and capabilities. Also, potential threats and vulnerabilities associated with its assets shall be monitored. Employees and contractors providing information technology and cybersecurity services shall also be identified and documented. Details on specific controls are contained in Appendix II. 3.2 Implement Preventive Controls An SFI shall implement appropriate measures/controls/safeguards for IT systems, processes and people to mitigate cyber risks. These can be administrative, logical or physical controls. Details on specific controls are contained in Appendix III. 3.3 Monitor and Detect An SFI shall establish capability for ongoing (24/7) monitoring of its IT systems, infrastructure, applications, services, and other relevant components to promptly detect anomalies or cyber incidents. This capability may be managed internally or outsourced to a third-party provider. Notwithstanding the approach chosen, monitoring should be adequate to detect cyber threats. 3.4 Respond and Remediate An SFI shall ensure that the capability for responding to cyber incidents is available in-house or, if outsourced, can be accessed at short notice. Details on specific controls are contained in Appendix III. 3.5 Restore Service Operations An SFI shall aim at recovering its operations timeously to reduce the overall impact of cyber incidents. 3.6 Cyber-Threat Intelligence An SFI is expected to possess knowledge of emerging threats, cyber-attacks, attack vectors, mechanisms and indicators of attack/compromise that may impact its information assets. 3.7 Sector-specific Cyber Resilience An SFI is required to participate in industry cyber exercises and programmes to evaluate its level of preparedness to recover from cyber incidents. These exercises may include cyber drills, war games or as defined by the CBN from time to time. SFIs shall avoid creating single points of failure in the industry and proactively define plans to mitigate such risks. | The bank must: 1. Maintain an updated inventory of all hardware, software, network components, and authorized personnel. 2. Implement and maintain preventive controls (administrative, physical, and logical) to secure IT systems, data, and personnel. 3. Ensure 24/7 monitoring to detect anomalies and cyber threats. 4. Establish in-house or outsourced incident response capabilities to contain threats. 5. Participate in cybersecurity simulations or sector-wide cyber drills. | Lack of asset tracking, insufficient preventive controls, delayed threat detection, or poor incident response can result in data breaches, operational disruptions, financial loss, and regulatory sanctions. | High | High | - IT & Cybersecurity Team - Risk & Compliance Officer - Incident Response Team | - Maintain real-time asset inventory tools and auditing schedules - Enforce layered security controls (firewalls, encryption, access control) - Use SIEM solutions and external SOC support where needed - Maintain an Incident Response Plan (IRP) and CSIRT or retainer with external experts - Participate in industry drills and simulate cyber scenarios internally | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | 4.2 | Open Banking | Open Banking refers to the practice of sharing financial data, such as account and transaction information, products and services with other financial institutions and third parties through API connections. The Regulatory Framework for Open Banking in Nigeria establishes principles for data sharing across the banking and payments system to promote innovation and broaden the range of financial products and services available to bank customers. Cyber-risks associated with open banking include data privacy, fraud, identity theft and API compromise. SFIs shall ensure compliance with the provisions of the Regulatory Framework for Open Banking in Nigeria and Operational Guidelines for Open Banking in Nigeria. | The bank must: 1. Comply with the Regulatory Framework for Open Banking in Nigeria and the Operational Guidelines for Open Banking in Nigeria. 2. Ensure that data sharing via APIs is secure, transparent, and consent-based. 3. Put controls in place to address cyber risks such as data privacy breaches, fraud, identity theft, and API compromise. | Failure to secure open banking APIs can lead to data breaches, regulatory violations, customer trust erosion, identity theft, fraud, and reputational damage. | High | High | - Chief Information Officer (CIO) - Chief Compliance Officer - API Management Team - IT Security Team | - Enforce strong API access control (authentication, authorization, encryption) - Conduct regular API vulnerability assessments and penetration testing - Apply data minimization and anonymization for customer data - Ensure customer consent management systems are implemented - Align internal processes with Open Banking regulations and train staff accordingly | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | 4.8 | Adoption of Emerging Technology | SFIs are required to comply with the following regulations in the use of emerging technologies: 1. obtain CBN approval before deploying emerging technologies or products. 2. ensure products and services are not provided by parties or countries on sanction lists. 3. refrain from establishing API connections or granting access to organisations not licensed by the CBN without prior regulatory approvals. 4. maintain professional due diligence and care in the adoption of emerging/evolving technologies. | The bank must: 1. Obtain CBN approval before deploying any new or emerging technology or product. 2. Ensure that no product or service is provided to or through parties or countries listed on sanction lists. 3. The metrics should help to identify deficiencies, failed security controls as well as highlight the progress made in resolving issues. iii. SFIs shall establish effective communication channels to disseminate relevant security requirements to employees for effective implementation of the cybersecurity programme. iv. The Board shall be provided with quarterly reports to inform them of the status of the Cybersecurity programme. SFIs are required to report all cyber incidents (as defined in Appendix I) not later than 24 hours after such incident is detected to the Director of Banking Supervision, Central Bank of Nigeria using the report format in Appendix VII or any other format that may be advised from time to time. Define and implement performance metrics (KPIs, KRIs, KGIs) to assess the effectiveness and efficiency of the cybersecurity programme. 2. Report all cyber incidents to the Director of Banking Supervision (CBN) within 24 hours of detection using the format in Appendix VII (or updated format), and provide additional information when necessary. | -  Ineffective or absent performance metrics may lead to poor cybersecurity oversight. - Lack of communication may result in employee non-compliance. - Delays in incident reporting could attract regulatory sanctions and damage reputation. - Absence of board-level visibility into cybersecurity posture may lead to poor risk governance. | - High | - High | - Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) - Cybersecurity Risk Officer - Head of Compliance - Internal Audit - IT Security Department - Board Secretariat | - Establish and maintain performance dashboards tracking KPIs/KRIs. - Schedule annual metric reviews and update as needed. - Use employee portals or emails to circulate cybersecurity obligations. - Adopt standardised reporting templates for quarterly board updates. - Maintain an Incident Response Plan with notification protocols to CBN. | - Medium | - Medium |

|  | 32 | Employee Compensation Act, 2010 | Section 1 (1,2) | Objectives of the Act | The objectives of the Act are to— (a) provide for an open and fair system of guaranteed and adequate compensation for all employees or their dependants for any death, injury, disease or disability arising out of or in the course of employment; (b) provide rehabilitation to employees with work-related disabilities as provided in this Act; (c) establish and maintain a solvent compensation fund managed in the interest of employees and employers; (d) provide for fair and adequate assessments for employers; (e) provide an appeal procedure that is simple, fair and accessible, with minimal delays; and (f) combine efforts and resources of relevant stakeholders for the prevention of workplace disabilities, including the enforcement of occupational safety and health standards | The Act aims to ensure that all employees, including those in banks, or their dependants, receive fair and guaranteed compensation in cases of death, injury, illness, or disability caused by work; it also provides for the rehabilitation of affected employees, requires the maintenance of a financially sound compensation fund, ensures that employer assessments are fair, establishes a simple and accessible appeals process, and mandates joint action among stakeholders to prevent workplace disabilities through the enforcement of safety and health standards. | Non-compliance with overall compensation principles could result in reputational/legal risks. | Medium | High | HR & Legal Compliance | Embed Act's principles into internal HR, health, and safety policies. | Low | Medium |

(2) In the case of a disabling occupational disease, the employer to be informed of the death or disability is the employer who last employed the employee in the employment to the nature of which the disease was due. The provisions of this Act are in lieu of any right of action, statutory or otherwise, founded on a breach of duty of care or any other cause of action, whether that duty or cause of action is imposed by or arises by reason of law or contract, express or implied, to which an employee, dependant or member of the family of the employee is or may be entitled against the employer of the employee, or against any employer within the scope of this Act, or against any employee, in respect of any death, injury or disability arising out of and in the course of employment and where no action in respect of it lies.  (2). The provisions of sub-section (1) of this section shall apply only when the action or conduct of the employer, the servant or agent of the employer or the employee, which caused the breach of duty, arose out of and in the course of employment within the scope of this Act.  (8). Nothing in this Act shall prevent an employer of the injured or deceased from maintaining an action upon contract or indemnity agreement against another employer or independent contractor in respect of the personal injury or death of an employee. | (1). This protection from legal action only applies if the incident (injury, disability, or death) happened while the bank, its staff, or agents were acting within the scope of their official duties. If the act occurred outside work responsibilities, this protection does not apply.  (8). The bank can still take legal action against another employer or an independent contractor if their actions led to the injury or death of the bank’s employee. |  |  |  | Section 22 (1-8) | Permanent Partial Disability or Disfigurement | (1) Subject to this Act, if a permanent partial disability results from the injury of the employee, the Board shall— (a) estimate the impairment of earning capacity from the nature and degree of the injury; and (b) pay the employee’s compensation that is a periodic payment equal to 90 per cent of an estimate of the loss of remuneration resulting from the impairment.  (2) The compensation referred to in sub-section (1) of this section shall be determined and calculated in accordance with the Second Schedule to this Act.  (3) The Board may, by regulations published in the Federal Gazette, revise or amend the Second Schedule to this Act.  (4) Subject to this Act, if— (a) a permanent partial disability results from the injury of an employee; and (b) the Board makes a determination under sub-section (5) of this section with respect to the employee, the Board may pay the employee compensation with a periodic payment that is equal to 90 per cent of the difference between the remuneration of the worker before the injury and whichever of the following amounts the Board considers better represents the loss of earnings of the employee the remuneration that— (i) the employee is earning after the injury; or (ii) the Board estimates the employee is capable of earning in a suitable occupation after the injury.  (5) A payment may be made under sub-section (4) of this section only if the Board determines that the combined effect of the occupation of the employee at the time of the injury and the disability resulting from the injury is so exceptional that an amount determined under sub-section (1) does not appropriately compensate the employee for the injury.  (6) In making a determination under sub-section (5) of this section, the Board shall consider the ability of the employee to continue in his or her occupation at the time of the injury or to adapt to another suitable occupation.  (7) Where permanent partial disability results from the injury, the minimum compensation awarded under this section shall be calculated in the same manner as provided by section 24 of this Act for temporary total disability but to the extent only of the partial disability. Earning Loss Estimation: The Employees’ Compensation Board will estimate how the injury has reduced the employee’s ability to earn based on the nature and extent of the injury.  2. Standard Compensation Payment: The employee will receive a regular (periodic) payment equal to 90% of the estimated loss in earnings. This is calculated according to the method outlined in the Second Schedule of the Act. The Board can revise that schedule if needed.  3. Exceptional Circumstances Adjustment: If the employee’s situation is exceptional (e.g., their injury and previous job type make continued employment or transition unusually difficult), and the standard formula under subsection (1) would not fairly compensate them, the Board may: - Compare what the employee earned before the injury with either: - what they are earning after the injury, or - what the Board believes they could earn in a suitable alternative job. Then, pay 90% of the income difference as compensation.  4. Occupation Suitability Check: The Board must assess whether the employee can continue in their previous job or reasonably adapt to another suitable occupation before deciding to apply this exceptional approach.  5. Minimum Compensation Rule: The minimum compensation for permanent partial disability must be calculated in the same way as temporary total disability under Section 24, but adjusted to reflect the level of partial disability.  6. Disfigurement Lump Sum: If the employee suffers a serious and permanent disfigurement (e.g. visible injury) that may reduce their ability to earn, the Board can also pay a lump sum—even if their current earnings haven’t decreased. | Failure to comply may lead to undercompensation, employee disputes, or litigation for neglecting statutory employee benefits. | Medium | High | HR Department / Legal Compliance | Maintain up-to-date records of employee duties, salaries, and injuries. Cooperate with Board assessments. Ensure HR is trained in handling such cases. | Low | Medium |

|  |  |  | Section 8.1 | Blacklisting by FIs | In order to ensure fairness and accountability, FIs shall adhere to the following procedure before the decision to blacklist an individual: i. Where an alleged offence as outlined in this Guidelines is discovered/reported/made against an individual, an investigation shall be conducted by the FI to determine the veracity of the allegations. ii. Upon verification of the existence of grounds for blacklisting, the FI shall notify the affected individual in writing, of the allegations timeously and he/she shall be required to respond to the allegations within 14 days from the receipt of the notification. iii. Upon receipt of the individual’s response, a Disciplinary Committee (DC) shall be setup to review the matter. iv. The individual shall be invited by the DC to present evidence that may aid in his/her defense. This invitation shall be received within 14 days prior to the sitting of the committee. v. Where an individual fails to appear before the DC after invitation, without any written notice stating the reasons for not appearing, the DC shall proceed with the process. However, where the individual has justifiable reasons for not appearing, the DC shall extend the invitation for a reasonable period that may allow the  individual to appear. vi. Based on the evidence presented during the hearing, the DC shall make a decision regarding the individual. vii. If the individual is indicted, the case shall be referred to an IRP for further review and validation. viii.In the course of the review, the IRP is at liberty to invite parties or call for any evidence presented at the sitting of the DC. ix. The decision(s) of the DC and the IRP shall be communicated to the individual involved. x. Where there is a conflict between the decisions of the DC and IRP, the decision of the IRP shall prevail. xi. The above procedure shall also apply to individuals who have resigned prior to discovery of an eligible offence. | The Bank must follow a documented, step-by-step process before blacklisting any individual (whether current or former staff). |  |  |  | Article 7 | General NDP Act Compliance Measures by Data Controllers and Data Processors | a) Register with the Commission as a data controller or data processor of major importance as the Commission may determine in accordance with the NDP Act. d) Identify all its obligations under the NDP Act and prepare schedules of compliance; f) Prepare and follow Schedules on Monitoring Evaluation and Maintenance of Data Security System in order to guarantee data confidentiality, integrity and availability; g) Prepare and follow schedules on organisation-wide, internal sensitisation and training on data privacy and protection in order to foster a culture of compliance with the NDP Act and best practices; i) In the case of a data controller or data processor of major importance, designate a Data Protection Officer (DPO). Associate DPOs/Privacy Champions may be designated to support the DPO where the data controller or the data processor carries out data processing or interfaces with data subjects on multiple platforms and places; j) Develop or review its organisational privacy policies, the privacy policy shall be in compliance with the NDP Act; k) Publish its organisational privacy policies on its platforms with a view to sensitising data subjects on data processing activities as well as rights and duties in connection therewith;  l) Provide privacy and cookie notices at the homepage of its website. The cookie notice should give a data subject the opportunity to decline or accept the notice; A cookie notice must be displayed in such a way that it significantly obstructs the middle, the left or the right side of the home page of a website. Displaying a cookie notice at the bottom of a webpage where it may be ignored or be  unnoticed by a data subject is tantamount to lack of transparency in data processing. m) Ensure that the privacy policy and notice is transparent and appropriately provided on platforms/places where data processing is taking place; and without prejudice to the NDP Act, it shall also take into account specific directions on privacy by relevant Application Hosting Platforms through which a data subject may access its services; n) Develop and circulate an internal data protection strategy or policy and basic privacy checklist to help members of staff and other relevant persons (such as vendors, agents and contractors) understand the organisation’s direction in connection with the processing of personal data and outline the steps they are to take to ensure the organisation’s direction is maintained; o) Conduct a Data Privacy Impact Assessment (DPIA) when required under the NDP Act, or when directed by the Commission; q) Notify a data subject immediately after becoming aware of a personal data breach that may pose high risk to his or her privacy; r) Update agreements with third party processors to ensure compliance with the NDP Act; s) Design systems and processes to make data requests and access seamless for data subjects; t) Design systems and processes to enable data subjects to easily correct or update their personal data; u) Design systems and processes to enable data subjects easily transfer data to another platform or person (natural or artificial); v) At least within the six (6) months of commencement of business and then, at the minimum, on an annual basis, train its personnel on data protection law and practices; and  w) Clearly explain the complaints process to data subjects including the right to lodge a complaint with the Commission. | 7(a) The bank must register with the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) as a data controller or processor of major importance, if so designated.  7(d) The bank must identify all its compliance obligations under the NDPA and create documented schedules to track and fulfill these obligations.  7(f) The bank must implement and maintain regular evaluation and monitoring procedures to ensure the security, confidentiality, and integrity of personal data.  7(g) The bank must organize ongoing internal training and awareness programs for staff to build a culture of data protection compliance.  7(i) If classified as a data controller/processor of major importance, the bank must appoint a Data Protection Officer (DPO). Where needed, assign supporting privacy champions.  7(j) The bank must develop or revise its internal privacy policy to ensure it aligns with the requirements of the NDPA.  7(k) The bank must publish its NDPA-compliant privacy policy on its platforms so that customers understand how their data is collected and used.  7(l) The bank must display cookie notices prominently on its website, allowing users to accept or reject cookies. It must not hide these notices at the bottom of the page.  7(m) The bank must ensure its privacy notices are clearly visible on any platform where personal data is collected, and must comply with relevant hosting platform requirements.  7(n) The bank must develop and distribute an internal privacy strategy and checklist for staff, vendors, and partners, outlining key data protection duties and procedures.  7(o) The bank must conduct a Data Privacy Impact Assessment (DPIA) when legally required or when directed by the NDPC.   7(q) The bank must notify affected data subjects immediately if a personal data breach that could harm their privacy occurs.  7(r)The bank must review and update contracts with third-party service providers to ensure their compliance with the NDPA.  7(s) The bank must implement systems that allow customers to easily request access to their personal data.  7(t) The bank must put in place systems that allow customers to update or correct their personal information easily.  7(u) The bank must provide customers with systems to enable the transfer of their data to another provider or platform (data portability).  7(v) The bank must train its staff on data protection laws and practices within six months of starting operations, and continue with yearly training sessions.  7(w) The bank must provide a clear and accessible complaint process for customers, including how they can escalate issues to the NDPC. | Failure to fully implement and maintain NDPA compliance systems may result in regulatory fines, reputational damage, and legal liability. | High | High | Compliance, Legal, HR, IT, Risk | Maintain NDPA compliance program with defined owners, training schedule, breach response plan, DPO structure, and contract review workflow | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 8 (1) | Designation of Data Controllers and Data Processors of Major Importance | (1) Section 65 of the NDP Act provides, “data controller or data processor of major importance” means a data controller or data processor that is domiciled, resident in, or operating in Nigeria and processes or intends to process personal data of more than such number of data subjects who are within Nigeria, as the Commission may prescribe, or such other class of data controller or data processor that is processing personal data of particular value or significance to the economy, society or security of Nigeria as the Commission may designate. | The Bank that processes the personal data of a large number of individuals in Nigeria — such as customers, employees, or vendors — or processes data that is critical to Nigeria’s economy, financial stability, or national security, may be classified by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) as a Data Controller or Data Processor of Major Importance (DCMI/DPMI).
