|  |  |  | Article 8 (2) | Designation of Data Controllers and Data Processors of Major Importance | (2) “Operating in Nigeria” as stated in section 65 includes a data controller or a data processor who targets a data subject in Nigeria. Such data controller or processor may not be domiciled in or resident in Nigeria. This is taking into consideration the provision of section 2(2)(a) of the NDP Act on the Application of the Act as well as sections 24(3) and 44 on the need to hold accountable data controllers and processors whose processing activities significantly impact the economy, society or security of Nigeria. | The Bank — even if not physically located or registered in Nigeria — is considered to be operating in Nigeria if it targets Nigerian data subjects, such as by offering banking products or services to individuals in Nigeria. |  |  |  | Article 8 (3) | Designation of Data Controllers and Data Processors of Major Importance | (3) In carrying out an objective assessment of what is of value or significance to the economy, society or security of Nigeria, the Commission shall take into consideration all relevant factors – including but not limited to the following: a) The risks that the data processing by a data controller or a data processor poses to a data subject if such data controller or data processor is not under the obligation imposed by the NDP Act on a data controller or a data processor of major importance as contemplated by section 29(1)(a) of the NDP Act; b) The implication for data sovereignty where data controllers or data processors may advertently or inadvertently transfer data outside Nigeria’s jurisdiction to the detriment of the economy, society or security of Nigeria; c) The sensitivity of the personal data involved;  d) Data driven financial assets entrusted by data subjects in the care of the data controller or data processor; e) Reliance on third party servers or cloud computing services for the purpose of substantial processing of personal data;  f) Substantial involvement in cross-border data flows; g) Use of filing systems and automation of data processing; h) Number of data subjects involved; and i) The need for international standard certifications for people, processes and technologies involved in data confidentiality, integrity and availability. | When determining whether The Bank is a Data Controller or Data Processor of Major Importance, the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) will assess how The Bank’s data activities may affect Nigeria’s economy, society, or security. This includes reviewing:  Risks to individuals if The Bank is not held to stricter standards, Whether data is being transferred outside Nigeria in a way that harms national interests, - How sensitive the personal data is (e.g., financial, biometric), - Whether The Bank holds data-driven financial assets on behalf of customers, - If it relies on cloud services or third-party servers for significant data processing, - The Bank’s level of cross-border data sharing, - Its use of automated systems and structured databases, - The number of data subjects affected, | Failure to self-assess and monitor eligibility for DCMI/DPMI designation may lead to non-compliance with stricter regulatory obligations. | High | High | Compliance, DPO, Risk Management | Conduct regular data impact and risk profiling reviews using the NDPC’s designation factors. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 8 (4) | Designation of Data Controllers and Data Processors of Major Importance | (4) In order to ensure proportionality of obligations in relation to various levels of major data processing, the Commission classifies data controllers and data processors into 3 (three) levels or categories of major data processing, namely: (a) Ultra-High Level (UHL) (b) Extra-High Level (EHL) (c) Ordinary-High Level (OHL) | The Bank should be aware that if it is classified as a Data Controller or Data Processor of Major Importance, it will fall into one of three categories based on the scale and sensitivity of its data processing: - Ultra-High Level (UHL) - Extra-High Level (EHL) - Ordinary-High Level (OHL) | Misclassification or failure to track classification status may result in non-compliance with proportional obligations under the NDPA. | Medium | High | Data Protection Officer (DPO), Compliance Team | Annual classification self-assessment and documentation; verify category with NDPC if unclear. | Low | Medium |

|  |  |  | Article 15 (1a-h) | Principles of Personal Data Protection | (1) The entire principle of data protection are obligatory in any form of data processing.  The principles under section 24 of the NDP Act are:  a) Fairness, lawfulness and transparency of data processing,  b) Purpose limitation,  c) Data minimisation and ethics,  d) Storage limitation,  e) Data accuracy,  f) Data confidentiality, integrity and availability,  g) Accountability, and  h) Duty of care. | The Bank must ensure that all personal data processing activities comply with the core principles set out in Section 24 of the NDPA, which include:  - Fairness, lawfulness, and transparency: Processing must be honest, legal, and clear to data subjects.  - Purpose limitation: Personal data should only be collected and used for specific, legitimate purposes.  - Data minimisation and ethics: Only collect data that is necessary, and process it ethically.  - Storage limitation: Keep data only as long as necessary.  - Data accuracy: Ensure personal data is accurate and up-to-date.  - Data confidentiality, integrity, and availability: Protect data from unauthorized access or loss and keep it accessible to authorized users.  - Accountability: The Bank must be able to demonstrate compliance with these principles.  - Duty of care: The Bank must take responsibility to protect data and avoid harm to data subjects. | Failure to comply with any of the eight core principles could result in regulatory sanctions, data breaches, reputational damage, and loss of trust. | High | High | All Departments (led by DPO) | Data Protection Policy, Data Retention Policy, RoPA, Employee Training, IT Security Controls, Privacy Notices | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 16 | Lawful Bases of Data Processing | (1) In line with Section 25 of the NDP Act, it is important for a data controller to carefully  assess the lawful bases of data processing before embarking on same.  (2) Subject to the provisions of the NDP Act and any regulatory instruments issued by  the Commission, a data controller shall carefully consider and choose the appropriate lawful bases of data processing in order to process personal data. The lawful bases  are:  a) Consent  b) Contractual Obligation  d) Legal Obligation  e) Valid Interest  f) Public Interest  g) Legitimate Interest.  (3) As the party who determines the purpose of data processing, the data controller is ultimately responsible for determining the lawful bases of data processing | Before processing personal data, The Bank must carefully assess and select the appropriate lawful basis for each data processing activity, as required under Section 25 of the NDPA. The lawful bases include: - Consent from the data subject, - Fulfillment of a contractual obligation, - Compliance with a legal obligation, - Acting in a valid interest, - Serving the public interest, - Or pursuing a legitimate interest.  Since The Bank decides why and how personal data is processed, it is ultimately responsible for ensuring the chosen lawful basis is valid and properly documented. | Processing personal data without a valid legal basis may lead to regulatory violations, invalid consent claims, data subject complaints, and sanctions. | High | High | Legal/Compliance Unit & DPO | Lawful Basis Register; Data Processing Inventory (RoPA); Standard Operating Procedures for data intake and processing | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 17 (1-7) | Reliance on Consent | 1) Considering that data privacy is a fundamental right to informational self-determination, it is prudent for a data controller to prioritize the interest of the data subject which may be effectively addressed through his or her informed consent.  (2) Where reliance on consent may effectively defeat the rule of law, another lawful basis may be considered.  (3) In any complaint to the Commission as to whether consent was not obtained before data processing, and the Commission is to make a determination whether reliance on consent would effectively defeat the rule of law, the Commission shall take into account: a) The clear and present risk to fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject and third parties; b) The security implication; c) Public welfare; d) The need for efficacy in the administration of justice - taking into account the need to: i. Uphold equality before the law, ii. Submit to the neutrality and impartiality of courts of competent jurisdiction; e) Sustainable development; f) Prior relationship between the data controller and the data subject; and g) Proportionality and necessity of the scope of the processing.  (4) The items listed in sub (3) above are hereafter referred to collectively as Special Rule of Law Indexes (SRLI).  (5) Reliance on any lawful bases of data processing which is not consent and not supported by any SRLI shall be strictly scrutinized during NDP Act compliance audits and in any proceeding where the conduct of a data controller or processor is called into question.  (6) Whenever a data controller relies on consent, it shall keep a proper record that guarantees accountability in respect of the consent.  (7) In determining whether a data controller is accountable in the mode of obtaining consent, the data controller shall: a) Provide appropriate information to the data subject such that the data subject, on the basis of the information, may make an informed decision; b) Make the process of withdrawal of consent as easy as giving consent; and c) Ensure that refusal of consent is not detrimental to the rights and interests of the data subject. | The Bank must prioritize obtaining informed consent from data subjects as a fundamental right, ensuring individuals clearly understand and agree to how their personal data is processed. However, if relying on consent conflicts with the rule of law, The Bank may use another lawful basis for data processing.  If there is a complaint regarding the absence of consent, the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) will evaluate whether consent is necessary by considering factors collectively called the Special Rule of Law Indexes (SRLI). These factors include:  - Risks to fundamental rights and freedoms of data subjects and third parties  - Security implications  - Public welfare  - Fair administration of justice  - Sustainable development  - The prior relationship between The Bank and the data subject  - Proportionality and necessity of the data processing  If The Bank relies on a lawful basis other than consent without support from any SRLI, this reliance will be strictly scrutinized during compliance audits and enforcement actions. Whenever The Bank relies on consent, it must keep proper records to demonstrate that valid consent was obtained, ensuring accountability.  To uphold accountability in obtaining consent, The Bank must:  - Provide clear and appropriate information to data subjects enabling informed decisions  - Make withdrawing consent as easy as giving consent  - Ensure refusal of consent does not negatively affect the rights or interests of data subjects | Failure to obtain or demonstrate valid consent, or improper use of alternative lawful bases, may result in enforcement action, reputational harm, or invalidation of data processing. | High | High | Data Protection Officer (DPO); Legal/Compliance Unit | Consent Management System; Privacy Notice with clear consent terms; Consent withdrawal process; Documentation of lawful basis with SRLI assessment | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 17 (8) | Reliance on Consent | (8) Nothing in this GAID shall prevent a data subject from giving a constructive or an implied consent to data processing in the following circumstances: a) A data subject’s acts of participation in a public event and the images taken in that event may be used for a report of that event – provided that such images shall not be used for profit or commerce-oriented advertisement without the express consent of the data subject. A data controller in this circumstance shall ensure that images captured do not portray data subjects in a bad light. In addition to other measures of duty of care, a data controller may put participants on notice that images captured may be used for reporting, journalistic or other purposes permitted by the NDP Act. | The Bank recognizes that a data subject may give constructive or implied consent in certain situations. For example, if a data subject participates in a public event where images are taken, those images may be used for event reporting provided they are not used for profit or commercial advertising without explicit consent. The Bank must ensure such images do not portray data subjects negatively and should, where applicable, notify participants that images may be used for reporting, journalism, or other lawful purposes under the NDPA. | Misuse of images without proper consent can lead to privacy violations, reputational damage, or regulatory penalties. | Medium | High | Corporate Communications; Legal/Compliance Unit | Public event notices; Image-use disclaimers; Non-commercial use policy; Pre-event DPO review | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 17 (9) | Reliance on Consent | (9) At all times where consent is required, a data subject shall be provided with a clear and explicit option to accept or to decline. | Whenever consent is required, The Bank must provide data subjects with a clear and explicit choice to accept or decline consent. | Obtaining consent without clarity may result in invalid consent and non-compliance with NDPA. | High | High | Legal/Compliance; Product Managers; IT | Use of opt-in forms with clear yes/no choices; No pre-checked boxes; UX testing for clarity | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 18 (1)(a–f) | Data Processing Which Requires Consent | (1) Without prejudice to the provisions of the NDP Act and in addition to other circumstances in which consent may be required under this GAID or by operation of law, consent is required: a) For any direct marketing activity; b) For the processing of sensitive personal data; c) For further processing that is incompatible with the original purpose of processing; d) For the processing of the personal data of a child; e) Before personal data may be transferred to a country in respect of which the Commission has not made an adequacy decision; and f) Before the data controller makes a decision based solely on automated processing which produces legal effects concerning or significantly affecting the data subject. | The Bank must obtain explicit consent in the following data processing cases, in addition to other situations required by law or GAID:  (a) Any direct marketing activity; (b) Processing of sensitive personal data; (c) Any further processing incompatible with the original purpose; (d) Processing personal data of a child; (e) Before transferring personal data to a country without an adequacy decision by the Commission; (f) Before making any automated decisions that have legal effects or significantly affect the data subject. | Non-compliance with consent obligations can result in privacy violations, regulatory fines, reputational harm, or data subject complaints — especially in cases involving minors, cross-border data transfers, sensitive data, or automated decisions. | High | High | Compliance; Marketing; IT; Legal; DPO | Consent management systems, parental consent tools, data flow checks, automated processing reviews, and legal adequacy assessments | Medium | Medium |

(3) The consent shall be freely given, informed and specific. | The Bank must ensure that the operation of cookies and other tracking tools complies with data protection principles (fairness, transparency, etc.). (5) Necessary cookies which do not process sensitive data, financial data or any data stored privately by a data subject does not need the ticking of a box or similar methods;  (6) In this article "necessary cookies" means cookies that enable core functionality such as security, network stability management, and accessibility. All other forms of cookies require a specific selection of "yes or no" (alternatively: "except" or "reject") options presented to the data subject. | The Bank should display a conspicuous cookie banner to website visitors, clearly notifying them about cookies.  Necessary cookies (which do not process sensitive, financial, or private data) do not require active consent (e.g., core functionality cookies). |  |  |  | Article 19 (7) | Consent to Cookies and other Tracking Tools | (7) In deploying cookies, website owners are required to:  a) Make cookies notice banner or display conspicuous. Similarly, every tracking tool shall be made known to the data subject at the section of the web page which appears first;  b) Make cookie listing onto clear and easy to understand;  c) Notify users of the presence and purpose of the cookies;  d) Identify the organisation responsible for the use of the cookies; and  e) Provide information on how to withdraw consent from the use of the cookies. | When deploying cookies, The Bank must: - Ensure cookie notices are immediately visible without scrolling; - Provide clear and easy-to-understand cookie listings; - Notify users of cookie purposes; - Identify the organisation responsible; - Explain how users can withdraw consent. | Users may unknowingly give consent or be misled if cookie banners or listings are unclear, leading to regulatory violations. | High | High | DPO; Web Development Team; Legal & Compliance | Deploy CMP (Consent Management Platform); Ensure banners are fixed at top or bottom of homepage and cookie info is clear. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 20 | Lawfulness of Purpose, Reliance on Consent, and Other Lawful Bases | (1) In addition to other obligations under the NDP Act and this GAID, every data processing shall only proceed from purposes that are: i. Lawful under the NDP Act; ii. Not in violation of other legislation for the time being in force in Nigeria, and iii. Not in violation of preemptory norms of general International Law.  (2) No consent shall be sought, given or accepted in any circumstance that may engender direct or indirect propagation of atrocities, hate, child rights violations and criminal acts. | (1) All personal data processing by The Bank must: - Be lawful under the NDPA; - Not violate any Nigerian laws; - Not breach established international legal norms.  (2) The Bank must never seek, accept, or rely on consent to process data in ways that promote atrocities, hate, child rights violations, or criminal acts. | Reputational, regulatory, and legal risks from unlawful processing or misuse of consent in harmful or illegal contexts. | Medium | High | Legal & Compliance Unit; DPO | Legal review of all data processing purposes; approval process for data processing justifications; periodic consent review and audit | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 21(1–3,5) | Lawful Basis Clarifications | (1) At the preliminary stage of a contract with a data subject, a data controller or data processor may carry out data processing on the data subject for the purpose of due diligence.  (2) Where the contract did not materialise, any personal data collected relating to the data subject shall be destroyed within six (6) months unless there is a justifiable ground to archive the data for the purposes of any future legal claim.  (3) A contract with a data subject involving data processing shall make provision for termination of the contract prior to the tenure of the contract.  (5) Pursuant to Section 46 of the 1999 Constitution and Section 34(1)(a)(v) of the NDP Act, a specific term of a contract on personal data processing that ousts or purports to oust the adjudicatory jurisdiction of Nigerian courts or the executive jurisdiction of the Commission shall be treated as void. | (1) The Bank may process personal data during contract negotiations with a data subject for due diligence purposes.  (2) If no contract results, any collected data must be destroyed within six months, unless there is a legitimate reason to keep it for future legal claims.  (3) Contracts involving data processing should include provisions for early termination of the contract.  (5) Any contract clause that tries to exclude Nigerian courts or NDPC jurisdiction over data protection matters is void and unenforceable. | Legal risk from retaining personal data beyond lawful period; invalid contract clauses could lead to regulatory penalties or nullity. | Medium | High | Legal & Compliance Department | Contract templates reviewed by Legal; pre-contract data retention policy with auto-delete; legal clause approval checklist | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 22(1–4) | Reliance on Legal Obligation | (1) A legal obligation means any one of the following: a) a specific duty imposed by law; b) an order of a court of competent jurisdiction; or c) a responsibility incidental to an obligation imposed by law to carry out an act which requires the processing of personal data.  (2) Where a legal obligation derogates from the general safeguards of the NDP Act, it shall be treated as a derogation from the right to privacy as enshrined under Section 37 of the 1999 Constitution, and accordingly, Section 45 of the 1999 Constitution applies.  (3) In line with Section 45 of the 1999 Constitution, data processing shall only take place in such circumstances of derogation as stipulated in Sub-Article (2) of this Article if the enabling law for the said legal obligation is reasonably justifiable in a democratic society attd: i. it is in the interest of defence, public safety, public order, public morality or public health; or ii. for the purpose of protecting the rights and freedom of other persons; accordingly, account shall be taken of practices in a democratic society where the rule of law is firmly entrenched.  (4) Data processing under legal obligation shall be strictly limited to the minimum requirement under a law in line with Sub-Article (3) above and shall not be used for a voyage of discovery into the privacy of a data subject or in circumstances of establishing a speculative claim. | (1) The Bank may process personal data where it has a legal obligation, such as: - A specific duty imposed by law, - A court order, or - A responsibility tied to a legal obligation.  (2–3) Such processing is a derogation from the right to privacy and must be:  - Justifiable in a democratic society, serving public safety, defense, public order, morality, health, or protecting others’ rights;  - Consistent with constitutional safeguards.  (4) The Bank must ensure that data processing under legal obligation is strictly limited to what is necessary and not used for speculative or intrusive purposes. | Unlawful data processing under the guise of legal obligation may violate constitutional rights and expose The Bank to sanctions. | Medium | High | Legal & Compliance Unit | Legal review and documentation of all legal obligations requiring data processing; obtain court orders in writing and file justification memos. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 23(1) | Evaluation of Lawful Bases of Data Processing | (1) In all adjudicatory or administrative proceedings pertaining to personal data processing, it shall be essential to the character of a democratic society to meticulously evaluate: (a) The necessity of processing of personal data – taking into consideration the risks and the alternatives (agency; (b) The duty of care and the standard of care employed to mitigate unnecessary, disproportionate risks of data processing; (c) The functional opportunity of redness accessible to an aggrieved person in accordance with Part 10 of the NDP Act and the Fundamental Rights Enforcement Procedure Rules for the time being in force; (d) The proportionality of the processing of personal data – taking into account: i. the scope of measures adopted or intended to be adopted for the processing of personal data in relation to the ii. the legitimate aim pursued. Duty of care shall be exercised in favour of the data subject and/or other data subjects whose fundamental rights and freedoms that may be affected. It is obligatory to avoid the setting of procedures which are prejudicial to fundamental rights and freedoms. It is prudent and obligatory to avoid any data processing that may undermine the adequacy of data protection which exists within the Federal Republic of Nigeria. | The bank must ensure that personal data is processed only when necessary, with care and proportionality, and that affected individuals have access to redress. These factors must guide data protection policies, DPIAs, and legal justifications. | Failure to justify data processing on grounds of necessity and proportionality may result in legal challenges, enforcement actions, or reputational damage. | Medium | High | Legal & Compliance Team | Integrate necessity and proportionality reviews into Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs); ensure procedures for redress are in place and accessible. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 23(2) | Evaluation of Lawful Bases of Data Processing | (2) Nothing in the NDP Act, this GAID, any legislation, or any legal instrument shall be deemed as authorising any form of data processing without compliance with Sections 37 and 45 of the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. For ease of reference, the sections provide:  Section 37 CERN 1999: The privacy of citizens, their homes, correspondences, telephone conversations and telegraphic communications is hereby guaranteed and protected.  Section 45(1) CERN 1999: Nothing in sections 37, 38, 39, 40 and 41 of this Constitution shall invalidate any law that is reasonably justifiable in a democratic society. (3) In the interest of defence, public safety, public order, public morality or public health; or (4) for the purpose of protecting the rights and freedom or other persons. | The bank must ensure that all data processing complies with constitutional privacy protections. Processing that limits privacy must meet legal standards of justification, necessity, and proportionality. | Risk of unconstitutional data processing that violates privacy rights, leading to litigation, regulatory sanctions, or public backlash. | Medium | High | Legal & Compliance Team | Incorporate constitutional rights checks (Section 37 and 45) into every data processing assessment, especially in high-risk or sensitive areas. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 24(1–4) | Reliance on Vital Interest | (1) A data controller may rely on vital interest as a lawful basis for the processing of personal data, particularly when circumstances do not permit the data subject to give consent to the processing.  (2) The vital interest referred to in Sub-Article (1) of this Article may be that of the data subject or of a third party and it shall meet the conditions stipulated below:  a) The processing is necessary for the preservation or protection of life or livelihood and failure or refusal to act may be harmful to the data subject or a third party;  b) There is a legitimate expectation based on relationship or connection, operation of law, convention or prevailing norms that personal data should be processed in such circumstances of vital interest; and  c) The data controller or data processor may be called into question as being negligent, unprofessional or reckless for failing to carry out the data processing in such adverse circumstances in which a vital interest is in jeopardy.  (3) The method of processing employed for the purposes of vital interest shall be necessary and proportionate.  (4) The data controller shall give an account of its processing to the affected data subject, his or her representative in interest, or to a competent authority upon request. | (1) The Bank may process personal data based on vital interest when the data subject cannot give consent, particularly during emergencies.  (2) This vital interest may relate to the data subject or a third party. It must meet the following criteria:  Processing is necessary to preserve life or livelihood and inaction may be harmful.  There is a legitimate expectation (from relationship, law, norms, etc.) that processing should occur in such a situation.  The Bank could be considered negligent for failing to act.  (3) The processing must be necessary and proportionate to the situation.  (4) The Bank must be able to justify and explain the processing to the data subject, their representative, or a competent authority upon request. | Unjustified or excessive reliance on vital interest may result in unlawful data processing, legal liability, and regulatory sanctions. | Medium | High | Legal & Compliance Team | Include "vital interest" scenarios in data processing policy. Apply strict review criteria before relying on this lawful basis. Maintain documentation. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 25(1–4) | Reliance on Public Interest | (1) Public interest may be relied upon as a lawful basis of data processing in circumstances where there is:  (a) a public health or humanitarian emergency; or  (b) there is a clear and present danger to public safety; or  (c) there is a need also address direction of destination or deprivation for the benefit of the data subject. In furtherance of the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy or Sustainable Development Goals.  (2) In addition to other obligations that may be imposed under the NDP Act, in any regulatory instrument issued by the Commission and any other legislation, a data controller shall take into account the safeguards in the provisions of Article 23 of this GAID when carrying out data processing on the ground of public interest.  (3) The method of processing employed for the purposes of public interest shall be necessary and proportionate.  (4) Article 23 of this GAID regarding the evaluation of legal obligation shall also apply to the evaluation of public interest when it is relied upon as a lawful basis of data processing. | (1) The Bank may process personal data based on public interest when:  - There's a public health or humanitarian emergency,  - There’s a danger to public safety, or  - The data processing addresses issues of deprivation, aligns with national development goals, or supports the Fundamental Objectives of the Nigerian Constitution.  (2–4) When relying on public interest:  - The Bank must implement safeguards (as outlined in Article 23) to protect rights.  - The processing must be necessary and proportionate.  - Legal obligation safeguards under Article 23 also apply here. | Improper or unjustified reliance on public interest may result in rights violations, regulatory breaches, or reputational damage. | Medium | High | Legal & Compliance Team | Document clear justification for invoking public interest. Ensure all Article 23 safeguards are reviewed and implemented in such cases. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 26(1–2) | Reliance on Legitimate Interest | (1) A data controller shall cautiously consider reliance on legitimate interest as a lawful basis for data processing and shall be required in a compliance audit to show the basis of its preference. A template of a Legitimate Interest Assessment is in Schedule 8.  (2) Section 25 (2) of the NDP Act makes compatibility with contract, vital interest, legal obligation or public interest, a basis for reliance on legitimate interest. Accordingly, it shall be mandatory for a data controller under the circumstances to: a) Carry out Legitimate Interest Assessment (as prescribed in Schedule 8) before embarking on data processing; b) Priorities privacy by design and by default – taking into consideration the suitability of anonymisation or pseudonymisation; c) Identify and document the lawful basis of processing which is compatible with the legitimate interest process; d) Identify and eliminate data processing that may overreach the fundamental rights and freedoms of data subjects – particularly such processing that may lead to behavioural monitoring or profiling, or lead to targeted advertisement by third parties or partners; e) Identify and eliminate data processing that may lead to a breach of data confidentiality, integrity and availability – taking into account vulnerable data subjects; f) Provide transparent information to data subjects in accordance with Section 27 of the NDP Act; g) Provide for prompt remediation of data subjects’ rights; and h) Priorities data ethics and utmost duty of care. | (1) The Bank must carefully consider using legitimate interest as a lawful basis. It will be required to justify its decision during audits.  (2) To rely on legitimate interest, The Bank must:  - Complete a Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA) as per Schedule 8.  - Apply privacy by design and default (e.g., anonymisation/pseudonymisation).  - Identify and document compatible lawful bases (e.g., contract, vital interest).  - Avoid processing that overreaches rights (e.g., profiling or targeted ads).  - Avoid processing that compromises confidentiality, integrity, or availability, especially for vulnerable individuals.  - Provide clear information to data subjects (per Section 27 of NDPA).  - Ensure remediation options for data subjects are available.  - Uphold data ethics and a high duty of care. | Relying on legitimate interest without proper LIA may result in unlawful data processing, breaches of data subjects’ rights, regulatory penalties, or reputational harm. | Medium | High | Legal & Compliance Team | Mandatory Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA) using Schedule 8 template; embed privacy by design; exclude profiling or sensitive targeting unless justified; provide data subject transparency and rights mechanisms. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 27 | Consideration Regarding Information to Data Subjects | (1) Provision of information to a data subject shall be in accordance with Section 27 of the NDP Act. The information shall be clear and shall take into consideration vulnerable data subjects.  (2) In circumstances of exclusive physical events, interviews or interactions where a data controller or data processor may not be able to provide data subjects with a privacy policy or if provided, the class of data subjects may not be able to understand the privacy policy without the aid of an interpreter, the data controller or data processor shall provide the information in the form that the data subject can understand.  (3) The information to be provided by the data controller or data processor includes but is not limited to the following:  a) The name of the data controller or data processor,  b) Lawful basis of data processing,  c) Types of personal data to be collected,  d) The purpose of the processing,  e) The means of processing,  f) Access to personal data by authorised third parties,  g) Purpose of access by third parties,  h) Data subject's rights,  i) Access to prompt internal remediation through contact to be supplied by the data controller or data processor, and  j) Right to lodge a complaint with the Nigeria Data Protection Commission.  (4) Information to data subjects does not constitute a request for consent. Consent shall be specifically requested and obtained when it is required by law and on the ground that the information which may guide the data subject in making an informed decision has been duly provided prior to the processing of personal data. | (1–2) The Bank must provide clear, accessible information to data subjects in line with Section 27 of the NDPA. This includes formats understandable to vulnerable or non-literate persons.  (3) The Bank must inform data subjects about:  - Its name (as controller or processor),  - The lawful basis for processing,  - The types of personal data collected,  - The purpose and means of processing,  - Third-party access, its purpose, and those authorised,  - Rights of the data subject,  - Internal complaint and remediation channels, and the right to lodge a complaint with the NDPC.  (4) Providing information is not the same as requesting consent. Consent must still be specifically obtained when required. | Failure to properly inform data subjects can result in non-compliance with the NDPA, especially where vulnerable individuals are involved. This may lead to sanctions, reputational damage, and inability to lawfully process data. | Medium | High | Legal & Compliance Team, DPO | Prepare standardised, accessible privacy notices in various formats; ensure field officers, agents, or event facilitators are trained to communicate these notices clearly to vulnerable audiences; separate consent process when required. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 28 (1-2) | Data Privacy Impact Assessment | (1) A Data Privacy Impact Assessment (DPIA) is mandated under Section 28 of the NDP Act when data processing may likely result in high risk to the rights and freedoms of a data subject by virtue of its nature, scope, context, and purposes.  (2) Introduction of new technologies or new processing techniques or directives mandating processing of personal data on a large scale requires a DPIA on the following grounds:  (a) Unintended, adverse consequences to the lives and livelihoods of data subjects may result from the data processing;  (b) Such adverse consequences are threats to fundamental rights and freedoms as well as to the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy - which Policy forms the basis of sustainable development, security and economic programmes of government; and  (c) In circumstances where data processing measures constitute a derogation from Section 37 of the 1999 Constitution, they shall comply with the safeguards under Section 45 of the 1999 Constitution. In this regard, the need to fulfil the conditions of necessity and proportionality and other safeguards stipulated under Article 29 of this GAID is obligatory. | The bank must conduct a Data Privacy Impact Assessment (DPIA) before initiating any data processing activity that is likely to result in a high risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms. This obligation applies when: - The bank introduces new technologies or new processing techniques. - The bank processes personal data on a large scale (e.g., automated profiling, credit scoring, biometrics).  The bank must particularly conduct a DPIA when: 1. The data processing could lead to unintended, adverse consequences to individuals’ lives or livelihoods.  2. These adverse outcomes could threaten fundamental rights and freedoms, or conflict with national development, economic, or security objectives.  3. The processing involves a derogation from the right to privacy under Section 37 of the 1999 Constitution—in such cases, the bank must ensure that: - The processing is necessary and proportionate, and - It includes safeguards required under Section 45 of the Constitution and Article 29 of this Directive. | Failing to conduct a DPIA for high-risk processing may lead to serious privacy breaches, regulatory action, reputational damage, or constitutional violations. | High | High | Data Protection Officer (DPO) | Embed DPIA requirement into internal project initiation processes; Train relevant teams (e.g., IT, legal, compliance) on DPIA triggers; Use standard DPIA templates approved by the DPCO; Review all tech or process changes for DPIA necessity. | Medium | Medium |

|  |  |  | Article 37 | Right to Data Portability | (1) A data subject has a right to data portability.  (2) The right to data portability shall apply where the data subject provided the personal data on the basis of his or her consent or the processing is necessary for the performance of a contract. It may not apply where processing is based on a legal ground other than consent or contract.  (3) The right to data portability may not apply against a data controller or data processor in the performance of its public duties; unless there is a compelling legitimate interest or right of a data subject that may be abridged by reason of denying the data subject's right of data portability.  (4) Where, in a certain set of personal data, more than one data subject is concerned, the right to receive the personal data should be without prejudice to the rights and freedoms of other data subjects in accordance with the NDP Act or any regulatory instrument issued by the Commission.  (5) The right to data portability shall not prejudice the right of the data subject to obtain the erasure of personal data and the limitations of that right as prescribed under the NDP Act.  (6) Nothing in this Article shall imply the erasure of personal data concerning the data subject which has been provided by him or her for the performance of a contract to the extent that and for as long as are necessary for the performance of that contract. | The bank must enable customers (data subjects) to obtain and reuse their personal data, where data was collected based on consent or contract. This data must be provided in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format. The bank must ensure the right is exercised without harming others’ data rights and must not refuse portability where required. Contractual obligations may justify retaining some data even after a portability reques | Failure to honor data portability rights may lead to regulatory sanctions, reputational damage, or customer dissatisfaction. | Medium | High | Data Protection Officer (DPO), IT, Customer Service | Implement a structured data export mechanism, validate legal basis, and review third-party data implications before export. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 38 (4 - 7, 9 - 11) | Exercise of Right to be Forgotten | 4.Upon the receipt of a complaint in line with Section 46 of the NDP Act, the Commission shall carry out a preliminary evaluation of the complaint - taking into account: a) The applicability of the NDP Act to the complaint; b) The urgency of the complaint and any urgent relief contained therein; c) The impact of the allegations on the complainant or on a third party on whose behalf the complaint is being lodged with the Commission; and d) The temporary remedy that may be provided pending the outcome of an investigation into the complaint.  5.When the Commission is convinced through a preliminary evaluation that there is a violation of the NDP Act, it shall open a case file for the complaint.  6.Upon the opening of a case file, the Commission shall immediately serve the affected data controller or data processor (hereafter referred to as the respondent) a notice of investigation.  7.The notice of investigation may require the respondent to provide, where applicable: a) The information itemised under this Sub-Aricle.  9.The Commission receives a appropriate, it shall invite the respondent to a Pre-Action Conference (PAC) in order to examine the facts and the available evidence provided by the parties or obtained by the Commission through investigation.  10.A PAC may take place as frequently as necessary in respect of a complaint or an investigation carried out by the Commission pursuant to Section 46(3) of the NDP Act.  (11) In line with the power vested in the Commission under Section 6(c) of the NDP Act, the Commission may direct a data controller or data processor to attend a PAC with any relevant person who is legally compeilable or competent to give evidence and who may provide relevant information in determining an issue relating to violation of the NDP Act. | If the Nigeria Data Protection Commission opens an investigation (after receiving a complaint), the bank — as a data controller or data processor must:  1.  Respond promptly to a notice of investigation served by the Commission.  2. Provide relevant information upon request, which may include: - List of engaged third-party data processors, agents, or contractors. - Copies of Data Processing Agreements and evidence of NDPA compliance. - Details of any cross-border data transfers and their legal basis. - The relevant Data Privacy Impact Assessment (DPIA). - Name and contact information of the designated Data Protection Officer (DPO).  3. Attend any Pre-Action Conference (PAC) if invited by the Commission to discuss facts or provide clarifications.  4. Ensure that relevant persons (e.g. officers, contractors) who can provide evidence or information also attend the PAC when required by the Commission. | Failure to respond or comply with the Commission's investigative process may lead to enforcement actions, fines, reputational harm, or operational disruptions. | Medium | High | Legal & Compliance, DPO, Data Governance Officer | Internal legal protocols, case management system, DPO oversight, pre-compiled response documents | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 39 (2) | Exercise of Right to Lodge a Complaint with the Commission | (2) Every regulation, policy, framework, or legal instrument which pertains to the processing of personal data shall in addition to all applicable data subject rights and safeguards contained a clause on the right to lodge a complaint with the Nigeria Data Protection Commission. | The bank must ensure that every policy, privacy notice, contract, or any other document related to personal data processing includes a clear clause informing individuals of their right to lodge a complaint with the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC). | Omission of the complaint clause may lead to NDPA non-compliance, limit data subject rights, and increase reputational and regulatory risks. | Medium | High | Legal & Compliance, Data Protection Officer (DPO) | Compliance checklists; Privacy Notice Template including NDPC contact info; Legal review of all policy documents | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 40 (2-4, 6, 8) | Data Subject's Standard Notice to Address Grievance | (2) An aggrieved data subject may cause SNAG to a data controller or a data processor where the data subject reasonably believes that the data controller or data processor violated his or her right to data privacy.  (3) SNAG shall not be regarded as a condition precedent for lodging a direct complaint with the Commission or for instituting an action, rather it shall be regarded as a standardised template for demanding internal remediation in an organisation which may be acting in violation of a data subject's privacy.  (4) SNAG may be served directly by a data subject or by a person acting under his or her authority or by a civil society organisation acting in the public interest.  (6) Upon receipt of a SNAG, a data controller or a data processor shall communicate its decision on the SNAG to the Commission through the designated electronic platform.  (8)A SNAG may be served on a data controller or a data processor via its physical sources, telephone messaging medium, e-mail address, courier service or other reasonable means of correspondence. | 1. The bank must be prepared to receive a Standard Notice to Address Grievance (SNAG) from any individual (data subject) who reasonably believes that the bank has violated their right to data privacy.  2. The bank must recognise that a SNAG is a standard internal grievance tool—even though it is not mandatory before a complaint is made to the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC), the bank is still required to treat it seriously and provide internal remediation.  3. The bank must accept SNAGs served by:  - The data subject, - A person authorized by the data subject (e.g., lawyer or agent), or - A civil society organization acting in the public interest.  4. The bank must acknowledge and receive SNAGs via any of the following channels: - Physical delivery (e.g., front desk), - SMS or telephone messaging, - Email, - Courier service, - Any other reasonable means of communication.  5. Once a SNAG is received, the bank must communicate its decision or response to the Commission through the designated electronic platform provided by the NDPC. | Failure to acknowledge or respond to SNAGs may breach privacy obligations, harm customer trust, and result in regulatory scrutiny from NDPC. | Medium | High | Data Protection Officer (DPO), Legal, Customer Care | Grievance handling policy; Multiple accessible complaint channels (physical, SMS, email, courier); Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for SNAG responses | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Article 44 | Parameters for Assessing Privacy and Public Interest in Emerging Technologies | (1) In line with Section 5(a) of the NDP Act, the Commission shall foster the development of personal data protection technologies, in accordance with recognised international best practices and applicable international law; accordingly, the Commission shall accord priority to ETs which strengthen data privacy.  (2) In furtherance of Section 1(b) of the NDP Act towards strengthening the legal foundations of the national digital economy and guaranteeing the participation of Nigeria in the regional and global economies through the beneficial and trusted use of personal data, the Commission shall take into account the utilitarian value of ETs in achieving sustainable development through lawful processing of personal data.  (3) A data controller or data processor who intends to process personal data in the circumstances contemplated by Article 44 (2), may benchmark with global consensus on ETs such as the United Nations Resolution on Artificial Intelligence. Accordingly, data controllers and data processors shall, among other self-correcting measures, remain from or cease the use of ET systems that are impossible to operate in compliance with international human rights law or that pose undue risks to the enjoyment of human rights. | If the bank plans to adopt emerging technologies (ETs)—such as AI, automated decision systems, advanced analytics, biometrics, etc.—it must ensure those technologies protect personal data privacy and comply with international human rights standards. The bank must avoid or stop using any technology that violates privacy laws or poses undue risks to individuals’ rights. It should also benchmark with global frameworks (e.g., the UN AI Resolution) to ensure its systems meet global ethical standards in personal data use. | Use of ETs without benchmarking to human rights or data protection standards can result in data breaches, regulatory sanctions, reputational damage, or civil liability. | High | High | CTO; DPO; Compliance | Pre-deployment risk assessments; Human rights and DPIA screening; Global standards benchmarking (e.g., UN, OECD) | Medium | High |

(3) All employees and other persons who are engaged by the data controller or data processor shall be trained and sensitized periodically on emerging developments in data processing and to such an extent that is reasonably relevant to their job descriptions respectively.  (4) The Commission may develop a mechanism in place for the training, and the award of certifications on Data Privacy and Protection. | The bank must ensure that all employees and persons it engages (e.g., contractors, consultants) are regularly trained on data protection, privacy rules, and new developments in data processing.
