Accordingly, a Data Subject shall have the option to:  a) object to the processing of Personal Data relating to him which the Data Controller intend to process for the purpose of marketing; | The Bank shall allow customers to object to the use of their data for marketing. | Breach of customer rights, reputational risk. | High | Medium | Marketing / DPO | Include opt-out options in all marketing messages (email, SMS, in-app); record opt-outs promptly. | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Section 2.8 (2) | Objections by the Data Subject | b) be expressly and manifestly offered the mechanism for objection to any form of data processing free of charge. | The Bank shall provide a clear, free, and simple mechanism for customers to opt-out of data processing. | Risk of non-compliance with objection rights. | Medium | Medium | DPO / IT | Web-based objection forms, call center scripts, and back-office response workflow. | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Section 2.9 | Advancement of Right to Privacy | Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this Regulation, the privacy right of a Data Subject shall be interpreted for the purpose of advancing and never for the purpose of restricting the safeguards Data Subject is entitled to under any data protection instrument made in furtherance of fundamental rights and the Nigerian laws. | The Bank must interpret the data subject’s right to privacy in a way that always strengthens their rights and never reduces them under this or any other Nigerian law | Regulatory risk from narrow or exploitative interpretation. | Medium | High | Legal / DPO | Privacy reviews of internal policies and changes in business processes. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (1) | Rights of Data Subject | (1) The Controller shall take appropriate measures to provide any information relating to processing to the Data Subject in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language, and for any information relating to a child. The information shall be provided in writing, or by other means, including, where appropriate, by electronic means. When requested by the Data Subject, the information may be provided orally, provided that the identity of the Data Subject is proven by other means. | The Bank shall provide information to data subjects in clear, accessible, and plain language, including in child-friendly formats where needed. | Risk of violating transparency obligations. | Medium | High | DPO / Customer Experience | Updated privacy notices, staff scripts, and website FAQs; multilingual and child-friendly materials if applicable. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (2) | Rights of Data Subject | (2) If the Controller does not act on the request of the Data Subject, the Controller shall inform the Data Subject without delay and at the latest within one month of receipt of the request of the reasons for not taking action and on the possibility of lodging a complaint with a supervisory authority. | If the Bank refuses a customer’s request under their data rights, it shall notify them within one month, with reasons and details of how to complain. | Legal breach, regulatory complaint, reputational risk | Medium | High | Legal / DPO | Data Rights SOP with complaint escalation channel | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (3) | Rights of Data Subject | (3) Except as otherwise provided by any public policy or Regulation, information provided to the Data Subject and any communication and any actions taken shall be provided free of charge. Where requests from a Data Subject are manifestly unfounded or excessive, in particular because of their repetitive character, the controller may either: a) Charge a reasonable fee considering the administrative costs of providing the information or communication or taking the action requested; or, b) Write a letter to the Data Subject stating refusal act on the request and copy The Agency on every such occasion through a dedicated channel which shall be provided for such purpose. | The Bank must provide all information free of charge, unless requests are excessive or unfounded, in which case it may charge a fee or refuse with justification and copy NITDA. | Cost management and compliance burden with repeated requests | Medium | Medium | DPO / Legal / Ops | Review thresholds for manifestly excessive requests; fee policy; refusal templates shared with NITDA | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (4) | Rights of Data Subject | (4) The Controller shall bear the burden of demonstrating the manifestly unfounded or excessive character of the request. | The Bank bears the burden of proof when claiming a request is excessive or unfounded. | Rejection of legitimate requests without evidence; audit liability | Medium | Medium | Legal / DPO | Maintain records and rationale of request refusals | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (5) | Rights of Data Subject | (5) Where the Controller has reasonable doubts concerning the identity of the natural person making the request for information, the Controller may request the provision of additional information necessary to confirm the identity of the Data Subject. | The Bank may ask for additional verification where there is doubt about the requester's identity | Risk of providing personal data to unauthorized persons | Medium | High | Customer Service / DPO | Identity verification SOP (e.g. KYC match, multi-factor checks) | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (6) | Rights of Data Subject | (6) The information to be provided to Data Subject may be provided in combination with standardized icons in order to give in an easily visible, intelligible and clearly legible manner a meaningful overview of the intended processing. Where the icons are presented electronically, they shall be machine-readable. | The Bank may use standard icons to provide customers a simplified overview of data processing, which must be clear and machine-readable online. | Incomplete or unclear communication to customers | Medium | Medium | Communications / DPO | Infographics in privacy notice, electronic display compliance | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (7a) | Rights of Data Subject | (7) Prior to collecting Personal Data from a Data Subject, the Controller shall provide the Data Subject with all the following information: a) the identity and the contact details of the Controller; | The Bank shall disclose its identity and contact details to the Data Subject before collecting any personal data. | Lack of transparency, potential regulatory breach | Medium | Medium | Customer Service / DPO | Include in online forms, T&Cs, privacy policies | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (7b) | Rights of Data Subject | b) the contact details of the Data Protection Officer; | The Bank shall provide the contact details of its designated Data Protection Officer (DPO) to the Data Subject. | Opaque DPO communication channel | Medium | Medium | DPO | Display DPO email/contact on website, app, and forms | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (7c) | Rights of Data Subject | c) the purpose(s) of the processing for which the Personal Data are intended as well as the legal basis for the processing; | The Bank shall disclose the purpose and legal basis of personal data collection. | Breach of lawful processing and consent requirements | Medium | High | Legal / Business Unit | Include purpose/legal basis in privacy statement | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (7d) | Rights of Data Subject | d) the legitimate interests pursued by the Controller or by a third party; | The Bank shall state any legitimate interests pursued (if applicable) when relying on legitimate interest as a basis for processing. | Data subjects may contest vague interest claims | Medium | Medium | Legal / DPO | Legitimate interest assessment (LIA) documentation | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (7e) | Rights of Data Subject | e) the recipients or categories of recipients of the Personal Data, if any; | The Bank shall inform the Data Subject about who (or which categories of persons) will receive their personal data. | Third-party risk, legal breach if undisclosed | Medium | High | Legal / DPO | Disclosure via privacy policy or contract | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (7f) | Rights of Data Subject | f) where applicable, the fact that the Controller intends to transfer Personal Data to a third country or international organization and the existence or absence of an adequacy decision by The Agency; | If data will be transferred to a foreign country or international organization, the Bank shall inform the Data Subject and state whether an adequacy decision exists. | Illegal data transfers, international risk exposure | Medium | High | DPO / Legal / IT | List of cross-border transfers and adequacy review | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (7g) | Rights of Data Subject | g) the period for which the Personal Data will be stored, or if that is not possible, the criteria used to determine that period; | The Bank shall inform the Data Subject how long their data will be stored or the criteria used to determine this period. | Over-retention of data, legal conflict | Medium | Medium | Records Management / Legal | Data retention policy published; data lifecycle mapping | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (7h) | Rights of Data Subject | h) the existence of the right to request from the Controller access to and rectification or erasure of Personal Data or restriction of processing concerning the Data Subject or to object to processing as well as the right to Data Portability; | The Bank shall inform the Data Subject of their rights to access, rectification, erasure, restriction, objection, and portability. | Omission may lead to complaints or enforcement actions | Medium | High | Legal / DPO | Updated privacy notice and onboarding scripts to include these rights | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (7i) | Rights of Data Subject | i) the existence of the right to withdraw consent at any time, without affecting the lawfulness of processing based on consent before its withdrawal; | The Bank shall inform the Data Subject of their right to withdraw consent at any time and that this withdrawal does not affect earlier lawful processing. | Failure to notify may result in consent deemed invalid | Medium | High | DPO / Customer Service | Consent withdrawal mechanism in forms and privacy notice | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (7j) | Rights of Data Subject | j) the right to lodge a complaint with a relevant authority; | The Bank shall inform the Data Subject of their right to lodge a complaint with the relevant supervisory authority. | Undermining Data Subject rights and exposing Bank to regulatory scrutiny | Medium | High | Compliance / Legal | Include complaint guidance and contact details in privacy policy | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (7k) | Rights of Data Subject | k) whether the provision of Personal Data is a statutory or contractual requirement, or a requirement necessary to enter into a contract, as well as whether the Data Subject is obliged to provide the Personal Data and of the possible consequences of failure to provide such data; | The Bank shall disclose whether providing data is required by law or contract, and the consequences of not providing it. | Informed consent invalidated if legal context is unclear | Medium | High | Business / Legal / Ops | Consent language in forms reviewed by legal team | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (7l) | Rights of Data Subject | l) the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling and, at least, in those cases, meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing for the Data Subject; | If the Bank uses automated decision-making or profiling, it shall provide the logic, significance, and consequences of such processing. | Regulatory risk for opaque profiling or denial of services | Medium | High | Data Science / DPO | Automated processing explanation embedded in consent and decision modules | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (7m) | Rights of Data Subject | m) Where the Controller intends to further process the Personal Data for a purpose other than that for which the Personal Data were collected, the controller shall provide the Data Subject prior to that further processing with information on that other purpose, and with any relevant further information; and | If the Bank intends to use data for another purpose beyond the original reason, it must notify the Data Subject in advance. | Scope creep without notice violates consent principle | Medium | High | Product / Legal / Compliance | Review & update privacy policy when changing data use | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (7n) | Rights of Data Subject | n) Where applicable, that the Controller intends to transfer Personal Data to a recipient in a foreign country or international organization and the existence or absence of an adequacy decision by The Agency. | Where applicable, the Bank must inform the Data Subject of foreign data transfer recipients and adequacy status under NDPR. | Unauthorized transfer or lack of transparency regarding jurisdiction | Medium | High | Compliance / IT Security | Standardized cross-border transfer disclosure template | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (8) | Rights of Data Subject | (8) Where Personal Data are transferred to a foreign country or to an international organization, the Data Subject shall have the right to be informed of the appropriate safeguards for data protection in the foreign country. The Data Subject shall have the right to obtain from the Controller without undue delay the rectification of inaccurate Personal Data concerning him or her. Considering the purposes of the processing, the Data Subject shall have the right to have incomplete Personal Data completed, including by means of providing a supplementary statement. | The Bank shall: (1) inform Data Subjects of appropriate safeguards when transferring personal data internationally; (2) promptly correct any inaccurate data; and (3) allow Data Subjects to complete their information if it's incomplete. | Risk of reputational and legal harm due to inaccurate or incomplete records or foreign transfer secrecy | High | High | Data Management / DPO | SOP for data accuracy review and disclosure of foreign safeguards | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (9) | Rights of Data Subject | (9) The Data Subject shall have the right to request the Controller to delete Personal Data without delay, and the Controller shall delete Personal Data where one of the following grounds applies: a) the Personal Data are no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which they were collected or processed; b) the Data Subject withdraws consent on which the processing is based; c) the Data Subject objects to the processing and there are no overriding legitimate grounds for the processing; d) the Personal Data have been unlawfully processed; and e) the Personal Data must be erased for compliance with a legal obligation in Nigeria. | The Bank shall promptly delete personal data when a Data Subject requests it and any of the listed conditions apply, including withdrawal of consent, data being unnecessary, unlawful processing, or a legal obligation to erase. | High litigation/regulatory risk for failure to erase data on request | High | High | Records Mgt / DPO | Right to erasure policy, workflow automation, and deletion logs | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (10) | Rights of Data Subject | 10) The Controller who has made the Personal Data public and is obliged to delete the Personal Data shall, take all reasonable steps, to inform Controllers processing the Personal Data of the Data Subject’s request. | The Bank shall, if it previously disclosed personal data publicly and is now required to delete it, take all reasonable steps to inform any third parties or data controllers that are also processing that data of the Data Subject’s deletion request. | Risk that third parties continue to process deleted data due to lack of notification from the Bank. | Medium | High | Data Protection Officer (DPO) | Add third-party notification steps to deletion process; track and document each notification. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (11) | Rights of Data Subject | (11) The Data Subject shall have the right to obtain from the Controller restriction of processing where one of the following applies: a) The accuracy of the Personal Data is contested by the Data Subject for a period enabling the Controller to verify the accuracy of the Personal Data; b) The processing is unlawful, and the Data Subject opposes the erasure of the Personal Data and requests the restriction of their use instead; c) The Controller no longer needs the Personal Data for the purposes of the processing, but they are required by the Data Subject for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims; and d) The Data Subject has objected to processing pending the verification whether the legitimate grounds of the Controller override those of the Data Subject. | The Bank shall restrict processing of a Data Subject’s personal data where any of the following apply: the accuracy is disputed; the Data Subject prefers restriction to deletion; the Bank no longer needs the data but the Data Subject does for legal purposes; or the Data Subject has objected while a decision is pending. | Unlawful or unwanted data processing may continue, violating Data Subject rights and regulatory obligations. | Medium | High | Data Protection Officer (DPO) | Include conditional processing flags in the system; review objection and verification procedures; retain flagged records securely until resolved. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (12) | Rights of Data Subject | (12) Where processing has been restricted such Personal Data shall, except for storage, only be processed with the Data Subject's consent or for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims or for the protection of the rights of another natural or legal person or for reasons of important public interest in Nigeria. | Once the Bank restricts a Data Subject’s data, it must not process it further—except for storage—unless: the Data Subject gives consent; it is needed for legal claims; it protects another person’s rights; or it serves Nigeria’s public interest. | Unauthorized processing of restricted data may violate data subject rights and regulatory obligations. | Medium | High | Data Protection Officer (DPO) | Restrict system permissions post-flagging; apply automated block on processing except for specified exemptions. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (13) | Rights of Data Subject | (13) The Controller shall communicate any rectification or erasure of Personal Data or restriction to each recipient to whom the Personal Data have been disclosed, unless this proves impossible or involves disproportionate effort. The controller shall inform the Data Subject about those recipients if the Data Subject requests it. | The Bank shall inform any party it has shared personal data with about any correction, deletion, or restriction placed on that data—unless doing so is impossible or requires unreasonable effort. The Bank must also tell the Data Subject who those recipients are, if asked. | Failure to inform third parties may result in continued misuse of outdated or restricted personal data. | Medium | High | Data Protection Officer (DPO) | Maintain a recipient log per data subject; automate alerts for updates/rectification notices to recipients; retain evidence of attempted notifications. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (14) | Rights of Data Subject | (14) The Data Subject shall have the right to receive the Personal Data concerning him or her, which he or she has provided to a controller, in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format, and have the right to transmit those data to another controller without hindrance from the controller to which the Personal Data have been provided, where: (a) The processing is based on consent, or (b) On a contract, and (c) The processing is carried out by automated means. | The Bank shall, upon request, provide personal data (originally supplied by the customer) in a structured, machine-readable format if processing is based on consent or contract and is automated. | Failure to provide machine-readable data may lead to data portability complaints and non-compliance. | Medium | High | Data Protection Officer (DPO) | Implement a secure, automated export system for data portability requests; verify eligibility (consent/contract/automated) before processing. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 3.1 (15) | Rights of Data Subject | (15) In exercising his right to Data Portability, the Data Subject shall have the right to have the Personal Data transmitted directly from one controller to another, where technically feasible. Provided that this right shall not apply to processing necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the Controller. | The Bank shall, where technically possible, transfer a Data Subject’s personal data directly to another Controller upon request, except where the Bank is acting under public interest or official mandate. | Failure to transmit data when technically feasible may violate data portability rights. | Medium | High | Data Protection Officer (DPO) | Integrate data export functionality and verify technical feasibility before declining. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 4.1 (3) | Implementation Mechanisms | . (3) A Data Controller or Processor shall ensure continuous capacity building for Data Protection Officers and the generality of her personnel involved in any form of data processing. | The Bank shall regularly train its DPO and all staff involved in data processing to maintain compliance and data protection awareness. | Lack of ongoing training may result in non-compliance and data breaches due to human error. | High | High | HR / Compliance / DPO | Establish mandatory annual data protection training; track attendance and completion. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 4.1 (4) | Implementation Mechanisms | (4) The Agency shall by this Regulation register and license Data Protection Compliance Organisations (DPCOs) who shall on behalf of the Agency monitor, audit, conduct training and data protection compliance consulting to all Data Controllers under this Regulation. The DPCOs shall be subject to Regulations and Directives of NITDA issued from time to time. | The Bank shall engage only registered DPCOs licensed by NITDA for data protection audits, monitoring, training, and compliance support, as required under this regulation. | Use of unregistered or unlicensed DPCOs may render compliance activities invalid and result in regulatory sanctions. | Medium | High | Compliance / Procurement | Maintain an up-to-date list of NITDA-licensed DPCOs; verify license before engagement. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 4.2 | Administrative Redress Panel | (1) Without prejudice to the right of a Data Subject to seek redress in a court of competent jurisdiction, the Agency shall set up an Administrative Redress Panel under the following terms of reference;  (2) Investigation of allegations of any breach of the provisions of this Regulation;  (3) Invitation of any party to respond to allegations made against it within seven days;  (4) Issuance of Administrative orders to protect the subject-matter of the allegation pending the outcome of investigation;  (5) Conclusion of investigation and determination of appropriate redress within twenty-eight (28) working days; and  (6) Any breach of this Regulation shall be construed as a breach of the provisions of the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) Act of 2007. | (1) The Bank must be aware that data subjects can file complaints before an Administrative Panel, and not only in court.  (2)  The Bank must be prepared for investigations by the Administrative Panel following any complaints.   (3) The Bank must be prepared to respond to NDPR complaints within 7 days of notice.  (4) The Bank must comply with temporary measures issued by the Panel during investigations.  (5) The Bank must cooperate and provide necessary documentation within investigation timelines.  (6) The Bank must treat any NDPR breach as a legal breach with serious regulatory consequences. | Failure to respond promptly or cooperate with the Panel could lead to sanctions or reputational damage. | Medium | High | Compliance / Legal / DPO | Establish internal NDPR complaint handling SOPs, designate responsible officer, track timelines, and maintain open communication with the Panel. | Low | Medium |
|  | 49 | Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) 2023 | Section 2 (1) | Application | (1) This Act shall apply to the processing of personal data, whether by automated means or not. | The bank must comply with the Act whenever it handles personal data—whether using digital systems (automated) or manually (e.g., paper records, physical forms). | Non-compliance may lead to regulatory sanctions, fines, and reputational damage. | Medium | High | Data Protection Officer | Implement policies covering all personal data processing, including manual and automated systems. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 2 (2) | Application | (2) This Act shall apply, where the— (a) data controller or the data processor is domiciled in, resident in, or operating in Nigeria; (b) processing of personal data occurs within Nigeria; or (c) the data controller or the data processor is not domiciled in, resident in, or operating in Nigeria, but is processing personal data of a data subject in Nigeria. | The bank must comply with this Act if it is based in Nigeria, operating in Nigeria, or processing personal data within Nigeria. Even if the bank is outside Nigeria, it must still comply if it handles the personal data of anyone located in Nigeria. | Risk of violating jurisdictional data protection requirements, potential cross-border legal exposure. | Medium | High | Compliance Officer | Maintain a register of data processing activities and locations; monitor cross-border data flows. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 24 (1a) | Principles of personal data processing | (1) A data controller or data processor shall ensure that personal data is—  (a) processed in a fair, lawful and transparent manner; | The bank must ensure that personal data is handled in a way that is fair to the customer, legally permitted, and clearly explained | Customer complaints, legal actions, fines, and loss of trust if data is mishandled or concealed. | Medium | High | Data Protection Officer | Develop and publish clear privacy policies; conduct privacy impact assessments; maintain consent records. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 24 (1b) | Principles of personal data processing | (b) collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes, and not to be further processed in a way incompatible with these purposes; | The bank must ensure that personal data is collected only for clearly stated, specific, and lawful purposes such as account opening, loan processing, or regulatory compliance and must not use that data later for unrelated purposes | Risk of data misuse, regulatory penalties, and breach of customer trust. | Medium | High | Business Unit Heads | Define and document processing purposes; restrict use via access controls and approval workflows. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 24 (1c) | Principles of personal data processing | (c) adequate, relevant, and limited to the minimum necessary for the purposes for which the personal data was collected or further processed; | The bank must only collect and use personal data that is necessary, relevant, and appropriate for the specific reason it was collected. It must not gather or keep more data than needed for that purpose. | Excessive data collection increases breach risk and regulatory penalties. | Medium | High | Data Protection Officer | Data collection forms reviewed for necessity; data minimization embedded in system design. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 24 (1d) | Principles of personal data processing | (d) retained for not longer than is necessary to achieve the lawful bases for which the personal data was collected or further processed; | The bank must not keep personal data longer than necessary. Once the reason for collecting or using the data has been fulfilled, the data must be securely deleted or anonymized, unless there is a lawful reason to retain it. | Retaining data too long risks breaches, fines, and non-compliance with retention laws. | Medium | High | Records Management Team | Implement data retention schedules and automated deletion/anonymization processes. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 24 (1e) | Principles of personal data processing | (e) accurate, complete, not misleading, and, where necessary, kept up to date having regard to the purposes for which the personal data is collected or is further processed; and | The bank must ensure that personal data it holds is accurate, complete, and not misleading. The bank must also update the data when necessary to keep it current for the purposes it was collected or used. | Inaccurate or outdated data can lead to wrong decisions, customer dissatisfaction, regulatory penalties. | Medium | High | Data Quality Manager | Implement data validation, regular updates, customer data verification processes. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 24 (1f) | Principles of personal data processing | (f) processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing, access, loss, destruction, damage, or any form of breach. | The bank must process personal data securely by implementing measures to protect it from unauthorized or illegal processing, access, loss, destruction, damage, or any form of data breach. | Data breaches can cause financial loss, legal sanctions, reputational harm. | High | Very High | Information Security Officer | Deploy encryption, access controls, intrusion detection, and incident response plans. | Medium | High |
|  |  |  | Section 24 (2) | Principles of personal data processing | (2) A data controller and data processor shall use appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure confidentiality, integrity, and availability of personal data. | The bank must implement suitable technical and organizational safeguards to ensure that personal data is kept confidential, accurate, and available when needed. | Failure may result in data breaches, loss of data integrity, service interruptions, regulatory fines. | High | Very High | IT Department / Data Protection Officer | Implement robust IT security infrastructure and organizational policies (e.g., access management, backups). | Medium | High |
|  |  |  | Section 25 (1a) | Lawful Basis of Personal Data Processing | (1) Without prejudice to the principles set out in this Act, data processing shall be lawful, where— (a) the data subject has given and not withdrawn consent for the specific purpose or purposes for which personal data is to be processed; | The bank must obtain explicit consent from individuals before processing their personal data. This consent must be for the specific purpose(s) for which the data will be used. | Lack of consent may cause legal non-compliance, fines, reputational damage, and customer complaints. | Medium | High | Compliance Officer / Customer Service | Obtain and document consent before data collection and processing; provide withdrawal options. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 25 (1bi) | Lawful Basis of Personal Data Processing | (b) the processing is necessary— (i) for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is a party or to take steps at the request of the data subject prior to entering into a contract, | The bank may process personal data without explicit consent when it is necessary to perform a contract with the individual (such as opening an account or providing a loan) or to take steps the individual has requested before entering into a contract | Incorrect data use could breach contract terms or customer trust, leading to disputes or fines. | Medium | High | Business Unit Heads | Ensure contract-related processing is documented and aligned with data protection policies. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 25 (1bii) | Lawful Basis of Personal Data Processing | (ii) for compliance with a legal obligation to which the data controller or data processor is subject, | The bank must process personal data when required by law. This means the bank needs to handle personal data as necessary to comply with any legal or regulatory obligations imposed on it, such as reporting requirements or tax laws. | Non-compliance risks legal sanctions, fines, and operational disruptions. | High | Very High | Legal / Compliance Teams | Maintain updated legal register; automate compliance reporting and data handling procedures. | Medium | High |
|  |  |  | Section 25 (1biii) | Lawful Basis of Personal Data Processing | (iii) to protect the vital interest of the data subject or another person, | The bank may process personal data without consent if it is necessary to protect the life or safety of the individual or another person, for example, in emergencies where consent cannot be obtained. | Failure to act in emergencies risks harm to individuals and potential liabilities. | Low | Very High | Customer Service / Risk Management | Define emergency data processing protocols and staff training on urgent data access procedures. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 25 (1biv) | Lawful Basis of Personal Data Processing | (iv) for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the data controller or data processor, or | The bank must process personal data when carrying out tasks that serve the public interest or when exercising official duties assigned by law, such as cooperating with government agencies on regulatory matters. | Failure may lead to legal penalties and loss of regulatory trust. | Medium | Very High | Compliance / Legal | Formalize cooperation protocols with authorities and document lawful data processing activities. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 25 (1bv) | Lawful Basis of Personal Data Processing | (v) for the purposes of the legitimate interests pursued by the data controller or data processor, or by a third party to whom the data is disclosed. | The bank may process personal data when it is necessary for its legitimate business interests or those of a third party, provided these interests do not override the rights and freedoms of the data subject. | Risk of violating data subject rights, leading to complaints and regulatory scrutiny. | Medium | High | Business Units / Compliance | Conduct Legitimate Interest Assessments (LIA); document balancing tests; provide opt-out options. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 25 (2a) | Lawful Basis of Personal Data Processing | (2) Interests in personal data processing shall not be legitimate for the purposes of subsection (1) (b) (v), where— (a) they override the fundamental rights, freedoms and the interests of the data subject; | The bank must ensure that any legitimate interest it relies on to process personal data does not violate the fundamental rights and freedoms of the individuals whose data is processed. | Risk of unlawful data use, complaints, sanctions, and reputational damage. | Medium | High | Compliance Officer | Review LIAs to ensure rights are respected; escalate conflicts for legal review. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 25 (2b) | Lawful Basis of Personal Data Processing | (b) they are incompatible with other lawful basis of processing under subsection subsection (1) (b) (i)-(iv); or | The bank must not process personal data based on legitimate interests if another lawful basis from sections (1)(b)(i) to (iv) applies instead. | Risk of incorrect legal basis use causing non-compliance and enforcement actions. | Medium | High | Legal / Compliance Teams | Maintain clear guidelines on basis prioritization; provide training on lawful basis selection. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 25 (2c) | Lawful Basis of Personal Data Processing | (c) the data subject would not have a reasonable expectation that the personal data would be processed in the manner envisaged. | The bank must only process personal data under legitimate interests when the data subject would reasonably expect such processing based on their relationship with the bank and the context. | Unexpected processing may cause loss of trust and regulatory penalties. | Medium | High | Customer Relations / Compliance | Provide clear privacy notices explaining legitimate interests; manage customer expectations effectively. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 26 (2) | Consent | (2) In determining whether consent was freely and intentionally given, account shall be taken of whether, the performance of a contract, including the provision of a service, is conditional upon consent to the processing of personal data that is not necessary for the performance of that contract. | The bank must not make consent for data processing a condition for providing a service or contract unless the data processing is necessary for that service or contract to be performed. | Invalid consent could lead to regulatory penalties and legal challenges. | Medium | High | Legal / Compliance Officer | Review consent requests and forms to ensure necessity; avoid bundling consent with non-essential processing. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 27 | Provision of information to the data subject | 1) Before a data controller collects personal data directly from a data subject, the data controller shall inform the data subject of the—  (a) identity, residence or place of business of, and means of communication with the data controller and its representatives, where necessary; | Before collecting personal data directly, the bank must clearly inform individuals who is collecting their data, including contact details and how to communicate with the bank about their data. | Poor disclosure can lead to mistrust and regulatory non-compliance. | Medium | High | Data Protection Officer | Update and publish contact details in all customer-facing platforms (e.g., privacy notices, forms). | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 27 (1b) | Provision of information to the data subject | (b) specific lawful basis of processing under section 25(1) or 30(1) of this Act, and the purposes for which the personal data are intended; | The bank must tell individuals the legal reason for processing their data and the purpose(s) for which the data will be used. | Vague or missing explanations may result in invalid processing and customer complaints. | Medium | High | Compliance Officer | Include lawful basis and purposes in privacy notices and customer onboarding materials. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 27 (1c) | Provision of information to the data subject | (c) recipients or categories of recipients of the personal data, if any; | The bank must inform individuals if their personal data will be shared with any third parties or categories of recipients. | Failure to notify may lead to breach of trust and compliance issues. | Medium | High | Legal / DPO | List categories of recipients in privacy notices; update as needed. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 27 (1d) | Provision of information to the data subject | (d) existence of the rights of the data subject under Part VI; | The bank must inform individuals of their rights related to their personal data, such as rights to access, correction, or deletion. | Uninformed customers may trigger complaints or regulatory investigation. | Medium | High | Compliance / Legal | Provide a user-friendly privacy rights guide via website and print materials. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 27 (1e) | Provision of information to the data subject | (e) retention period for the personal data; | The bank must disclose how long it intends to keep the personal data. | Failure to disclose or improper retention practices can cause regulatory action. | Medium | High | Records Management / Legal | Embed retention details in privacy notices; align with internal retention schedule. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 27 (1f) | Provision of information to the data subject | (f) right to lodge a complaint with the Commission in accordance with section 46 (1) of this Act; and | The bank must inform individuals of their right to complain to the relevant data protection authority if they believe their data rights have been violated. | Lack of awareness may erode trust and trigger regulatory pressure. | Medium | High | Customer Experience / DPO | Include complaint options in privacy policy and customer service communications. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 27 (1g) | Provision of information to the data subject | (g) existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, the significance and envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject, and the right to object to and challenge such processing. | If the bank uses automated decision-making or profiling that affects individuals, it must inform them about this, explain its impact, and advise them of their right to object or challenge the process. | Potential claims of discrimination or lack of transparency. | Medium | High | Credit Risk / Compliance | Publish clear explanation of automated decision systems and opt-out procedures. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 27 (2) | Provision of information to the data subject | (2) Before a data controller collects personal data, other than directly from the data subject, the data controller shall inform the data subject of the matters set out in subsection (1), except where the— (a) data subject already has been provided with such information; or (b) provision of such information is impossible or would involve a disproportionate effort or expense. | When the bank collects personal data indirectly, it must still inform the individual about the data processing unless the person has already been informed or providing the information is impractical. | Non-disclosure may lead to complaints and regulatory non-compliance. | Medium | High | Compliance Officer / DPO | Implement workflow to identify indirect data sources and trigger notification. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 27(3) | Provision of information to the data subject | (3) The information referred to in subsection (1) shall be contained in a privacy policy and expressed in clear, concise, transparent, intelligible, and easily accessible format, taking into consideration the class of data subjects targeted by the data processing. | The bank must publish a clear and accessible privacy policy containing all required information, tailored to the audience’s understanding. | Complex language may mislead customers and result in penalties. | Medium | High | Corporate Communications | Design privacy notices using plain language principles; test with customer focus groups. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 28 (1) | Data privacy impact assessment | (1) Where the processing of personal data may likely result in high risk to the rights and freedoms of a data subject by virtue of its nature, scope, context, and purposes, a data controller shall, prior to the processing, carry out a data privacy impact assessment. | The bank must conduct a Data Privacy Impact Assessment (DPIA) before starting any data processing that could pose a high risk to individuals’ privacy rights. | Skipping DPIAs can lead to data breaches or unlawful processing. | Medium | Very High | Risk Management / Compliance | Embed DPIA as a step in all new high-risk data initiatives or product launches. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 28 (2) | Data privacy impact assessment | (2) The data controller shall consult the Commission prior to the processing if, notwithstanding the measures envisaged under this section, the data protection impact assessment indicates that the processing of the data would result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of a data subject. | If a DPIA shows high residual risk after controls, the bank must consult the data protection authority before proceeding with the data processing. | Proceeding without clearance could attract enforcement or sanctions. | Low | Very High | DPO / Legal | Establish trigger thresholds for consultation and escalate high-risk DPIAs to regulator. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 29 (1a) | Obligations of the data controller and data processor | (1) Where a data controller engages the services of a data processor, or a data processor engages the services of another data processor, the data controller or data processor engaging another shall ensure that the engaged data processor —  (a) complies with the principles and obligations set out in this Act as applicable to the data controller; | When the bank outsources data processing to third parties, it must ensure those parties comply with all applicable data protection laws and principles. | Processors may mishandle data, leading to joint liability for the bank. | High | High | Procurement / DPO | Include data protection clauses in all vendor contracts; conduct due diligence and audits. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 29 (1b) | Obligations of the data controller and data processor | (b) assists the data controller or data processor, as the case may be, by the use of appropriate technical and organisational measures, in the fulfilment of the data controller's obligations to honour the rights of a data subject under Part VI; | The bank must ensure its data processors help it respect individuals’ data rights through proper technical and organizational safeguards. | Failure to respond to rights requests may breach the law. | Medium | High | Procurement / Compliance | Review third-party capabilities before contracting; monitor their performance regularly. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 29 (1c) | Obligations of the data controller and data processor | (c) implements appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the security, integrity, and confidentiality of personal data as required in Part VII; | The bank and its processors must implement robust security measures to protect personal data from unauthorized access, loss, or damage. | Invalid consent could lead to regulatory penalties and legal challenges. | Medium | High | Legal / Compliance Officer | Review consent requests and forms to ensure necessity; avoid bundling consent with non-essential processing. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 29 (1d) | Obligations of the data controller and data processor | (d) provides the data controller or engaging data processor, where applicable, with information reasonably required to comply and demonstrate compliance with this Act; and | The bank must require data processors to provide necessary information to demonstrate compliance with data protection laws. | Poor disclosure can lead to mistrust and regulatory non-compliance. | Medium | High | Data Protection Officer | Update and publish contact details in all customer-facing platforms (e.g., privacy notices, forms). | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 29 (1e) | Obligations of the data controller and data processor | (e) notifies the data controller or engaging data processor, where applicable, when a new data processor is engaged. | The bank must be informed whenever a data processor appoints another processor and ensure that the same compliance standards are maintained. | Vague or missing explanations may result in invalid processing and customer complaints. | Medium | High | Compliance Officer | Include lawful basis and purposes in privacy notices and customer onboarding materials. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 29 (2) | Obligations of the data controller and data processor | (2) The measures under subsection (1) include a written agreement between the data controller and the data processor, or between data processors, as the case may be, | The bank must have written contracts with all data processors that clearly set out data protection responsibilities and requirements. | Failure to notify may lead to breach of trust and compliance issues. | Medium | High | Legal / DPO | List categories of recipients in privacy notices; update as needed. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 30 (1a) | Sensitive Personal Data | 1) Without prejudice to the principles set out in this Act, a data controller or data processor shall not process or permit the processing of a data subject's processing of sensitive personal data, unless the— (a) data subject has given and not withdrawn consent to the processing for the specific purpose or purposes for which it will be processed. | The bank must obtain explicit consent before processing any sensitive personal data (such as health, biometric, or religious information) and must respect withdrawal of that consent. | Uninformed customers may trigger complaints or regulatory investigation. | Medium | High | Compliance / Legal | Provide a user-friendly privacy rights guide via website and print materials. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 30 (1b) | Sensitive Personal Data | (b) processing is necessary for the purposes of performing the obligations of the data controller or exercising right of the data subject under employment or social security laws or any other similar laws; | The bank may process sensitive personal data without consent if it is necessary to fulfill legal employment or social security obligations. | Failure to disclose or improper retention practices can cause regulatory action. | Medium | High | Records Management / Legal | Embed retention details in privacy notices; align with internal retention schedule. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 30 (1c) | Sensitive Personal Data | The bank must stay updated on any additional categories of sensitive personal data, legal grounds for processing such data, and safeguards issued by the data protection authority (the Commission). The bank must comply with these additional regulations and directives as they are issued. | The bank may process sensitive personal data without consent to protect life or safety when the individual cannot give consent. | Lack of awareness may erode trust and trigger regulatory pressure. | Medium | High | Customer Experience / DPO | Include complaint options in privacy policy and customer service communications. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 30 (1e) | Sensitive Personal Data | (e) processing is necessary for the establishment, exercise, or defence of a legal claim, obtaining legal advice, or conduct of a legal proceeding; | The bank may process sensitive personal data without consent for legal claims or court cases. | Potential claims of discrimination or lack of transparency. | Medium | High | Credit Risk / Compliance | Publish clear explanation of automated decision systems and opt-out procedures. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 30 (1f) | Sensitive Personal Data | (f) processing is necessary for reasons of substantial public interest, on the basis of a law, which shall be proportionate to the aim pursued, and provides for suitable and specific measures to safeguard the fundamental rights, freedoms and interests of the data subject; | The bank may process sensitive personal data without consent for important public interest reasons, following the law and with safeguards to protect individuals’ rights. | Non-disclosure may lead to complaints and regulatory non-compliance. | Medium | High | Compliance Officer / DPO | Implement workflow to identify indirect data sources and trigger notification. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 30 (1g) | Sensitive Personal Data | (g) processing is carried out for purposes of medical care or community welfare, and undertaken by or under the responsibility of a professional or similar service provider owing a duty of confidentiality; | If the bank processes sensitive data related to medical or welfare services, it must ensure such processing is done responsibly and confidentially by qualified professionals. | Complex language may mislead customers and result in penalties. | Medium | High | Corporate Communications | Design privacy notices using plain language principles; test with customer focus groups. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 30 (2) | Sensitive Personal Data | (2) The Commission may make regulations or issue directives prescribing— (a) further categories of personal data that may be classified as sensitive personal data; (b) further grounds on which such personal data may be processed; and (c) safeguards that may apply. | The bank must stay updated on any additional categories of sensitive personal data, legal grounds for processing such data, and safeguards issued by the data protection authority (the Commission). The bank must comply with these additional regulations and directives as they are issued. | Skipping DPIAs can lead to data breaches or unlawful processing. | Medium | Very High | Risk Management / Compliance | Embed DPIA as a step in all new high-risk data initiatives or product launches. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 32 | Data Protection Officers | (1) A data controller of major importance shall designate a Data Protection Officer or expert knowledge of data protection law and practices, and the ability to carry out the tasks prescribed under this Act and subsidiary legislation made under it.  (2) The Data Protection Officer may be an employee of a data controller or engaged by a service contract. (3) The Data Protection Officer shall— (a) advise the data controller or the data processor, and their employees, who carry out processing made under this Act; (b) monitor compliance with this Act and related policies of the data controller or data processor; and (c) act as the contact point for the Commission on issues relating to data processing. | If the bank is classified as a “data controller of major importance” (i.e., handling significant volumes or sensitive data), it must appoint a qualified Data Protection Officer (DPO) either as an employee or via contract. The DPO will advise the bank on data protection compliance, monitor adherence to data laws and policies, and serve as the official contact point with the data protection authority | Proceeding without clearance could attract enforcement or sanctions. | Low | Very High | DPO / Legal | Establish trigger thresholds for consultation and escalate high-risk DPIAs to regulator. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 33 | Data protection compliance services | The Commission may license a person having a requisite level of expertise, in relation to data protection and this Act, to monitor, audit and report on compliance by data controllers and data processors with— (a) this Act; and (b) regulations, guidelines, directives, and codes of conduct issued by the Commission made under the provisions of this Act. | The bank must cooperate with licensed compliance experts appointed by the Commission who audit and report on the bank’s adherence to data protection laws, regulations, and guidelines. | Processors may mishandle data, leading to joint liability for the bank. | High | High | Procurement / DPO | Include data protection clauses in all vendor contracts; conduct due diligence and audits. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 34 (1ai) | Rights of a Data Subject | (1) A data subject has the right to obtain from a data controller, without constraint or unreasonable delay— (a) confirmation as to whether the data controller or a data processor operating on its behalf, is storing or otherwise processing personal data relating to the data subject, and where that is the case— (i) the purposes of the processing, | Upon request, the bank must promptly confirm whether it is storing or processing an individual’s personal data. If so, the bank must inform the individual of the specific purposes for which their data is being processed. | Failure to respond to rights requests may breach the law. | Medium | High | Procurement / Compliance | Review third-party capabilities before contracting; monitor their performance regularly. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 34 (1aii) | Rights of a Data Subject | (ii) the categories of personal data concerned, | The bank must provide information about the types or categories of personal data it holds or processes about the individual. | Failure to disclose may breach transparency rights. | Medium | High | DPO / Legal | Maintain clear data inventory mapped to data types. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 34 (1aiii) | Rights of a Data Subject | (iii) the recipients or categories of recipient to whom the personal data have been or will be disclosed, particularly recipients in third countries or international organisations, | The bank must disclose who the personal data has been or will be shared with, including any third parties or organizations in other countries. | Opaque sharing practices may violate fair processing duties. | Medium | High | Compliance / Legal | Maintain updated register of third-party recipients. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 34 (1aiv) | Rights of a Data Subject | (iv) where possible, the period for which the personal data will be stored, or, if not possible, the criteria used to determine that period, | The bank must inform the individual how long their personal data will be stored. If this is not possible, the bank must explain the criteria used to determine the retention period. | Poor or undefined retention practices risk over-retention. | Medium | High | Records Management | Define and publish data retention schedule. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 34 (1av) | Rights of a Data Subject | (v) the existence of the right to request from the data controller rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing of personal data concerning the data subject or to object to such processing, | The bank must inform individuals about their rights to request correction, deletion, restriction of processing, or to object to the processing of their personal data. | Lack of awareness may lead to regulatory complaints. | Medium | High | DPO / Customer Service | Update privacy policy and training materials to reflect rights. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 34 (1avi) | Rights of a Data Subject | (vi) the right to lodge a complaint with the Commission; | The bank must inform individuals of their right to file a complaint with the data protection authority (the Commission) if they believe their data rights have been violated. | Non-disclosure erodes trust and may delay redress. | Medium | Medium | Compliance / Legal | Privacy notice includes complaint procedures. | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Section 34 (1avii) | Rights of a Data Subject | (vii) where the personal data is not collected from the data subject, any available information as to their source; and | If the bank collected personal data from sources other than the individual, it must disclose the source of that data, where this information is available. | Lack of transparency could lead to trust and legal issues. | Medium | High | DPO / Compliance | Record and track source metadata for all personal data. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 34 (1aviii) | Rights of a Data Subject | (viii) the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, the significance and envisaged consequences for the data subject; | The bank must inform individuals if their personal data is subject to automated decision-making or profiling, including the significance and potential impact of such processing on the individual. | Profiling without notification can lead to legal claims. | Medium | High | Risk / Product / Compliance | Implement explanation feature in systems with automated decisions. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 34 (b) | Rights of a Data Subject | (b) a copy of data subject's personal data in a commonly used electronic format, except to the extent that providing such data would impose unreasonable costs on the data controller, in which case the data subject may be required by the data controller to pay all or part of such costs; | The bank must provide a copy of the individual's personal data in a commonly used electronic format upon request, unless this imposes unreasonable costs. If costs apply, the bank may ask the individual to cover them. | Denial or delay may trigger enforcement action. | Medium | High | DPO / IT / Customer Service | Self-service data download options or request portals. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 34 (1c) | Rights of a Data Subject | (c) the correction or, if correction is not feasible or suitable, deletion of the data subject's personal data that is inaccurate, out of date, incomplete, or misleading; | The bank must correct any personal data about an individual that is inaccurate, outdated, incomplete, or misleading. If correcting the data is not feasible or appropriate, the bank must delete such data. | Retention of false data can mislead decisions and violate rights. | Medium | High | Data Stewards / Compliance | Data accuracy reviews and edit logs. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 34 (1d) | Rights of a Data Subject | (d) the erasure of personal data concerning the data subject, without undue delay; and | The bank must erase an individual’s personal data without unnecessary delay when requested, provided there is a lawful basis to do so. | Failure to erase may lead to data hoarding and regulatory fines. | Medium | High | Records Management / Legal | Implement deletion workflows with verification. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 34 (1e) | Rights of a Data Subject | (e) restriction of data processing pending— (i) the resolution of a request, (ii) objection by the data subject under this Act, or (iii) the establishment, exercise, or defence of legal claims. | The bank must restrict the processing of personal data when requested by the individual in any of the following situations: - While a request regarding their data is being resolved - When the individual objects to the processing - During the establishment, exercise, or defence of legal claims involving the individual | Processing despite restriction can constitute a breach. | Medium | High | Compliance / IT | Apply flags or locks to restricted data fields. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 34 (2) | Rights of a Data Subject | (2) A data controller shall erase personal data without undue delay, where— (a) the personal data is no longer necessary, in relation to the purposes for which it was collected or processed; or (b) the data controller has no other lawful basis to retain the personal data. | The bank must erase personal data without undue delay when: - The data is no longer needed for the purpose it was collected or processed - There is no lawful basis for the bank to retain the data | Retaining data beyond lawful basis risks penalties. | High | High | Records Management / DPO | Periodic data reviews and auto-expiry configurations. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 35 | Withdrawal of Consent | (1) A data subject shall have the right to withdraw, at any time, consent to the processing of personal data under this Act. (2) The data controller shall ensure that it is as easy for the data subject to withdraw, as to give consent. | The bank must allow individuals to withdraw their consent to data processing at any time and make this withdrawal process as easy as giving consent. | Retaining data post-consent withdrawal may trigger fines. | High | High | IT / Compliance / Product Teams | Build opt-out functionality across all touchpoints. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 36 (1) | Right to Object | 1) A data subject shall have the right to object to the processing of personal data relating to the data subject. | The bank must respect and act on an individual’s right to object to the processing of their personal data, stopping the processing unless there are overriding legitimate grounds. | Continuing processing after objection is unlawful. | Medium | High | Legal / Compliance | Enable processing flag to block activity after objection. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 36 (2) | Right to Object | (2) A data controller shall discontinue the processing of personal data, unless the data controller demonstrates a compelling public interest or other lawful grounds, which overrides the fundamental rights and freedoms, and the interests of the data subject. | If an individual objects to the processing of their personal data, the bank must stop processing it unless the bank can prove there is a compelling public interest or another lawful reason that outweighs the individual’s rights and freedoms. | Weak justification may be rejected by NDPC. | Medium | High | Legal / Data Governance | Require Legal review before overriding objection. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 36 (3) | Right to Object | (3) Where personal data is processed for direct marketing purposes, the data subject shall have the right to object, at any time, to the processing of personal data concerning the data subject, which includes profiling, in so far as it is related to such direct marketing. | The bank must allow individuals to object at any time to the use of their personal data for direct marketing purposes, including profiling related to direct marketing. | Marketing without opt-out can trigger fines and complaints. | High | High | Marketing / DPO | Add unsubscribe links and opt-out toggles. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 36 (4) | Right to Object | (4) Where the data subject objects to processing for direct marketing purposes, the personal data shall no longer be processed for such purposes. | If an individual objects to direct marketing, the bank must immediately stop processing their personal data for direct marketing purposes. | Continued marketing after opt-out is a clear breach. | High | High | Marketing / CRM Systems | Maintain dynamic opt-out database across all platforms. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 37 (1) | Automated Decision-Making | (1) A data subject shall have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing of personal data, which produces legal or similarly significant effects concerning the data subject. | The bank must not make decisions solely based on automated processing of personal data if those decisions produce legal effects or significantly affect the individual. | Unlawful use of fully automated decisions affecting rights or obligations | Medium | High | DPO / IT / Legal | Restrict fully automated decision-making with legal/rights impact unless permitted by law or consent | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 37 (2a) | Automated Decision-Making | (2) Subsection (1) shall not apply, where the decision is— (a) necessary for entering into or the performance of a contract between the data subject and a data controller; (b) authorised by a written law, which establishes suitable measures to safeguard the fundamental rights and freedoms, and the interests of the data subject; or (c) authorised by the consent of the data subject. | The bank may use automated decision-making only if: - It is necessary for entering into or performing a contract with the individual; - It is authorized by law with safeguards for the individual’s rights; or - The individual has given explicit consent. | Automation without meeting exemption criteria (contract, law, consent) | Medium | High | DPO / Legal | Validate exemption prior to any automated decision | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 37 (3) | Automated Decision-Making | (3) The data controller shall implement suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's fundamental rights, freedoms and interests, including the rights to— (a) obtain human intervention on the part of the data controller; (b) express the data subject's point of view; and (c) contest the decision. | The bank must ensure the individual’s rights are protected by: - Allowing human review of automated decisions; - Letting individuals express their views; - Enabling individuals to challenge the decision. | Lack of safeguards for automated decisions (no human review or appeal) | Medium | High | DPO / Customer Service | Human-in-the-loop controls and right to challenge mechanism | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 39 (1a-e) | Security, Integrity, and Confidentiality | (1) A data controller and data processor shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the security, integrity and confidentiality of personal data in its possession or under its control, including protection against accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, misuse, alteration, unauthorised disclosure, or access, taking into account—  (a) the amount and sensitivity of the personal data; (b) the nature, degree and likelihood of harm to a data subject that could result from the loss, disclosure, or other misuse of the personal data; (c) the extent of the processing; (d) the period of data retention; and (e) the availability and cost of any technologies, tools, or other measures to be implemented relative to the size of the data controller or data processor. | The bank must implement appropriate technical and organizational controls to protect personal data from unauthorized access, loss, or damage. The measures should consider: - The sensitivity and volume of data; - Potential harm to individuals if data is mishandled; - The scale and duration of data processing; - Available and cost-effective security technologies. | Weak security framework increases exposure to data breaches | High | High | CISO / DPO | Risk-based technical and organisational measures | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 39 (2a-g) | Security, Integrity, and Confidentiality | (2) Measures implemented under subsection (1) may include— (a) pseudonymisation or other methods of de-identification of personal data; (b) encryption of personal data; (c) processes to ensure security, integrity, confidentiality, availability and resilience of processing systems and services; (d) processes to restore availability of and access to personal data in a timely manner, in the event of a physical or technical incident; (e) periodic assessment of risks to processing systems and services, including where the processing involves the transmission of data over an electronic communications network; (f) regular testing, assessing, and evaluation of the effectiveness of the measures implemented against current and evolving risks identified; (g) regular updating of the measures and introduction of new measures to address shortcomings in effectiveness, and accommodate evolving risks. | The bank should apply measures such as: - De-identifying data (pseudonymisation); - Encrypting personal data; - Ensuring system resilience and availability; - Having processes to quickly restore data access after incidents; - Periodically assessing risks and testing security controls; - Updating security measures regularly to address new threats. | Failure to use encryption, de-ID, or recovery plans | High | High | IT Security | Encryption, pseudonymisation, backups, testing | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 40 (1) | Personal Data Breaches | (1) Where personal data breach has occurred with respect to personal data being stored or processed by a data controller or data processor, the data processor shall, on becoming aware of a breach—  (a) notify the data controller or data processor that engaged it, describing the nature of the personal data breach including, where possible, the categories and approximate numbers of data subjects and personal data records concerned; and (b) respond to all information requests from the data controller or data processor that engaged it, as they may require to comply with their obligations under this section. | When a data processor becomes aware of a data breach, it must promptly notify the bank (data controller) and provide details about the breach, including affected data categories and numbers, and assist the bank in fulfilling its legal obligations. | Processor fails to notify the bank about breach | High | High | DPO / Procurement | Contractual obligation for processors to notify bank | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 40 (2) | Personal Data Breaches | (2) A data controller shall, within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach which is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, notify the Commission of the breach and, where feasible, describe the nature of the personal data breach including, where possible, the categories and approximate numbers of data subjects and personal data records concerned. | If the bank becomes aware of a data breach likely to harm individuals’ rights or freedoms, it must notify the data protection Commission within 72 hours, describing the breach and affected data as fully as possible. | Delay in breach notification to Commission | High | High | DPO / Legal | Incident response procedure with 72-hour breach alert | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Section 40 (3) | Personal Data Breaches | (3) Where a personal data breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of a data subject the data controller shall immediately communicate the personal data breach to the data subject in plain and clear language, including advice about measures the data subject should take to mitigate the possible adverse effects of the personal data breach and if a direct communications to the data subject would involve disproportionate effort or expense, or is otherwise not feasible, the data controller may instead make a public communication in one or more widely used media sources such that the data subject is likely to be informed. | If a breach is likely to pose a high risk to individuals, the bank must immediately inform affected individuals clearly and simply, advising them on steps to protect themselves. If direct notification is impractical or costly, the bank may issue a public notice through widely accessible media. | Failure to notify affected individuals of high-risk breach | High | High | DPO / Corporate Comms | Breach notification templates for individuals | Low | Medium |
