|  |  |  | Reg. 3 | Application | These Regulations shall apply to all Financial Institutions (FIs) under the regulatory purview of the Central Bank of Nigeria. | The Bank is mandatorily covered by these regulations if they are regulated by the CBN. | Failure to recognize applicability could lead to complete non-compliance or regulatory penalties. | Low | High | Executive Management / Compliance | Regulatory scope assessments; inclusion in compliance charter. | Very Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 4 | Prohibition of opening anonymous accounts | FIs shall not establish or keep anonymous accounts, numbered accounts or accounts in fictitious names. | The Bank shall not open or maintain any account that is anonymous, uses only numbers, or is registered under a fictitious or false name. All accounts must be linked to a verifiable natural or legal person, and full Know Your Customer (KYC) procedures must be completed before account activation. | Risk of money laundering or terrorist financing through accounts not linked to verified individuals. | High | High | Compliance / Operations | KYC verification at onboarding; system blocks incomplete KYC accounts; regular audit trail on onboarding documentation. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg, 5 (1a) | Customer  Due  Diligence measures | (1) FIs shall undertake CDD measures when— (a) establishing business relationships ; | The Bank must perform CDD checks when opening any new customer account or business relationship | Unidentified or misidentified customers create AML/CFT vulnerabilities. | High | High | Onboarding / Compliance | KYC onboarding checklist and mandatory identity verification. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg, 5 (1b) | Customer  Due  Diligence measures | (b) carrying out occasional transactions above the applicable and designated threshold of US$1,000 or its equivalent in other currencies or as may be determined by the CBN from time to time, including where the  transaction is carried out in a single or several transactions or operations that appear to be linked ; | The Bank must verify customer identity when handling one-time transactions over $1,000 (or equivalent) — even if the amount is broken into multiple linked transactions | Structuring transactions to evade CDD checks; regulatory breach. | Medium | High | Operations / Compliance | Threshold transaction monitoring; alerts for linked transactions. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg, 5 (1c) | Customer  Due  Diligence measures | (c) carrying out occasional transactions that are wire transfers, including cross-border and domestic transfers between FIs and when credit or debit cards are used as a payment method to effect money transfer ; | The Bank must apply CDD to wire transfers, including local or cross-border transfers, even when using cards to transfer money | Anonymous money movement and risk of cross-border illicit flows. | Medium | High | Compliance / IT Ops | Payment channel monitoring; KYC flag before wire initiation. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg, 5 (1d) | Customer  Due  Diligence measures | (d) there are doubts as to the veracity or adequacy of previously obtained customer identification data ; or | If the Bank has doubts about previously collected customer identification, it must re-verify the customer’s identity. | Using outdated, incorrect, or fraudulent identity data. | Medium | High | KYC / Compliance | Trigger-driven KYC refresh based on red flags. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg, 5 (1e) | Customer  Due  Diligence measures | (e) there is a suspicion of ML, TF and PF regardless of any exemptions or any other thresholds referred to in these Regulations or the CBN AML, CFT and CPF Regulations. | If there is suspicion of money laundering, terrorism financing, or proliferation financing, the Bank must conduct full CDD immediately — regardless of any threshold or exemption. | Failure to act on suspicious behavior; regulatory censure. | Medium | High | AML / Compliance | Immediate full CDD trigger in suspicious transaction reporting (STR) workflow. | Low | High |
|  |  |  | Reg, 5 (2) | Customer  Due  Diligence measures | (2) FIs shall establish internal processes and procedures for conducting CDD measures for all potential and existing customers, including occasional customers. | The Bank must establish internal policies and procedures to ensure consistent CDD is conducted for all customers, including walk-ins and one-time users. | Lack of consistency in CDD approach across departments or branches. | Medium | High | Compliance / Risk | Documented CDD SOPs; periodic training. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg, 5 (3a-e) | Customer  Due  Diligence measures | (3) CDD measures shall include — (a) customer identification and verification of identity ; (b) identification and verification of identity of beneficial owners (BOs) ; (c) understanding nature and purpose of business ; (d) understanding the sources of funds ; and (e) conducting ongoing due diligence on the business relationship and monitoring for suspicious activities. | The Bank’s CDD measures must include: (a) verifying customer identity, (b) identifying beneficial owners, (c) understanding the nature/purpose of the business, (d) knowing the source of funds, and (e) ongoing monitoring for suspicious activities. | Failure to execute full CDD increases exposure to money laundering, terrorist financing, and regulatory sanctions. | High | High | Compliance / KYC / Relationship Managers | Full KYC onboarding checklist including BO, source of funds, and business purpose fields; integrated AML monitoring system. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 6 (a) | Customer identification | FIs shall identify their customer (whether permanent or occasional,and whether natural or legal persons or legal arrangements) and obtain the following information — (a) for Individuals — (i) legal name and any other names used (such as maiden name), (ii) permanent address (full physical address), (iii) residential address (where the customer can be located), (iv) telephone number, e-mail address and social media handle, (v) date and place of birth, (vi) Bank Verification Number (BVN), (vii) Tax Identification Number (TIN), (viii) nationality, (ix) occupation, public position held and name of employer, (x) an official personal identification number or other unique identifier contained in an unexpired document issued by a government agency, that bears a name, photograph and signature of the customer such as a passport, national identification card, residence permit, social security records or drivers’ license, (xi) type of account and nature of the banking relationship, and (xii) signature, and (xiii) politically exposed persons (PEPs) status ; | The Bank must collect and verify full identification information for every individual customer, whether they are permanent or occasional. This applies to all natural persons opening an account or conducting transactions. The required information includes: 1. Full legal name and any other names used (e.g., maiden name) 2. Permanent and residential address 3. Telephone number, email address, and social media handle 4. Date and place of birth 5. Bank Verification Number (BVN) 6. Tax Identification Number (TIN) 7. Nationality 8. Occupation, public position held, and employer name 9. A valid government-issued ID with photo, name, and signature (e.g., passport, driver’s license, national ID) 10. Type of account and purpose of the banking relationship 11. Customer’s signature 12. Politically Exposed Person (PEP) status  The Bank must ensure that all the above information is properly documented and verified during account opening or onboarding, in compliance with KYC and AML/CFT requirements | Incomplete or unverified identity data could lead to onboarding of high-risk or illicit customers, facilitating ML/TF/PF. | High | High | KYC Unit / Branch Operations / Compliance | KYC checklist with mandatory fields, ID validation tools, BVN/TIN verification portals | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 6 (b) | Customer identification | (b) for legal persons and legal arrangements — (i) name of institution, (ii) mailing address, (iii) e-mail and social media address, (iv) phone numbers, (v) registration number, (vi) registered address, (vii) business address, (viii) valid identification, such as tax identification number, (ix) nature and purpose of business or activities, (x) certified true copy of documentary evidence confirming legal existence such as certificate of incorporation, (xi) certified true copy of memorandum and articles of association or other similar documents, (xii) certified true copy of the list of directors and shareholders or similar documents, (xiii) board resolution to open the account, (xiv) identification of those who have authority to operate the account, (xv) legal documents indicating persons exercising control or significant influence over the legal persons and legal arrangement’s assets, (xvi) valid means of identification of persons mentioned in subparagraph (xv) of this paragraph, (xvii) names and identification documents of the relevant persons having a senior management position in the legal persons and legal arrangements, and (xviii) the original documents referred to in subparagraphs (x) to (xiv) of this paragraph, shall be sighted and documented. | The Bank must collect and verify detailed information before opening an account for any legal entity or legal arrangement (e.g., companies, partnerships, NGOs, trusts). The following information must be obtained and documented: 1. Name of the institution or entity 2. Mailing address 3. Email address and social media handle 4. Phone numbers 5. Corporate registration number 6. Registered address 7. Business/operational address 8. Valid legal identifier, such as a Tax Identification Number (TIN) 9. Nature and purpose of the business or legal activity 10. Certified true copy of incorporation documents (e.g., certificate of incorporation) 11. Certified true copy of the memorandum and articles of association (or similar founding documents) 12. Certified true copy of the list of directors and shareholders (or similar documentation) 13. Board resolution authorizing the opening of the account 14. Identification of authorized signatories (those allowed to operate the account) 15. Legal documents identifying persons who control or influence the entity’s assets (e.g., beneficial owners, trustees) 16. Valid ID documents for those individuals identified in item 15 17. Names and valid ID documents of all individuals in senior management positions 18. The Bank must sight and retain the original versions of all documents listed in items 10–14.  All this information must be collected, verified, and securely documented to establish the legitimacy, control structure, and risk profile of the legal entity. This ensures compliance with CBN’s Know Your Customer (KYC), AML, and CFT requirements. | Failure to identify the true owners or controllers of legal entities may enable shell companies or front entities to facilitate ML/TF/PF. | High | Very High | Compliance / Legal / KYC / Corporate Banking | CDD checklist, documentation requirements, company registry cross-check, physical sighting of documents | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 7 (1) | Verification of customer identity | —(1) FIs shall verify the identity of customers and BOs using reliable, independent source documents, data or information (identification data). | The Bank must confirm the identity of both the customer and any beneficial owners by collecting and verifying documents, data, or information from trustworthy and independent source | False identity use; regulatory non-compliance | Medium | High | Compliance / Ops Team | ID verification using BVN/NIMC, utility bill, passport, CAC docs, KYC database | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 7 (2a) | Verification of customer identity | (2) FIs shall verify the identity of individuals by confirming the — (a) date of birth from a valid official document, such as birth certificate, passport, identity card and national or social security records ; Verification of customer identity | The Bank must confirm the customer’s date of birth using valid documents such as a birth certificate, passport, national ID card, or any government-issued document that clearly shows the date of birth. | Incorrect DOB entry; fake identity; weak KYC process | Low | Medium | Operations | Collect and record birth documents; cross-check with BVN/NIMC | Very Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Reg. 7 (2b) | Verification of customer identity | (b) residential address through physical visitation and use of other sources, including utility bill, tax assessment, bank statement, or letter from a public authority ; | The Bank must confirm the customer’s current residential address by physically visiting the address or checking utility bills, tax documents, bank statements, or a letter from a public authority. | Fake address or unverifiable customer location | Medium | High | Field Verification | Field visit, utility bill check, verification against external address database | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 7 (2c) | Verification of customer identity | (c) contact details provided by the customer through positive feedback from phone call, email or physical letter to the residential address ; | The Bank must verify the phone number, email, or postal address provided by the customer by contacting them directly through a call, email, or a physical letter sent to the address. | Inability to contact customer; invalid contact details | Medium | Medium | Customer Service | Phone call confirmation, email bounce-back checks, postal mail record | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Reg. 7 (2d) | Verification of customer identity | (d) validity of the official documentation provided through certification by an authorized person such as embassy official, notary public (in the case of foreign nationals) ; and | The Bank must ensure that any official documents submitted, especially by foreign customers, are certified by a recognized authority such as an embassy official | Forged documentation from foreign customers | Medium | High | Compliance | Accept only embassy/notary-certified documents; document and archive verification | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 7 (2e) | Verification of customer identity | (e) phone numbers, particularly for wallet providers, through independent process, including validation against the NCC database or geo-mapping. | The Bank must confirm that the customer’s phone number is valid using independent verification methods such as checking against the NCC database | Invalid/fraudulent phone numbers; ghost wallet accounts | Medium | High | IT / Risk | API integration with NCC; Phone verification process during onboarding | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 7 (3a) | Verification of customer identity | (3) FIs shall verify the identity of a legal person or legal arrangement by — (a) undertaking search on public registry or database such as CAC or similar database, other commercial enquiries and through any other available sources of information to confirm — (i) the existence of the legal person or legal arrangement, (ii) whether the legal person or legal arrangement has not been, or is not in the process of being dissolved, struck off, wound up or terminated, (iii) the information on the directors and shareholders or persons or entities holding similar positions, including their PEP status, (iv) information on person with significant control, and (v) information on BO, and its PEP status ; | The Bank must verify the identity of a corporate or legal customer by conducting a search on public registries (like CAC) or similar databases. This verification must confirm: • That the entity exists and is not in the process of being dissolved or wound up; • The identity of its directors and shareholders, including if they are politically exposed persons (PEPs); • The persons with significant control; • The beneficial owners (BOs) and whether they are PEPs. | Shell companies; Unverified BOs; Hidden PEPs | High | High | Compliance / Legal | CAC verification; PEP screening; BO declaration; documentation and registry reports | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 7 (3b) | Verification of customer identity | (b) reviewing a copy of the latest annual report, audited accounts or relevant financial statement, where applicable ; | The bank should collect and review the most recent financial documents of the customer (e.g., annual report or audited statements), especially where required for risk profiling or verification of financial standing. | Inability to assess financial health; misrepresentation of income level | Medium | High | Credit / Compliance | Require financial statement during onboarding for corporate accounts | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 7 (3c) | Verification of customer identity | (c) reviewing a copy of the board resolution or applicable resolution ; | The bank must request and examine a valid board resolution or similar authorization that confirms the legal entity’s intent to open and operate an account or engage in a business relationship. | Unauthorized account opening; misrepresentation of authority | Medium | High | Legal / Compliance | Mandatory submission of board resolution for corporate onboarding | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 7 (3d) | Verification of customer identity | (d) utilizing the documentation from a reliable independent source proving the name, form and current existence of the customer ; | The bank should verify the customer's legal existence and structure using credible third-party sources (e.g., CAC certificate, business license, court registration). | Dealings with non-existent/fake companies | Medium | High | Compliance | Mandatory CAC/doc verification; archive checks in customer file | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 7 (3e) | Verification of customer identity | (e) utilizing an independent information verification process, such as accessing public and private databases ; | The bank must independently confirm the customer's information by consulting databases like CAC, tax authority, or private credit registries. | Undetected false information; onboarding high-risk entities | Medium | High | Risk / IT / Compliance | Access CAC, FIRS, SCUML, and credit registry for independent verification | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 7 (3f) | Verification of customer identity | (f ) obtaining prior bank references, where applicable ; | Where relevant, the bank should obtain a reference letter or history from a previous bank that had a relationship with the customer. | High-risk customer not detected; lack of credit behavior history | Low | Medium | Credit / Relationship Mgt | Request bank reference for new business customers over threshold | Very Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Reg. 7 (3g) | Verification of customer identity | (g) visiting the entity ; and | The bank should physically visit the business premises of the customer to verify its existence and operations, particularly for medium/high-risk accounts. | Fake business front; onboarding of ghost companies | Medium | High | Field Ops / Compliance | Field visit logbook; signed inspection report; photographic evidence | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 7 (3h) | Verification of customer identity | (h) confirming the contact details provided through phone call, email and physical letter to the business address. | The bank must confirm that the contact information provided by the customer is active and correct, using at least one independent channel. | Invalid or unreachable contact details; inability to trace customer | Medium | Medium | Customer Service / Onboarding | Perform contact confirmation using 2-factor methods (e.g., call + letter) | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Reg. 8 (a) | Identification and verification of signatories, directors, and  beneficial owners of legal persons and legal arrangements | When conducting CDD measures in relation to customers that are legal persons or legal arrangements, FIs shall — (a) understand the ownership and control structure ; | The Bank must obtain a clear understanding of who owns, controls, or has significant influence over a company or legal arrangement, including the structure of ownership and decision-making hierarchy. | Hidden beneficial owners; exposure to shell companies | Medium | High | Compliance / Onboarding | Request detailed organogram, shareholding structure, and legal formation documents | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 8 (b) | Identification and verification of signatories, directors, and  beneficial owners of legal persons and legal arrangements | (b) at the time of establishing new relationships or whenever there is a change in ownership, identify and verify the identity of the BOs who exercise control through ownership or controlling interest, including voting rights ; | The Bank must identify and verify the individuals who own or control the customer at account opening or when there's a change in ownership. This includes verifying those with voting rights or influence. | Failure to identify high-risk or sanctioned BOs | Medium | High | Compliance / KYC | Mandatory BO declaration form + ID verification | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 8 (c) | Identification and verification of signatories, directors, and  beneficial owners of legal persons and legal arrangements | (c) subject all account signatories, Directors and BOs to the requirements for identification and verification of individuals provided in regulations 6 and 7 of these Regulations ; | The Bank must carry out the full identity verification steps (as required under Regs 6 and 7) for all individuals who are account signatories, directors, or beneficial owners of legal entities before onboarding them | Onboarding of unauthenticated individuals; regulatory non-compliance | Medium | High | KYC / Compliance | Require full Reg. 6 & 7-compliant documents from each person | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 8 (d) | Identification and verification of signatories, directors, and  beneficial owners of legal persons and legal arrangements | (d) conduct status enquiry from CRMS and at least two Credit Bureaux to determine their credit status ; | The Bank must check the credit status of account signatories, directors, and beneficial owners by querying the CRMS and at least two licensed credit bureaus before establishing or continuing a relationship. | Relationship with high-risk or indebted individuals | Medium | Medium | Credit Risk / Compliance | Check CRMS, CRC Credit Bureau, and one other licensed bureau before onboarding | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Reg. 8 (e) | Identification and verification of signatories, directors, and  beneficial owners of legal persons and legal arrangements | (e) ascertain that the customer is not banned from the use of clearing system due to issuance of dud cheque ; and | The Bank must confirm that the customer has not been blacklisted or restricted from using the clearing system as a result of issuing dud (bounced) cheques. | Operational risk from customers with history of dud cheques | Medium | Medium | Operations / Compliance | Verify against cheque system blacklist or relevant CBN database | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Reg. 9 (1) | Authority of Third Party | (1) FIs shall verify — (a) that any person purporting to act on behalf of a customer is so authorized ; and (b) the identity of the person purporting to act on behalf of a customer. | The bank must confirm that anyone claiming to act on behalf of a customer has been properly authorized to do so and must verify the person’s identity. | Fraudulent access to account or misrepresentation | Medium | High | Compliance / Legal | Request power of attorney or board resolution + confirm with customer and external validation | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 9 (2) | Authority of Third Party | (2) The verification referred to in subregulation (1) of this regulation shall be done through confirmation from the customer the third party is purporting to represent and from other independent sources. | The bank must confirm the third party’s authority both by contacting the customer directly and through other independent sources. | False representation or manipulation of authority. | Medium | High | Compliance | Call-back confirmations, external verification (e.g., board resolution, POA). | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 10 (1) | Nature and Purpose of Business | (1) FIs shall understand and obtain sufficient information on the nature and purpose of the business that its customer intends to undertake, including expected or predictable patterns of transactions. | The bank must understand what the customer’s business is, why they are opening the account, and what kinds of transactions are expected. | Misuse of account for illegal purposes; non-alignment with business profile | Medium | High | Relationship Manager / KYC | Capture business description, expected volume and frequency of transactions during onboarding | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 10 (2) | Nature and Purpose of Business | (2) FIs shall be at alert to circumstances that may indicate any significant changes in the nature of a business or its ownership | The bank must watch out for and investigate any major changes in the customer’s business activities or ownership. | ML/TF risks may increase if changes go unnoticed. | Medium | High | Compliance / Transaction Monitoring | Ongoing transaction reviews; periodic profile reviews. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 11 (1) | Understanding sources of funds | (1) FIs shall understand and obtain sufficient information on the source of funds into the customer’s account. | The bank must know where the money coming into the customer’s account is coming from and gather enough information to understand it clearly. | Unexplained wealth or money laundering through the account | High | High | KYC / Compliance | Mandatory source of wealth and income disclosure + document review | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 11 (2) | Understanding sources of funds | (2) The information to be obtained before the commencement of the relationship shall include— (a) details of occupation, employment or business activities and sources of wealth and income ; and (b) expected origin of the funds to be used in the operation of the account during the relationship. | Before opening an account, the bank must collect information about: - The customer’s job, business, or how they earn their money (source of wealth and income); and - Where the money that will be used in the account is expected to come from. | Risk of onboarding customers with unexplained or suspicious sources of funds. | Medium | High | Relationship Managers / Compliance | Mandatory CDD form and pre-account-opening KYC checks. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 12 (1) | Ongoing Due Diligence | (1) FIs shall conduct ongoing due diligence on a business relationship and scrutinize transactions undertaken throughout the course of the relationship to ensure that the transactions being conducted are consistent with the — (a) FI’s knowledge of the customer ; (b) customer’s business and risk profile ; and (c) source of funds. | The bank must continuously monitor customer transactions to ensure they match what it knows about the customer’s identity, business, risk profile, and the source of their funds. | Undetected suspicious activity; outdated customer data | High | High | AML Compliance / Operations | Ongoing monitoring using automated systems; periodic KYC reviews | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | 12 (2) | Ongoing Due Diligence | (2) FIs shall take reasonable steps to keep the information up-to-date, and as the need arises, including where an existing customer opens a new account. | The bank must take reasonable steps to keep customer information updated, especially when the customer opens a new account or when changes occur. | Risk of outdated customer profiles, leading to regulatory and financial crime exposure. | Medium | Medium | Relationship Managers / Branch Operations | Periodic KYC refresh cycles; trigger-based CDD reviews. | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Reg. 13 (1) | Application of CDD to existing customers | (1) FIs shall apply CDD requirements to existing customers on the basis of materiality and risk and continue to conduct due diligence on such existing relationship at appropriate times. | The bank must apply customer due diligence (CDD) to existing customers based on the risk level and continue to monitor the relationship as necessary. | Financial crime risk due to outdated or inaccurate customer information | Medium | High | Compliance / Relationship Teams | Periodic KYC review, event-based trigger alerts | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 13 (2) | Application of CDD to existing customers | (2) The appropriate time to conduct CDD for existing customers include, but not limited to when — (a) transaction of significant value or an unusual transaction occurs ; (b) there is significant change in the customer’s profile ; (c) there is a material change in the way that the account is operated ; or (d) the FIs become aware that it lacks sufficient information about an existing customer. | The bank must review and update customer due diligence (CDD) when: - There’s a large or unusual transaction; - The customer’s personal or business information changes significantly; - The way the account is being used changes in a major way; or - The bank discovers it doesn’t have enough information about the customer | Failure to detect red flags due to outdated or incomplete customer records. | High | High | Compliance / Relationship Managers | Transaction monitoring rules; review alerts trigger CDD refresh. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 18 (1) | Reliance on identification and verification already performed | (1) FIs may rely on the identification and verification steps that it had previously undertaken, unless it has doubts about the veracity of that information or where there is a material change in the circumstances or profile of the customer. | The bank can rely on customer identification and verification already completed unless: - There is a reason to doubt the accuracy of the information; or - The customer’s situation or profile has significantly changed. | Relying on outdated/inaccurate data leading to non-compliance or financial crime exposure | Medium | High | Compliance / Risk | Trigger alerts when suspicious activity or deviation from known profile is observed | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 18 (2) | Reliance on identification and verification already performed | (2) The situations that may lead a FI to have doubts about the veracity of an information include where there is a — (a) suspicion of ML, TF or PF in relation to that customer ; or (b) material change in the way that the customer’s account is operated, which is not consistent with the customer’s business profile. | The bank must re-verify customer identity if: - There is suspicion of money laundering, terrorist financing, or proliferation financing; or - The way the account is being used changes significantly and does not match the customer’s known business profile. | Risk of continuing relationship with a customer under suspicion or whose activities no longer match known profile. | High | High | AML Compliance / Branch Staff | Escalation to AML Unit; trigger EDD upon suspicion. | Medium | High |
|  |  |  | Reg. 20 (1a) | Reliance on third party | (1) In addition to the provisions of regulation 27 of the CBN AML, CFT and CPF Regulations where a FI relies on other FIs and DNFBPs to conduct its CDD, it shall — (a) immediately obtain the necessary information concerning the identification and verification of the customer and BO and the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship ; | The Bank must ensure that it immediately gets full CDD information from the third party, including customer ID, beneficial owner details, and purpose of the business relationship. | Incomplete CDD due to third-party delays or data gaps | Medium | High | Compliance / Legal | Service-level agreement (SLA) with third parties ensuring immediate info transfer | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 20 (1b) | Reliance on third party | (b) take adequate steps to satisfy itself that copies of identification data and other relevant documentation relating to the CDD requirements is going to be made available from the third party upon request without delay ; | The Bank must take steps to confirm that it can quickly retrieve all CDD documentation from the third party when needed. | Delay in obtaining KYC records when required (e.g., for audit or investigation) | Medium | Medium | Compliance / Onboarding | Written assurance from third party + test access to documents | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Reg. 20 (1c) | Reliance on third party | (c) satisfy itself that the third party is regulated, supervised or monitored for, and has measures in place for compliance with, the CDD and record keeping requirements set out in these Regulations and the CBN AML, CFT and CPF Regulations ; and | The Bank must ensure the third party is properly regulated, supervised, and has effective CDD and recordkeeping practices aligned with regulations. | Using non-compliant third parties for KYC increases exposure to legal and operational risk | Medium | High | Compliance / Vendor Management | Third-party AML/CFT due diligence and certification review | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 20 (1d) | Reliance on third party | (d) ensure that adequate KYC provisions are applied to the third party in order to obtain account information for competent authorities. | The Bank must ensure that the third party applies adequate KYC policies to make customer/account information available to authorities. | Non-compliance with regulatory data requests due to poor third-party controls | Medium | High | Compliance / Legal | Assess third-party KYC frameworks during onboarding | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 20 (2) | Reliance on third party | (2) Notwithstanding the conditions specified in sub-regulation (1) (a) to (d) of this regulation, the ultimate responsibility for customer identification and verification shall be with the FI relying on the third party. | The Bank remains fully responsible for ensuring proper customer identification, even when it relies on a third party to conduct due diligence. | Liability for AML/CFT breaches due to over-reliance on third parties | Medium | High | Compliance / Risk | Final CDD review and approval by Bank compliance | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 21 (1) | Timing of Verification | (1) FIs shall obtain and verify the identity of the customer, beneficialowner and occasional customers before or during the course of establishing a business relationship or conducting transactions for them. | The Bank must identify and verify the customer, BO, or occasional customer before or while the relationship is being set up or a transaction is being conducted. | Onboarding unverified customers exposes bank to criminal risk and regulatory breach | Medium | High | Operations / Onboarding | Pre-onboarding checklist and real-time ID verification | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 21 (2) | Timing of Verification | (2) FIs are permitted to complete the verification of the identity of the customer and BO following the establishment of the business based on criteria set out in regulation 22 of the CBN AML, CFT and CPF Regulations. | The Bank may complete verification after account opening, but only if it meets the exception conditions defined in Regulation 22 of the CBN AML, CFT and CPF Regulations. | Delay in verification may result in servicing high-risk customers temporarily | Medium | Medium | Compliance / Risk | Conditional verification workflow with time-limited exceptions | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Reg. 22 (1a) | Tipping off | (1) Where a FI suspects that a transaction relates to ML, TF or PF and it believes that performing the CDD process may tip-off the customer, it shall— (a) not pursue the CDD process ; and | Do not continue CDD if you think doing so could alert the customer involved in a suspicious transaction. | Risk of tipping off a suspect, interfering with an investigation | Medium | High | Compliance / Staff | Employee STR decision-making training and escalation protocol | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg 22 (2) | Tipping off | (2) FIs shall ensure that their employees are aware of, and sensitive to, the issues referred to in subregulation (1) of this regulation when conducting CDD. | Ensure employee training on how to avoid tipping off during CDD and when STRs are being considered. | Inadvertent tipping off may alert customers under investigation. | Medium | High | Compliance / AML Dept | Mandatory periodic AML training with real-case examples on tipping off. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg 23 (a) | Record-Keeping | In addition to the provisions of regulation 35 of the CBN AML, CFT and CPF Regulations, FIs shall — (a) keep all records obtained through CDD measures, account files and business correspondence, and results of any analysis undertaken, either in electronic or written form for at least five years following the termination or cessation of the business relationship or after the date of the occasional transaction ; and | The Bank must retain all customer due diligence (CDD) records, account files, correspondence, and analysis (in physical or digital format) for at least five (5) years after the account is closed or after any one-off transaction. | Non-compliance could lead to sanctions and loss of historical audit trail. | Low | High | Operations / Compliance | Automated archiving system with date stamps; periodic backup to secure servers. | Very Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg 23 (b) | Record-Keeping | (b) ensure that documents, data or information collected under the CDD process is kept up-to-date and relevant, by undertaking reviews of existing records of customers as stipulated below or whenever the need arises, | The Bank must regularly review and update customer information collected during the CDD (Customer Due Diligence) process to ensure it remains accurate and relevant. | Outdated information could lead to failure in risk detection and STR delays. | Medium | High | Compliance / Business Units | Trigger-based update alerts in the system; standard review policy per risk rating. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg 23 (b(i)) | Record-Keeping | (i) for high risk customers, every 12months, | The Bank must review and update information for high-risk customers at least once every 12 months. | Regulatory breach or exposure due to outdated high-risk profiles. | Medium | High | Compliance / RM | Risk engine to flag due reviews; quarterly review calendar; mandatory update tracking. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 23 (b(ii)) | Record-Keeping | (ii) for medium risk customers, every 18months, and | The Bank must review and update information for medium-risk customers at least once every 18 months. | Delays or missed reviews may cause non-compliance or reputational risks. | Medium | Medium | Compliance / RM | CRM-based tracking system for customer review cycles. | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Reg. 23 (b(iii)) | Record-Keeping | (iii) for low risk customers, every 3years. | The Bank  must review and update information for low-risk customers at least once every 3 years. | Potential for outdated data on long-standing customers. | Low | Medium | Compliance / RM | System-based review triggers; periodic review logs. | Very Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Reg. 24 | Additional Measures for Special Customers and businesses | In addition to identification documentations listed in regulation 6 of these Regulations, additional measures on some specific customers and businesses as provided under this Part shall apply | The Bank must apply extra identification and verification steps to certain high-risk customers or businesses, beyond what is already required under Regulation 6. These additional steps are specified in the next part of the regulation. | Failure to apply enhanced measures may result in onboarding high-risk entities with insufficient controls, exposing the bank to financial crime or regulatory breach. | Medium | High | Compliance / Business Units | Risk-based Customer Acceptance Policy; Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) Checklist; Compliance oversight during onboarding. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 25 (1) | External and Non-Resident Non-Nigerians Accounts | (1) In line with Memorandum 17 of the CBN Foreign Exchange Manual, FI shall satisfy itself that a customer is permanently resident outside Nigeria when establishing a banking relationship for external and non-resident non-Nigerian customers. | The bank must ensure that the customer truly lives permanently outside Nigeria before opening an account for them. | Risk of opening external accounts for ineligible or misrepresented individuals. | Medium | High | Compliance / Operations | Review of valid foreign residential documentation; verification through embassy or other reputable institution. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 25 (2) | External and Non-Resident Non-Nigerians Accounts | (2) The following are eligible to open external accounts— (a) Embassies; (b) High Commissions; (c) Legations or consulates; (d) career and established members of Embassies, High Commissions, and Legation or Consulates; and (e) other international organisations recognized and accorded diplomatic status and their expatriate officials, such as African Union, United Nations or Commonwealth of Nations. | The bank may open external (non-resident) accounts only for the following eligible persons or entities: - Embassies - High Commissions - Legations or Consulates - Official, established members of diplomatic missions (e.g., Embassy or Consulate staff) - Recognized international organizations with diplomatic status (e.g., African Union, United Nations, Commonwealth) and their expatriate officials | Opening accounts for ineligible individuals or organizations, leading to regulatory breach. | Low | High | Compliance / Legal | Maintain updated list of eligible entities; require documentary proof of diplomatic status. | Very Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 25 (3) | External and Non-Resident Non-Nigerians Accounts | (3) FIs shall obtain the following documentation for external accounts— (a) applicant’s letter of request, showing official position or status and the probable duration of stay in Nigeria; (b) letter of introduction from the relevant Diplomatic Mission or International Organisation certifying the accredited status of the applicant; and (c) relevant pages of the applicant’s international passport. | The Bank must collect: - A written request from the customer that states their role and how long they’ll be in Nigeria; - An introduction letter from their embassy or international organization confirming who they are; - Passport pages that show identity and visa/travel details. | Risk of incomplete or falsified documentation, which may lead to unauthorized account opening. | Medium | High | Branch Operations / Compliance | Document checklist; dual-review process before onboarding; verify letterhead authenticity. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 25 (4) | External and Non-Resident Non-Nigerians Accounts | (4) The following are eligible to open non-resident accounts— (a) overseas correspondence and examination bodies; (b) foreign companies executing approved contracts in Nigeria; and (c) foreign professional bodies. | The bank must only open non-resident accounts for these categories: • Overseas correspondence and examination bodies • Foreign companies with approved contracts in Nigeria • Foreign professional bodies. | Opening accounts for ineligible entities or with incomplete documentation could enable fraud, illegal operations, or regulatory breaches. | Medium | High | Retail / Corporate / Intl Desk | Defined document checklist tailored to customer category; review and approval by both onboarding and Compliance teams before account activation. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 25 (5a) | External and Non-Resident Non-Nigerians Accounts | (5) FIs shall obtain the following documentation for non-resident accounts— (a) for overseas correspondence and examination bodies, letters of request from applicant, memorandum and articles of the overseas company, letter of accreditation from the Federal Ministry of Education, and Power of Attorney to the Agent in Nigeria; | The bank must collect all 4 documents before opening an account for overseas correspondence/exam bodies. No exceptions. | Risk of onboarding unverified foreign educational bodies, leading to regulatory breaches or fraud. | Medium | High | Branch Ops / Compliance | Document checklist and validation before account opening. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 25 (5b) | External and Non-Resident Non-Nigerians Accounts | (b) for foreign companies executing approved contracts in Nigeria, contract document, letter of request from applicant, and Memorandum and Articles of Association of the company; and | The bank must confirm contract approval status and ensure all documents are submitted and verified before account opening. | Risk of enabling money laundering or illegal inflows via sham contracts or entities. | High | High | Business Development / Compliance | Validate with contract award authorities and verify company documents. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 25 (5c) | External and Non-Resident Non-Nigerians Accounts | (c) for foreign professional bodies, letters of request from applicant, memorandum and articles of the overseas company, letter of accreditation from the Federal Ministry of Education, Power of Attorney to the Agent in Nigeria and letter of certification from a relevant body in Nigeria. | The bank must confirm the professional body's legitimacy and accreditation, and gather all 5 documents before onboarding. | Risk of opening accounts for fake or unauthorized foreign institutions. | Medium | High | Compliance / KYC Desk | Mandatory document verification with relevant Nigerian bodies. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 25 (6a) | External and Non-Resident Non-Nigerians Accounts | (6) FIs shall— (a) obtain and verify identification directly from the customer’s embassy or through a reputable FI in the applicant’s home country or country of residence, provided that particular care shall be taken when relying on identification evidence obtained from other countries | The Bnak must get the applicant’s ID either from their embassy or a trusted bank in their home/residence country. Be cautious when using foreign documents. | Risk of onboarding impersonated or fraudulent non-resident customers using unverifiable or forged documentation. | Medium | High | Compliance / Branch Operations | Use of an onboarding checklist for non-resident customers; notarization requirement; due diligence standards for accepting foreign documentation; maintain approved list of foreign FIs and embassies; document validation steps. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 25 (6b) | External and Non-Resident Non-Nigerians Accounts | (b) obtain and verify separate evidence of an applicant’s permanent residential address which shall be notarized; and | The Bank must collect a notarized document confirming the applicant's home address abroad. | Risk of identity fraud or impersonation if address is falsified. | Medium | High | Account Officer / Compliance | Require notarized address documentation before onboarding. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 25 (6c) | External and Non-Resident Non-Nigerians Accounts | (c) obtain additional comfort by confirming the customer’s identity and address from a reputable credit institution in the customer’s home country, where necessary | When needed, The Bank should cross-check the applicant’s ID and address with a trusted financial institution in the applicant’s country. | Risk of relying solely on customer-submitted documents which may be fraudulent. | Medium | High | Compliance Unit | Use reputable foreign banks or credit bureaus to verify identity/address. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 25 (9) | External and Non-Resident Non-Nigerians Accounts | (9) Where approvals are granted for individuals (including directors of legal persons) that are non-Nigerian and non-resident, the requirements of regulations 6 and 7 of these Regulations shall apply and the appropriate category of BVN as relates to non-resident individuals shall apply. | When non-Nigerian, non-resident individuals (including directors of companies) are approved for accounts, The Bank must follow Regulations 6 and 7 (general CDD/KYC obligations) and apply the appropriate BVN category for non-resident individuals. | Inadequate due diligence on non-resident individuals could lead to ML/TF exposure, regulatory breaches, or reputational harm. | Medium | High | Compliance / Branch Ops | Use of onboarding checklist for non-resident individuals; ensure proper CDD under Regs 6 & 7; validate BVN as per non-resident classification. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg, 26 (1) | Non-Resident Nigerians | (1) FIs shall obtain and verify applicant’s name, date of birth and permanent residential address (in host country) directly through a reputable Credit Institution or FI in the applicant’s country of residence or a correspondent bank, provided that particular care shall be taken when relying on identification evidence obtained from other countries. | The Bank must obtain and verify the name, date of birth, and permanent residential address (in the host country) of non-resident Nigerian applicants.  This should be done through a reputable Credit Institution, financial institution, or correspondent bank in the applicant's country of residence.  The Bank must exercise extra caution when using foreign-sourced identification evidence. | Weak verification of identity or source of funds may enable fraud, ML/TF, or misuse of the banking system. | Medium | High | Compliance / Branch Ops | Onboarding procedure includes mandatory verification with reputable foreign FI or correspondent bank and mandatory documentation of source of funds as per the regulation. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg, 26 (2) | Non-Resident Nigerians | (2) FIs shall validate the source of funds by obtaining identification issued by employer, payslips or statements of accounts from a bank in the country of residence. | The bank must confirm where the applicant’s money is coming from by collecting: - A valid ID issued by the applicant’s employer, - Recent payslips, or - Bank statements from the applicant’s financial institution in their country of residence. | Risk of onboarding individuals with illicit or unverifiable income. | Medium | High | Account Officer / KYC Desk | Require one or more of the listed documents for validation of source of funds. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 27 (1) | Resident Non-Nigerians | (1) FIs shall, as part of CDD measures, obtain and verify the valid Resident Permit of resident non-Nigerians. | The bank must collect and verify a valid Resident Permit from any non-Nigerian applying to open an account or use banking services in Nigeria. | Failure to verify residency or identity may result in onboarding illegal migrants or impersonators. | Medium | High | Compliance / Branch Ops | Include Resident Permit verification in onboarding checklist. Require notarized home country address for new arrivals. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 27 (2) | Resident Non-Nigerians | (2) Where a foreign national has recently arrived in Nigeria, the residential address in the applicant’s home country shall be notarized. | If the foreign national has just arrived in Nigeria, the bank must collect a notarized proof of their home-country residential address. | Risk of false identity or unverifiable residential information being used for account creation. | Medium | High | Account Officer / Onboarding Officer | Mandatory submission of notarized foreign address prior to account activation. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 28 (1) | Correspondent Banking Relationship | (1) Transactions conducted through correspondent relationships shall be managed in accordance with a risk-based approach. | The bank must manage all correspondent banking relationships using a risk-based approach to identify and respond to potential money laundering or terrorism financing risks. | Risk of exposure to money laundering, terrorist financing, or dealing with shell banks through unregulated or high-risk correspondent relationships. | Medium | High | Compliance / Risk / Operations | - Risk-based due diligence - Verification of AML regulation status - Internal AML/KYC policy checks - Recordkeeping - Staff training - STR reporting - Termination of risky relationships | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 28 (2) | Correspondent Banking Relationship | (2) Due diligence procedures shall be established to ascertain whether or not the correspondent bank or the counter-party is itself regulated for prevention of ML, TF or PF, and where regulated, the correspondent respondent shall verify the identity of its customers in accordance with FATF standards. | Before entering into a correspondent banking relationship, the bank must confirm that the correspondent bank is regulated for AML/CFT, and ensure it verifies the identity of its own customers using FATF standards. | Entering into a relationship with an unregulated or non-compliant correspondent bank may expose the bank to ML/TF/PF risks, enforcement penalties, or reputational damage. | Medium | High | Compliance / Correspondent Banking Unit | Perform and document AML/CFT checks on counterparties; require CDD/EDD reports from correspondents; review FATF alignment | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 28 (3) | Correspondent Banking Relationship | (3) Where the correspondent bank or the counter-party is itself unregulated, additional due diligence shall be required to ascertain and assess the correspondent or respondent’s internal policy for prevention of ML, TF or PF and KYC procedures. | If the correspondent bank is unregulated, the bank must carry out enhanced due diligence to evaluate the bank’s internal AML/CFT and KYC policies before proceeding. | Partnering with an unregulated entity without strong internal controls could facilitate ML/TF/PF and result in regulatory sanctions or reputational harm. | High | High | Compliance / Risk / Legal / Business Unit | Perform enhanced due diligence, including review of internal AML/CFT and KYC policies, governance framework, and effectiveness of controls | Medium | High |
|  |  |  | Reg. 28 (5) | Correspondent Banking Relationship | (5) FIs shall maintain records and ensure that sufficient due diligence has been undertaken by the remitting bank on the underlying client and the origin of the funds in respect of the funds passed through their accounts. | The bank must keep proper records and ensure that the remitting bank has verified both the identity of the customer and the source of the funds before accepting any transaction. | Risk of processing illicit or unverified funds due to weak checks by the remitting institution, leading to AML/CFT breaches. | Medium | High | Operations / Compliance / Risk | Require remitting bank to provide evidence of KYC and source of funds checks before processing; periodic audits | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 28 (6) | Correspondent Banking Relationship | (6) FIs shall guard against establishing correspondent relationships with high risk foreign banks such as shell banks or with correspondent banks that permit their accounts to be used by such banks. | The bank must avoid establishing relationships with shell banks or any correspondent bank that allows access to shell banks or other high-risk institutions. | Risk of being used as a conduit for money laundering or terrorist financing through relationships with non-transparent or unregulated entities. | High | High | Compliance / Risk / Legal | Conduct thorough background checks; maintain a list of prohibited entities; update risk appetite criteria | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 28 (7) | Correspondent Banking Relationship | (7) Staff dealing with correspondent banking accounts shall be trained to recognize higher risk circumstances and be prepared to challenge the correspondents over irregular activity whether isolated transactions or trend and to submit a suspicious transaction report to the NFIU. | Staff handling correspondent accounts must be trained to detect high-risk activity, challenge unusual transactions, and report suspicious activity to the NFIU when needed. | Risk of undetected suspicious transactions due to untrained or unaware staff, leading to regulatory breaches or ML/TF exposure. | High | High | Compliance / AML Unit / Training Department | Targeted AML/CFT training for relevant staff; escalation procedures; STR reporting protocols | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 28 (8) | Correspondent Banking Relationship | (8) FIs shall terminate an account with a correspondent bank that fails to provide satisfactory answers to questions including confirming the identity of customers involved in unusual or suspicious circumstances. | The bank must immediately terminate any correspondent relationship if the other bank fails to provide clear information or refuses to confirm customer identities in suspicious circumstances. | Risk of continued exposure to ML/TF activity by maintaining relationships with non-cooperative or non-transparent banks. | Medium | High | AML/Compliance / Relationship Management | Clear policy and procedure for termination of non-compliant correspondent relationships; escalation protocol | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg, 29 | Trusts | Where the arrangement for a Foreign Trust or Foundation is opaque or information on the parties to the legal arrangements cannot be provided because it is incorporated in a jurisdiction (such as tax havens and off-shore financial centres) that makes it impractical to do so, the FI shall decline to open an account for the legal arrangement. | The bank must not open an account for a foreign trust or foundation if the ownership or control structure is unclear or if required information about the parties involved cannot be obtained due to the trust being based in a secrecy jurisdiction. | Risk of facilitating money laundering or tax evasion through untraceable legal arrangements or offshore secrecy structures. | High | High | Compliance / Legal | Prohibit onboarding of opaque foreign trusts; require full disclosure and verification of UBOs before onboarding. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 30 (1) | Blind Trusts | (1) FIs shall obtain and understand the Trust Agreement in a Blind Trust such that the grantor, settlor or trustor and beneficiary are identified. | The Bank must obtain and review the Blind Trust agreement and ensure they can identify the grantor (settlor/trustor) and the beneficiary. | Risk of concealment of beneficial ownership or PEP status. | Medium | High | Compliance / Account Opening Unit | Mandatory review and KYC of trust parties. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 30 (2) | Blind Trusts | (2) Where the grantor or beneficiary is a PEP, the FI shall apply EDD measures. | If the grantor or beneficiary is a Politically Exposed Person (PEP), the FI must apply Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD). | Risk of misuse of blind trusts by PEPs to hide assets. | Medium | High | Compliance | Apply full EDD process. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 30 (3) | Blind Trusts | (3) FIs shall understand the structure of a Blind Trust and determine whether it is revocable or irrevocable. | The Bank must understand how the Blind Trust is structured and whether it is revocable or irrevocable. | Risk of misclassification of trust type leading to weak controls. | Medium | Medium | Legal / Compliance | Legal review and documentation checklists. | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Reg. 30 (4) | Blind Trusts | (4) Where the customer is a Revocable Blind Trust, the FI shall apply EDD measures to the customer. | If it is a Revocable Blind Trust, the Bank must apply EDD to the customer. | Revocable trusts pose higher control risk. | Medium | High | Compliance | EDD workflow for revocable trusts. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 30 (5) | Blind Trusts | (5) FIs shall apply EDD where the BOs of a customer is a Blind Trust and identify the ultimate BO. | If the Beneficial Owner (BO) of a customer is a Blind Trust, the FI must apply EDD and identify the ultimate beneficial owner. | Risk of hidden ownership or shell arrangements. | High | High | Compliance / Legal | EDD checklist and ownership tracing. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 31 (1) | Nominee Directors and Nominee Shareholders | (1) FIs shall require customers that are legal persons to disclose nominee shareholders and nominee directors, if any. | The Bank must require companies or legal persons to disclose any nominee shareholders or nominee directors. | Hidden control or ownership risks. | High | High | Relationship Manager / KYC | Legal declaration forms and KYC procedures. | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 31 (2) | Nominee Directors and Nominee Shareholders | (2) FIs shall obtain and verify the identification of nominee directors and shareholders in a legal person or legal arrangement. | The Bank must obtain and verify the identity of nominee directors and shareholders involved in the legal person or legal arrangement. | Use of proxies for concealment. | Medium | High | KYC Unit | Mandatory ID check and documentary review. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 31 (3) | Nominee Directors and Nominee Shareholders | (3) FIs shall obtain information on the status of nominees and their nominator to company. | The Bank must collect information on the role and relationship between nominees and the person or entity that nominated them. | Concealed influence or control risk. | Medium | Medium | Relationship Officer / Compliance | Questionnaire on nominee-nominator links. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 32 (1) | Refugees or Asylum Seekers | 1) FIs shall use identification issued by the Nigerian Immigration Services or other recognizable government agency to render banking service to refugees or asylum seekers. | The Bank must use ID documents issued by the Nigerian Immigration Services or other recognized government agencies to provide banking services to refugees or asylum seekers. | Risk of insufficient KYC for displaced individuals. | Medium | High | Customer Service / KYC | Acceptable documents list and verification process. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 32 (2) | Refugees or Asylum Seekers | (2) FIs shall undertake additional monitoring procedures in respect of sub-regulation (1) of this regulation to ensure that the use of the account is consistent with the customer’s circumstances. | The Bank must carry out additional monitoring to ensure that account activity aligns with the refugee/asylum seeker’s expected financial behavior and profile. | Risk of account misuse for illegitimate activity. | Medium | High | Transaction Monitoring / KYC | Profile-based transaction alerts. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 33 (1a) | Foreign Students | (1) FIs shall, as part of CDD measures— (a) obtain and verify the valid Study Permit of prospective customers that are non-Nigerian students; | The bank must collect and verify a valid Study Permit from any non-Nigerian student applying for an account. | Risk of onboarding ineligible students or non-residents. | Medium | Medium | KYC / Onboarding Officer | Permit verification with NIS portal. | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Reg. 33 (1b) | Foreign Students | (b) obtain and verify identification directly from the customer’s embassy or through a reputable FI in the applicant’s home country or country of residence, provided that particular care shall be taken when relying on identification evidence obtained from other countries; and | The bank must confirm the student's identity using either: - Their embassy, or - A reputable bank/financial institution in the student’s home country or country of residence. Caution must be exercised when accepting documents from foreign sources. | Risk of identity fraud or reliance on unreliable foreign sources. | Medium | High | KYC / Compliance | Embassy confirmation or verification from trusted FIs. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 33 (2) | Foreign Students | (2) All accounts of foreign students shall, on completion of the applicant’s studies in Nigeria, be closed. | The student’s account must be closed once they complete their studies in Nigeria. | Dormant or inactive accounts can be misused post-graduation. | High | Medium | Relationship Manager / Compliance | Monitor study permit expiry or graduation confirmation. | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Reg. 34 (1) | Minors | (1) For banking relationships for a minor, FIs shall obtain the birth certificate and passport photo of the minor. | The bank must collect the birth certificate and a passport photo of the minor. | Incomplete identity verification of minors. | Medium | Medium | KYC / Account Opening | Document checklist and validation. | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Reg. 34 (2) | Minors | (2) FIs shall obtain and verify the identification and home address of the parent or guardian of a minor. | The bank must verify the identity and residential address of the minor’s parent or guardian. | Risk of onboarding under fraudulent guardianship. | Medium | High | KYC | Full KYC procedures for parent/guardian. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 34 (3) | Minors | (3) For accounts opened through a school-related scheme, the school shall provide the date of birth and permanent address of the minor and complete the standard account opening documentation on behalf of the minor. | If the account is opened through a school program, the school must provide: - The minor’s date of birth, - Permanent address, and - Complete all standard account opening forms on behalf of the minor. | Risk of poor documentation or misinformation from third parties (schools). | Medium | Medium | Relationship Officer / KYC | Pre-approval of school as onboarding partner. | Low | Low |
|  |  |  | Reg. 34 (4) | Minors | (4) FIs shall continuously monitor account of a minor to ensure that— (a) it is not used for the purposes of ML or TF; (b) the transactions on the account are in line with the purpose for which the account was opened; and (c) transactions on the account does not exceed a limit pre-determined by the FI in line with its established risk assessment criteria. | The bank must regularly review a minor’s account to ensure: - It is not being used for money laundering or terrorism financing, - Transactions match the stated purpose of the account, and - Transaction volume stays within pre-set limits based on the bank’s risk assessment. | Risk of misuse of minor accounts for illicit activities. | Medium | High | Transaction Monitoring / Compliance | Risk-based transaction limits and automated alerts. | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 35 (a) | Non-Face-to-Face Customers Identification | FIs shall— (a) in respect of a non-face-to-face customer, undertake additional measures or checks to supplement the documentary or electronic evidence to ensure that an applicant is who he/she claims to be; | For customers who open accounts remotely (without face-to-face interaction), the bank must conduct extra checks to confirm the person is who they claim to be, beyond standard document or electronic evidence. | Risk of impersonation or fake identity in remote onboarding. | High | High | Onboarding / Compliance | Enhanced verification steps (biometrics, OTP, selfie+ID) | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 35 (b) | Non-Face-to-Face Customers Identification | (b) apply the additional measures in paragraph (a) of this regulation, whether the applicant is resident in Nigeria or elsewhere, where the applicant is requesting a bank account or other product or service that offers money transmission or third party payments; | These additional verification steps must be applied whether the customer lives in Nigeria or abroad, if the service involves money transfers or third-party payments. | Regulatory exposure due to inconsistent due diligence across borders. | Medium | High | Onboarding / Product Ops | Standardized KYC protocol across channels | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg, 35 (c) | Non-Face-to-Face Customers Identification | (c) ensure that there is sufficient evidence either documentary or electronic in its procedures for identification and authentication of its customers, to confirm their address and personal identity and to undertake at least one additional check to guard against impersonation or fraud; | The bank must ensure there’s enough documentary or electronic proof of both: - The customer's identity, and their address. Additionally, at least one more security check must be done to guard against fraud or impersonation. | Risk of fraud or identity spoofing due to weak evidence standards. | High | High | Onboarding / Compliance | Multi-factor KYC, address proof validation, selfie-ID | Medium | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 35 (e) | Non-Face-to-Face Customers Identification | (e) undertake checks to ensure that, where reliance is placed on intermediaries to undertake the processing of applications on the customer’s behalf, the intermediaries are regulated for the prevention of ML, TF or PF and that the relevant identification procedures are applied; | If another party (an intermediary) is helping to open the account, the bank must confirm the intermediary is: - Regulated for anti-money laundering and terrorism financing, and has followed proper identification procedures. | Risk of poor due diligence or abuse when relying on unregulated third parties. | Medium | High | Business Partnerships / Compliance | Intermediary vetting, SLA for AML standards, regular audits | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 35 (f) | Non-Face-to-Face Customers Identification | (f) conduct regular monitoring of internet-based business or customers and where a significant proportion of the business is operated electronically, computerized monitoring systems or solutions that are designed to recognize unusual transactions and related patterns of transactions shall be put in place to recognize suspicious transactions; and | The bank must monitor internet-based businesses or online customers regularly, and if most of the business is online, it must use automated systems to detect suspicious or unusual transactions | Online customers can mask identities and engage in layering. | High | High | Transaction Monitoring / IT | Use of rule-based or AI transaction monitoring systems | Medium | High |
|  |  |  | Reg. 35 (g) | Non-Face-to-Face Customers Identification | (g) ensure that in all cases, evidence as to how identity has been verified shall be obtained and retained with the account opening records. | The bank must keep clear evidence of how each non-face-to-face customer's identity was verified as part of the account opening documents. | Lack of audit trail may expose bank to regulatory penalties. | Medium | High | Onboarding / Records Mgmt | Attach verification proof (screenshots, recordings, system logs) to records | Low | Medium |
|  |  |  | Reg. 36 (1) | Introductions from authorized financial  intermediaries | (1) An introductory letter shall be issued by the introducing financial intermediary or person in respect of each applicant for business. | When a financial intermediary introduces a customer, the bank must receive a formal introductory letter for that customer. | Risk of onboarding customers without accountability or traceability. | Medium | High | Relationship Management / Compliance | Accept only letters from vetted, regulated intermediaries. | Low | Medium |

In this regard, your organisation is expected to get in touch with NIBSS PLC, for the needed training and access rights to the portal, amongst others. | The Bank must digitize and upload their authorized signatories to the NIBSS portal and ensure continuous updates as staff change roles. | Failure to digitize or update signatories may lead to fraud, forged authorizations, and regulatory breaches. | Medium | High | Compliance / Operations / HR / IT | Upload initial authorized signatories; assign admin role; establish SOP for periodic updates; train relevant staff | Low | Medium |
| Fraud Management | 62 | Establishment of Industry Fraud Desks |  | BPS/DIR/GEN/CIR/02/004 | The Central Bank of Nigeria, in furtherance of its efforts at combating fraud within the Banking Industry, established the Nigeria Electronic Fraud Forum (NeFF) to proffer solutions towards addressing frauds arising from the increased adoption of electronic payments. Following submissions to the Bank by NeFF and consultations with DMBs and electronic payments service providers, it has become imperative that an effective mechanism for receiving and responding promptly to fraud alerts be set up within the Nigerian Banking industry, towards managing and reducing successful electronic payments fraud rate in the Nigerian Banking Industry.  To this end, all DMBs, MMOs, Switches and all payments service providers are hereby directed to maintain a dedicated Fraud Desk in their respective organisations. The Fraud Desk shall be appropriately staffed with personnel that have requisite training on emerging fraud trends on various electronic payments channels. The desk shall, at a minimum, offer the following services:  1. Provide support to customers on electronic frauds with a minimum of 10 dedicated phone lines, manned and available to customers at all times; 2. Make available the option for calls to contact centre, in respect of fraud alerts or complaints, to be redirected to fraud desk; 3. Block and/or Place No Debit restrictions on accounts upon receipt of fraud complaint; 4. Receive customers’ stop-transaction instructions to block their accounts through short codes service provided to customers by the banks; 5. Log all customer fraud alert and/or complain and escalate in line with internally predefined escalation path; 6. Submit reports to the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) Plc on fraud information logged by the fraud desk; 7. Honour “hold” instructions from NIBSS with respect to fraud matters and grant NIBSS permissions to view details on logged transactions; 8. Sensitise customers on e-Fraud and Fraud Desk services; 9. Manage/Resolve all intra-bank fraud issues leveraging an enterprise fraud management system; 10. Maintain a mail group mapped to members of the fraud desk team.  Further to the above: Banks shall implement across all electronic channels, an enterprise fraud monitoring system, which ensures behavioural monitoring, patterns and hold/block controls on transactions suspected to be fraudulent, etc. Banks may subscribe to NIBSS’ central anti-fraud solution for this purpose. | The bank must: 1. Establish and maintain a dedicated Fraud Desk. 2. Staff the desk with trained personnel on emerging e-fraud trends. 3. Provide at least 10 dedicated phone lines available 24/7 to customers. 4. Redirect fraud-related calls from the contact center to the Fraud Desk. 5. Place No Debit restrictions or block accounts immediately upon receiving fraud complaints. 6. Enable customers to stop transactions via short code services. 7. Log and escalate all fraud alerts/complaints based on internal escalation procedures. 8. Report fraud cases to NIBSS. 9. Honour “hold” instructions from NIBSS and grant it access to logged transaction details. 10. Sensitize customers regularly about e-fraud and Fraud Desk services. 11. Resolve intra-bank frauds using an enterprise fraud management system (EFMS). 12. Maintain a functional email group for the fraud desk team. 13. Implement a centralized enterprise fraud monitoring system across all e-channels (or subscribe to NIBSS’ anti-fraud solution). | - May lead to financial losses, regulatory penalties, reputational damage, and loss of customer confidence. - Poor fraud escalation or failure to honour NIBSS instructions may be seen as regulatory non-compliance. - Lack of real-time fraud monitoring tools may allow fraudulent activities to go undetected. | High | High | - Chief Compliance Officer - Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) - Head of Fraud Management - IT Operations Lead - Customer Experience/Call Centre Manager | - Deploy an enterprise fraud management system (EFMS). - Set up 24/7 fraud desk with dedicated infrastructure and escalation workflows. - Integrate fraud desk lines with short code service. - Ensure regulatory reporting link with NIBSS. - Conduct fraud awareness training for staff and customers. | Medium | Medium |
