| 2 |  | Issuance of Risk-Based Cybersecurity Framework and Guidelines for Deposit Money Banks and Payment Service Providers | 1.1 | Respinsibilities of the Board | 1.0 Board Oversight and Cybersecurity Governance Responsibilities  The Board, through the Board Risk or Information Technology Committee, shall have oversight and responsibility for the cybersecurity programme of the Systemically Important Financial Institution (SFI). The Board shall provide leadership, direction, and resources for the effective implementation of cybersecurity processes and ensure that cybersecurity governance is integrated into the SFI’s organisational structure.  To this end, the Board shall be responsible for ensuring that:  i. At least two Non-Executive Directors (NEDs), one of whom shall be an Independent NED, possess requisite knowledge and experience in innovative financial technology, Information Communication Technology (ICT), and/or cybersecurity. ii. Cybersecurity is integrated with business functions and effectively managed across the SFI. iii. Cybersecurity governance aligns with Corporate and Information Technology (IT) governance and is driven by business objectives. iv. Cybersecurity management processes align with business requirements and applicable laws and regulations, while security targets are defined and met across the SFI. v. Senior Management provides central oversight for the cybersecurity programme, assigns responsibilities, and ensures the effectiveness of cybersecurity management processes. vi. The audit function remains independent and is staffed with skilled professionals who possess relevant qualifications and experience. vii. Cybersecurity governance documents (such as cybersecurity strategy, framework, and policies) are established and aligned with the SFI’s business goals and objectives. viii. Quarterly cybersecurity reports are presented by Senior Management to the Board. These reports shall include, at a minimum:  * a. Cyber risk assessment updates. * b. Status of security initiatives to address cyber risks. * c. Summary of incidents, including loss status and recovery efforts. * d. Vulnerability management and penetration testing reports, including remediation actions and compensating controls. * e. Compliance status with Board-approved cyber risk thresholds. * f. Status of implementation of recommendations from the CBN Cybersecurity Supervisory Review and Evaluation.  ix. A qualified individual is appointed as the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) on the recommendation of Senior Management. The CISO shall be responsible for overseeing and implementing the SFI’s cybersecurity programme.  x. In the case of banking groups, while SFIs may collaborate with the group-level CISO, a dedicated CISO shall still be appointed in accordance with Section 1.4 of this Framework.  xi. A stand-alone cybersecurity budget, distinct from the IT or Risk Management budget, is approved by the Board.  xii. The cybersecurity risk appetite is clearly defined and documented in the SFI’s Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework.  ---  ## **1.1.1 Cybersecurity Strategy and Framework**  The Board is responsible for the SFI’s cybersecurity strategy and shall ensure that:  i. The strategy defines how cybersecurity goals will be achieved, risks mitigated, and compliance with legal, regulatory, contractual, and statutory obligations ensured. ii. The cybersecurity framework aligns with business objectives and technology needs, and clearly defines key cybersecurity roles and responsibilities. iii. The cybersecurity policy clearly articulates the institution’s intent and approach toward achieving its cybersecurity objectives, including:  * Risk assessment * Security policy development * Incident response planning * Vulnerability management * Log monitoring   iv. The cybersecurity policy is reviewed at least annually, or upon significant changes to the SFI’s cyber risk exposure.  ---  ## **1.1.2 Cybersecurity Programme Requirements**  SFIs shall implement a comprehensive cybersecurity programme which shall, at a minimum, include:  * Data backup and recovery plans * Security awareness and training programmes * Initiatives to attain the target cybersecurity maturity level * Metrics to assess the effectiveness of the cybersecurity programme | The Bank shall:  1. Ensure that at least two Non-Executive Directors (including one Independent Director) have relevant experience in financial technology, ICT, or cybersecurity.  2. Integrate cybersecurity into all business activities and manage it effectively.  3. Align its cybersecurity governance with overall business and IT goals.  4. Make sure cybersecurity processes follow legal requirements and business needs, and that defined security targets are met.  5. Assign central oversight of the cybersecurity programme to Senior Management, who shall ensure it runs effectively.  6. Maintain an independent audit function staffed with skilled and qualified professionals to review cybersecurity processes.  7. Establish and maintain cybersecurity strategy, framework, and policies that align with the Bank’s business goals.  8. Receive quarterly cybersecurity reports from Senior Management, which shall include:    - Cyber risk assessment updates      - Progress on key cybersecurity initiatives      - Summary of security incidents, including losses and recovery efforts      - Reports on system weaknesses and test results, including remedial actions      - Status of compliance with Board-approved cyber risk thresholds      - Implementation updates from CBN supervisory reviews  9. Appoint a qualified Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), based on Senior Management’s recommendation, to oversee and implement the cybersecurity programme.  10. Appoint a dedicated CISO even when operating as part of a larger banking group, in line with regulatory requirements.  11. Approve a separate and dedicated budget for cybersecurity, independent of the IT or Risk Management budget.  12. Define and document its cybersecurity risk appetite within the Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework.  The Bank shall also ensure that its cybersecurity strategy:  - Clearly outlines how to meet cybersecurity goals and legal obligations   - Aligns with business and technology objectives   - Clearly defines cybersecurity responsibilities   - Covers areas such as risk assessments, security policies, incident response, vulnerability management, and activity monitoring   - Is reviewed at least annually or when there are major changes in cyber risk exposure  Furthermore, the Bank shall implement a cybersecurity programme that includes:  - A data backup and recovery plan   - Security awareness and training for staff   - Initiatives to reach target maturity levels in cybersecurity   - Clear metrics to measure how well the programme is working | Poor cybersecurity governance may result in regulatory non-compliance, reputational damage, and financial loss due to cyber incidents. | Medium | High | Board of Directors; Board Risk/IT Committee | Board-approved cybersecurity strategy, policies, and risk appetite; appointment of qualified CISO; dedicated cybersecurity budget; quarterly reporting; independence of audit function. | Low | Medium | Board oversight of security maturity, incident trends, penetration testing, compliance reviews, and risk mitigation tracking. | Quarterly (Ongoing oversight) | Board; MD/CEO; CISO; Senior Management |
|  |  |  | 1.2 | Responsibilities of senior management | 1.2 Responsibilities of Senior Management**  Senior Management shall be responsible for the effective implementation of Board-approved cybersecurity policies, programmes, standards, and the clear assignment of cybersecurity responsibilities within the organisation.  To fulfill this responsibility, Senior Management shall:  i. Recommend to the Board the appointment of a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) who meets the applicable regulatory qualifications and standards. ii. Obtain the Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) approval for the appointment of the CISO. iii. Provide periodic reports, at least quarterly, to the Board on the overall status of the cybersecurity programme, as specified in Section 1.1(viii). iv. Ensure that Information Security personnel undergo relevant and regular training programmes to maintain technical competence and awareness of emerging threats. v. Incorporate cybersecurity risk management into the Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework and governance structures to ensure consistent and holistic management of cyber risks across the SFI. vi. Drive cyber risk management processes to ensure effective adherence to the institution’s defined cybersecurity risk appetite. | The Bank shall ensure that Senior Management:  1. Recommends to the Board the appointment of a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) who meets regulatory qualifications and standards.  2. Obtains approval from the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) for the CISO’s appointment.  3. Submits regular cybersecurity status reports—at least quarterly—to the Board, covering progress and updates as required under Section 1.1(viii).  4. Ensures that Information Security staff receive ongoing, relevant training to maintain their skills and stay informed about current cyber threats.  5. Integrates cybersecurity risk management into the Bank’s overall Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework and governance systems to ensure risks are consistently managed across all areas.  6. Leads the implementation of cybersecurity risk processes that ensure the Bank stays within its defined cyber risk appetite. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  | 1.3 | Responsibilities of the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) | 1.3 Responsibilities of the Chief Information Security Officer**  The Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) shall be responsible for the day-to-day management of cybersecurity operations and the mitigation of cyber risks within the Specialized Financial Institution (SFI). The CISO shall ensure that the SFI’s information assets are adequately protected from internal and external threats.  Accordingly, the CISO shall:  i. Oversee and implement the Board-approved cybersecurity programme and strategy, ensuring alignment with the institution’s business objectives and risk appetite. ii. Develop and promote secure business and communication practices; define security objectives and performance metrics; and recommend the acquisition and deployment of appropriate cybersecurity tools and technologies to safeguard the SFI’s information assets. iii. Ensure the SFI maintains compliance with data privacy requirements and oversee the implementation of periodic cybersecurity awareness and training programmes for all employees. | The Bank shall ensure that the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO):  1. Oversees and implements the cybersecurity programme and strategy approved by the Board, making sure it aligns with the Bank’s business goals and risk tolerance.  2. Establishes secure business and communication practices, sets cybersecurity goals and performance measures, and recommends suitable tools and technologies to protect the Bank’s information systems.  3. Ensures compliance with data privacy regulations and leads regular cybersecurity training and awareness programmes for all employees. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  | 1.4 | Requirements for appointment as a Chief Information Security Officer | 1.4. Requirements for appointment as a Chief Information Security Officer** The SFI shall appoint a CISO who meets the under-listed requirements subject to CBN approval:  i. The CISO shall possess adequate authority, experience, independence and shall be of appropriate grade to function effectively. The minimum grade of staff to be appointed as CISO shall be as specified below or as may be approved by the CBN from time to time: a. Commercial Bank with International Authorisation – Senior Manager b. Commercial Bank with National Authorisation – Senior Manager c. Non-Interest Bank with National Authorisation – Manager d. Commercial Bank with Regional Authorisation – Manager e. Merchant Bank – Manager f. Payment Service Bank – Manager g. Non-Interest Bank with Regional Authorisation – Manager  ii. The CISO shall report directly/functionally to the Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer.  iii. To avoid conflict of interest, the CISO shall not report directly or indirectly to the Head of Information Technology (IT) operations or Chief Risk Officer.  iv. The Appointment of a CISO shall be in line with the provisions of the Revised Assessment Criteria for Approved Persons’ Regime for Financial Institutions, 2015 or any subsequent regulation.  v. Where the SFI is part of a Group that has a Group CISO charged with establishing and maintaining an enterprise vision, strategy and programme, the SFI’s CISO is required to replicate the responsibilities as required in Section 1.3 of this Framework.  vi. The CISO shall possess relevant qualifications with Information Security Certifications such as Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP), Certified Information Security Manager (CISM) and Certified Chief Information Security Officer (CCISO) among others and a minimum of ten year’s in-depth experience in any of the following roles: Cybersecurity, Information Technology, IT Risk Management, Information Security Risk Management or IT Audit. | The Bank shall:  Appoint a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) who has enough authority, experience, and independence to perform the role effectively. The CISO must hold at least the position of Senior Manager for commercial banks with international or national licenses, and Manager for those with regional licenses, in line with CBN requirements.  Ensure that the CISO reports directly to the Managing Director or Chief Executive Officer, not through the Head of IT or Chief Risk Officer, to maintain independence.  Appoint the CISO in accordance with the CBN’s Approved Persons Regime guidelines or any updated regulation.  If the Bank is part of a larger banking group with a Group CISO, the Bank shall still have its own CISO who performs all required responsibilities as outlined in the cybersecurity governance framework.  Ensure that the CISO has the right qualifications, such as professional certifications like CISSP, CISM, or CCISO, and at least 10 years of strong experience in areas such as cybersecurity, IT, IT risk management, information security, or IT audit. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  | 1.5 | The Information Security Steering Committee | 1.5. The Information Security Steering Committee** Every SFI shall establish an Information Security Steering Committee (ISSC) that shall be responsible for the governance of the cybersecurity programme. The committee shall meet the following requirements:  i. It shall comprise senior representatives of relevant departments within the SFI and be chaired by the MD/CEO, while the Executive Director in charge of Technology/Operations may serve as the alternate chairman. ii. The roles, responsibilities, scope and activities of the ISSC shall be as defined in the Terms of Reference. iii. The ISSC shall meet at least once in a quarter. iv. The agenda for the meeting shall include a presentation on the “State of cybersecurity” and address recent cyber events, vulnerabilities and proposals for controls to reduce cyber risks. The summary of the report shall be included in the reports to the Board referenced in Section 1.1(viii).  ---  **1.5.1. Terms of Reference of the ISSC**  The ISSC shall be responsible for:  i. ensuring that the SFI’s security policies and processes align with its business objectives. ii. evaluating, approving and sponsoring institution-wide security investment. iii. enforcing implementation of policies for investment prioritisation and security risk management. iv. providing strategic direction and cybersecurity governance for the SFI. v. recommend cybersecurity risk acceptance level to the Board for approval. | The Bank shall:  1. Set up an **Information Security Steering Committee (ISSC)** to oversee its cybersecurity programme.  2. Ensure the Committee is led by the **Managing Director/CEO**, and if unavailable, the **Executive Director responsible for Technology or Operations** may act as chair.  3. Include senior staff from key departments as members of the Committee.  4. Clearly define the Committee’s roles, responsibilities, and scope in a **Terms of Reference** document.  5. Hold Committee meetings **at least once every quarter**.  6. Ensure that each meeting covers the **current state of cybersecurity**, including recent threats, system weaknesses, and recommendations for improving controls. A summary of this discussion shall be included in quarterly cybersecurity reports to the Board.  ---  **The Bank shall ensure that the ISSC is responsible for:**  1. Making sure cybersecurity policies and processes support the Bank’s business goals.  2. Reviewing and approving major cybersecurity investments.  3. Enforcing policies that prioritize and manage cybersecurity risks.  4. Providing overall strategic guidance for the Bank’s cybersecurity programme.  5. Recommending the Bank’s level of acceptable cyber risk to the Board for approval. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

|  |  |  | 2.1 (2.1.1, 2.1.2 & 2.1.4) | The Risk Management System | 2.1.1. Risk Identification SFIs shall identify associated threats and vulnerabilities to the confidentiality, integrity and availability of their information assets to determine their cyber risk exposure.  2.1.2. Risk assessment SFIs are required to evaluate risks to their operations, probability of occurrence, impact of risk crystallisation, and security controls to mitigate identified risks. This process should be carried out annually and whenever major changes occur within the institution such as an acquisition, merger or when new technology is deployed to handle key business processes. The outcome of this process should be documented in a Cybersecurity Risk Control Self-Assessment. An independent Audit function shall be responsible for ensuring that the methodology used in risk assessment is reviewed periodically.  2.1.4. Risk mitigation/Risk treatment SFIs should implement risk mitigation and control measures consistent with the criticality of information assets. Risk treatment options such as risk reduction, acceptance, avoidance, transfer and management of residual risk should be selected based on the outcome of the risk assessment. Risk acceptance criteria should be as defined and approved by the Board. In cases where the SFI chooses to transfer risk, a detailed risk assessment for outsourcing or cyber risk insurance should be documented. | The Bank shall: 1. |  |  |  | 3 (3.1-3.4 & 3.7) | Enhancing Cybersecurity Resilience | Cyber resilience is the SFI’s ability to prevent, withstand and recover from cyber incidents. SFIs are required to establish procedures to enhance their cyber resilience. This will ultimately strengthen the financial industry’s cybersecurity posture. The following are the minimum controls that an SFI shall put in place to ensure the confidentiality, integrity and availability of critical information assets among others. 3.1 Know Your Environment An SFI shall proactively familiarise itself with its business environment and identify its critical assets. To ensure effective security measures, an SFI shall establish mechanisms for maintaining up-to-date inventory of authorised software, hardware as well as internal and external network connections. Additionally, an SFI shall identify and document its data, assets and capabilities. Also, potential threats and vulnerabilities associated with its assets shall be monitored. Employees and contractors providing information technology and cybersecurity services shall also be identified and documented. Details on specific controls are contained in Appendix II. 3.2 Implement Preventive Controls An SFI shall implement appropriate measures/controls/safeguards for IT systems, processes and people to mitigate cyber risks. These can be administrative, logical or physical controls. Details on specific controls are contained in Appendix III. 3.3 Monitor and Detect An SFI shall establish capability for ongoing (24/7) monitoring of its IT systems, infrastructure, applications, services, and other relevant components to promptly detect anomalies or cyber incidents. This capability may be managed internally or outsourced to a third-party provider. Notwithstanding the approach chosen, monitoring should be adequate to detect cyber threats. 3.4 Respond and Remediate An SFI shall ensure that the capability for responding to cyber incidents is available in-house or, if outsourced, can be accessed at short notice. Details on specific controls are contained in Appendix III. 3.5 Restore Service Operations An SFI shall aim at recovering its operations timeously to reduce the overall impact of cyber incidents. 3.6 Cyber-Threat Intelligence An SFI is expected to possess knowledge of emerging threats, cyber-attacks, attack vectors, mechanisms and indicators of attack/compromise that may impact its information assets. 3.7 Sector-specific Cyber Resilience An SFI is required to participate in industry cyber exercises and programmes to evaluate its level of preparedness to recover from cyber incidents. These exercises may include cyber drills, war games or as defined by the CBN from time to time. SFIs shall avoid creating single points of failure in the industry and proactively define plans to mitigate such risks. | The Bank shall establish, implement, and maintain a cybersecurity resilience framework to prevent, withstand, and recover from cyber incidents, as follows:  1. Identify and document its critical assets, including data, hardware, software, networks, and capabilities. It shall maintain an up-to-date inventory of these assets and their associated threats and vulnerabilities. Employees and contractors involved in IT and cybersecurity services shall also be documented.  2.  Apply appropriate administrative, logical, or physical safeguards to protect its IT systems, processes, and people against cyber risks.  3. Maintain continuous (24/7) monitoring capabilities across its IT systems, infrastructure, and applications to promptly detect anomalies or cyber incidents, whether through internal resources or qualified third-party providers.  4.  Ensure that adequate resources and plans for responding to cyber incidents are available in-house or can be accessed at short notice if outsourced.  5. Recover operations promptly to minimize the overall impact of cyber incidents.  6. Maintain knowledge of emerging threats, attack methods, indicators of compromise, and other cyber risks relevant to its information assets.  7. Participate in industry-wide cyber exercises, drills, and programs to test its preparedness for recovering from cyber incidents, and shall develop plans to avoid industry-wide single points of failure. | Lack of asset tracking, insufficient preventive controls, delayed threat detection, or poor incident response can result in data breaches, operational disruptions, financial loss, and regulatory sanctions. | High | High | - IT & Cybersecurity Team - Risk & Compliance Officer - Incident Response Team | - Maintain real-time asset inventory tools and auditing schedules - Enforce layered security controls (firewalls, encryption, access control) - Use SIEM solutions and external SOC support where needed - Maintain an Incident Response Plan (IRP) and CSIRT or retainer with external experts - Participate in industry drills and simulate cyber scenarios internally | Medium | Medium | - Automate asset discovery and unauthorized access alerts - Integrate AI-driven anomaly detection - Conduct frequent control effectiveness reviews - Share insights and best practices from sector exercises | - Asset review: Quarterly - Control audit: Bi-annually - Monitoring & IRP: Continuous - Simulation/drills: Annually | - CIO/Head of IT - Chief Compliance Officer - Cybersecurity Manager - Risk & Strategy Lead |

| 1 | CONSUMER PROTECTION | Exposure Draft of the Revised Consumer Protection Regulations 2.0 | 4.1 | FAIR TREATMENT | The bank shall comply with the following minimum standards at all stages of the relationship with consumers:  4.1.1 Treat consumers with courtesy and honesty.  4.1.2 Communicate in plain language, devoid of technical terms that would make it difficult for consumers to understand their rights and obligations.  4.1.3 Provide access to basic financial services without regard to demographic status such as gender, age, religion, literacy level, region and disability.  4.1.4 Provide support to consumers with special needs such as multilingual assistance, ramp, visual and hearing aids.  4.1.5 Promptly oblige consumers’ request for account closure or to switch providers, without unreasonable closing/switching barriers.  4.1.6 Execute variations to contracts, including interest rate, fees or charges, only if expressly provided for in the contract and notify customers at least five (5) working days in advance of execution.  4.1.7 Acknowledge enquiries from consumers within 24 hours.  4.1.8 Respond to customers’ enquiries within five (5) working days of receipt.  4.1.9 Not charge early liquidation fee on Consumer and Micro, Small and Medium Enterprise loans with variable interest rate.  4.1.10 Be accountable for improper functioning of their banking applications.  4.1.11 Deploy flexible banking applications to meet regulatory requirements for good consumer outcomes.  4.1.12 Disclose similar product offerings within the institution to enable consumers to make comparisons and informed choices.  4.1.13 Not engage in bundling or cross-selling practices that unduly limit consumer choices.  4.1.14 Be held accountable for employing any practice that could be considered unfair. | The Bank shall: 1. Treat customers with courtesy and honesty. 2. Use plain language and avoid technical jargon in all communication. 3. Ensure equal access to basic services regardless of gender, age, religion, disability, or literacy level. 4. Make contract variations (e.g., interest or fees) only if provided for, and notify customers at least 5 working days prior. 7. Acknowledge all customer enquiries within 24 hours. 8. Respond to all customer enquiries within 5 working days. 9. Do not charge early liquidation fees on MSME/consumer loans with variable interest rates. 10. Take responsibility for any failures or issues with the bank’s mobile or web applications. 11. Ensure bank apps are flexible and support regulatory consumer outcomes. 12. Disclose similar products for comparison and informed customer decisions. 13. Avoid forced product bundling or cross-selling that limits consumer choice. 14. Avoid all forms of unfair treatment and be accountable for misconduct. | - Breach of these standards can lead to: ▪ Regulatory sanctions ▪ Erosion of customer trust ▪ Customer attrition and reputational damage ▪ Fines or license limitations ▪ Negative media and public backlash | High | High | - Chief Compliance Officer- Head of Customer Experience- Branch Managers- Head of Digital Channels- Legal and Contracting Team | - Deploy customer-friendly communication templates and training for frontline staff. - Periodic testing of app accessibility and compliance with special-needs support. - Track response times to enquiries and escalate delays. - Ensure disclosure templates for similar products exist. - Set up independent compliance reviews of switching/closure procedures. - Embed interest and fee variation protocols into core banking system with alert triggers. - Conduct annual reviews of bundled offerings to check for undue customer restriction. | Medium | Medium | - Customer satisfaction surveys tied to compliance dashboards. - Language-check algorithms on digital communication templates. - Real-time analytics on enquiry acknowledgment and resolution timelines. - Periodic regulatory training on fairness and anti-discrimination for staff. - Compliance alerts for fee adjustments or closure delays. | - Continuous (daily operational standard)- Specific timelines:    - 24-hour enquiry acknowledgment    - 5-day enquiry resolution    - 5-day advance notice before variation | - Executive Management- Consumer Protection Compliance Officer- Head of Operations- IT & App Support Leads |
|  |  |  | 4.2 | BUSINESS ETHICS | To promote good business practices, FSPs shall comply with the following minimum standards:  4.2.1 Conduct business in a responsible, professional, and ethical manner.  4.2.2 Train staff to promote competence, efficiency, and professionalism in the discharge of their duties.  4.2.3 Provide clear information about product features, terms and conditions as channel on consumers.  4.2.7 Not charge fees for issuance and renewal of products or services which have not been requested by the customer.  4.2.8 Not compel consumers to buy a product or service as for waivers, extensions, and other concessions to a customer within ten (10) working days, otherwise the application shall be deemed granted.  4.2.11 Be responsible for digitally generated advise, Assess impact across similar accounts and notify affected customers when systemic issues are discovered. | - Regulatory non-compliance due to unethical practices. - Loss of customer trust and public backlash. - Legal action from mis-selling or improper charges. - Potential fines, reputational damage, or loss of license. - Staff behavior leading to operational misconduct. | High | High | - Chief Compliance Officer- Head of Customer Experience- Product Managers- Sales/Relationship Management Heads- Internal Audit- Legal & Digital Operations Units | - Enforce Code of Business Conduct and Ethics. - Mandatory onboarding and annual ethical conduct training. - Automate disclosure of terms and fees in onboarding portals. - Review compensation models to remove misconduct-inducing incentives. - Integrate financial suitability assessments into product advisory tools. - Enforce system-based application tracking for waivers/extensions. - Deploy real-time notification systems for service disruptions. - Implement system-based checks to block tied product sales unless linked. - Embed conflict-of-interest disclosures in CRM processes. | Medium | Medium | - Conduct routine audits of product sales scripts and application outcomes. - Independent ethics review board for high-risk cases. - Whistleblower platform with escalation process. - Set up digital product disclaimers with confirmation checks. - Require documented customer financial profiling in advisory processes. | - Continuous compliance.- Time-bound obligations:     - Customer application response: 10 working days     - Disruption notice: within 12 hours (unplanned) or 48 hours (planned) | - Executive Management- Ethics and Compliance Team- Customer Protection Unit- HR & Training Department- Digital Channels Lead- Audit and Internal Control Team |
|  |  |  | 4.3 | SALES PROMOTION AND ADVERTISEMENT | FSPs shall be required to ensure that their advertising and promotional materials comply with the following minimum standards:  4.3.1 Disclose |  |  |  | 4.4 | UNFAIR CONTRACT TERMS | FSPs shall comply with the following minimum standards to ensure that terms and conditions in contracts are fair and reasonable:  4.4.1 Contracts with consumers shall not contain unfair terms. A contract term shall be considered unfair if it:  a. Eliminates or limits the liability of an FSP to loss caused to a consumer by misrepresentation, negligence or misleading information on its products or services.  b. Binds a consumer to an obligation while the corresponding obligation on the FSP is conditional.  c. Eliminates or limits FSP’s liability with respect to actions or commitments undertaken by their employees, agents, or intermediaries.  d. Allows unilateral change to a contract without stating the circumstances under which the change could be made.  e. Excludes or restricts any legal requirement on the part of an FSP to act with skill, care, diligence, or professionalism toward the consumer in connection with the provision of any product or service and/or any liability for failing to do so.  4.4.2 Unfair terms used in contracts are void and shall not be binding on consumers.  4.4.3 Where there is any doubt or ambiguity about the meaning of a term used in a contract, the interpretation most favorable to the consumer shall prevail. | The Bank must: 1. Ensure all consumer contracts do not contain unfair terms, such as:  a. Clauses that eliminate/limit liability for losses caused by misrepresentation, negligence, or misleading information.  b. Obligations imposed on the consumer while making the bank’s obligation conditional or unclear.  c. Clauses that limit the bank's liability for staff, agents, or intermediaries’ conduct.  d. Allowing unilateral contract changes without stating clear conditions.  e. Excluding the bank’s legal duty to act with skill, care, and diligence. 2. Recognize that unfair contract terms are void and unenforceable. 3. Ensure the interpretation most favorable to the consumer must apply if contract terms are ambiguous. | - Use of unfair terms can result in:  - Regulatory sanctions  - Legal challenges or lawsuits  - Loss of customer trust and reputational damage  - Contracts being declared void and unenforceable | High | High | - Head, Legal & Compliance- Head of Products- Contract Management Unit- Risk Management Department | - Standardized contract templates vetted by Legal and Compliance. - Checklist for unfair terms during contract drafting and review. - Consumer-facing documents written in plain, clear language. - Legal review of all amendments or unilateral changes to consumer contracts. - Establish approval workflow for all new or revised contract terms. - Regular updates of contract templates based on evolving regulatory standards. | Medium | Medium | - Annual contract audit to identify and correct potentially unfair terms. - Consumer feedback loop to flag difficult or ambiguous terms. - Legal advisory notes issued to internal stakeholders outlining current regulatory expectations. - Pre-launch Legal/Compliance sign-off for all consumer product documents. | - At the contract drafting stage. - On a continuous basis for contract reviews and customer feedback. - Upon CBN or NDIC regulation updates impacting contract content. | - Legal & Compliance Team- Risk & Internal Audit- Product Development Heads- Executive Management for Oversight |
|  |  |  | 4.5 | LENDING PRACTICES | FSPs shall comply with the following requirements:  4.5.1 Apply lending fees only to the extent of the amount disbursed in respect of term loans, except for fees that are applicable to committed facility.  4.5.2 Obtain customers’ written authorization where repayment of facility is sought before due date.  4.5.3 Assess customers’ capability to repay facilities in a sustainable manner taking into consideration their financial circumstances.  4.5.4 Monitor loan performance and upon early detection of repayment difficulties, engage customers on repayment options.  4.5.5 Not compel consumers to buy products or services, such as insurance or valuation from a particular third-party provider as a pre-condition for the grant of a credit facility, but can provide the option to choose from at least three (3) providers or as may be prescribed by CBN from time to time.  4.5.6 Ensure that guarantors confirm in writing that they have read and understood their commitments, potential implications, and the maximum amount they are guaranteeing.  4.5.7 Provide update to Guarantors immediately a facility is in default to enable parties (lender, borrower and guarantor) engage on repayment options, until the facility returns to performing status and the likelihood of the guarantors being called upon to discharge their commitments in the loan agreement becomes minimal.  4.5.8 Issue a Discharge Letter at no cost to customers within 5 working days after loan liquidation, and where the loan is guaranteed, the guarantor be notified accordingly.  4.5.9 Notify customers where loan requests are declined with reason(s) within 10 working days from the date of receipt. | The Bank must: 1. Only apply lending fees on the actual disbursed amount for term loans (except committed facilities). 2. Get written authorization from customers before collecting loan repayments earlier than due date. 3. Assess customer affordability based on their financial situation before granting loans. 4. Monitor loans and engage borrowers early when signs of difficulty in repayment are detected. 5. Allow customers to choose from at least three third-party providers (e.g. insurance, valuation) where services are required as part of a loan process. 6. Ensure guarantors confirm in writing that they understand their obligations and the guaranteed amount. 7. Update guarantors immediately when a loan is in default and continue engagement until the loan performs again. 8. Issue a Discharge Letter at no cost within 5 working days of loan repayment; guarantors must also be notified. 9. Inform customers within 10 working days with reasons when their loan application is declined. | Non-compliance could result in regulatory penalties, reputational damage, customer dissatisfaction, legal liability from aggrieved customers or guarantors, and increased default rates due to poor lending decisions. | Medium | High | - Head of Retail/Consumer Lending- Legal & Compliance Unit- Credit Risk Department- Loan Operations Team- Relationship Managers | - Lending policy approved by Board - Affordability checks in loan origination system - Automated loan tracking tools - Loan decline templates- Standard operating procedure for loan closure | Low | Medium | - Update lending SOPs and digital workflows to reflect all 4.5 obligations. - Include guarantor acknowledgment templates and early default alert protocols.  - Automate loan decline notices and discharge letter issuance in core banking system. - Train relationship managers and credit officers on fair lending expectations and 3rd-party provider flexibility. - Monitor compliance quarterly through internal audit or compliance reviews. | Upon finalization of Regulation 2.0 or as directed by CBN | Chief Risk Officer, Head of Credit Operations, Chief Compliance Officer, Head of Legal, Product Managers |
|  |  |  | 4.6 | DEBT RECOVERY | To ensure that debt recovery processes are transparent, courteous, and fair, regulated entities shall:  4.6.1 Engage and give customers notice(s) of outstanding obligations prior to the commencement of a debt collection.  4.6.2 Initiate foreclosures only when other recovery options have been unsuccessful.  4.6.3 Give customers the option of a private sale, to be exercised within 30 days before commencing foreclosure, except where the customer waives the right.  4.6.4 Ensure that the net proceeds from foreclosures are immediately applied to the loan account and customers informed of the balance.  4.6.5 Provide customers with a report of the sale of the collateral. At a minimum, the report shall state the process, proceeds, incidental expenses, and net proceeds.  4.6.6 Be liable for the actions of their agents engaged for debt collection.  4.6.7 Not contact friends, employer, relatives, or neighbors of a customer for any information other than information on employment status, telephone numbers or address, except where the person has guaranteed the loan or has consented to be contacted. | The Bank as a regulated entity must: 1. Notify customers of unpaid debts before starting debt recovery actions. 2. Only initiate foreclosure if all other recovery methods have failed. 3. Offer customers a 30-day window to sell the collateral privately before foreclosure, unless they waive the right. 4. Immediately apply any foreclosure sale proceeds to the loan and inform the customer of the remaining balance. 5. Provide a detailed report to the customer after the sale of collateral, including process, proceeds, expenses, and net amount. 6. Be responsible for the conduct and actions of third-party agents or debt collectors. 7. Do not contact a borrower's relatives, neighbors, friends, or employer except to confirm address, phone, or employment – unless they are guarantors or have consented. | Improper or aggressive debt recovery practices can lead to regulatory sanctions, lawsuits, reputational harm, customer complaints, and loss of business license. | Medium | High | - Credit Recovery & Collections Unit- Legal Department- Compliance Department- Customer Experience Unit- Third-party Collection Agents | - Standard notice templates for overdue accounts- Escalation procedures for foreclosure approval- Agent Code of Conduct- Collateral sales reporting template- Call logs and CRM audit trails | Low | Medium | - Embed foreclosure timing and private sale option into recovery workflow.- Train collection teams and vendors on fair recovery practices.- Automate issuance of debt notices and post-sale reports.- Add clauses in debt collection contracts holding agents accountable for misconduct.- Conduct periodic audit and mystery shopper checks on recovery practices. | Upon adoption of Regulation 2.0 or as directed by CBN | Chief Compliance Officer, Head of Recovery, Chief Risk Officer, Head of Legal, Collections Manager |
|  |  |  | 5.1 | FORMAT AND MANNER OF DISCLOSURE | 5.1.1 Documents provided to consumers shall:  a. Be written in clear, simple English language and legible with a minimum font size of 10 and spacing of 1.0.  b. Not be misleading or deceptive.  c. Be provided in a durable form for ease of future reference.  d. State the name and contact details of the FSP.  e. State the type of license of the FSP and provide the name as well as contact details of the regulatory authority.  5.1.2 Clearly explain technical terms to consumers to aid understanding and decision.  5.1.3 Disclose the agreed communication channel(s) to be used for all correspondences and adopt same for information dissemination.  5.1.4 Display at customer engagement points, accurate information on all products and services, including:  a. Prime and maximum lending rates.  b. Deposit rates.  c. Applicable exchange rates for transactions that require currency conversion.  d. How to lodge a complaint to the FSP and escalation option to the CBN where necessary.  5.1.5 Ensure that their websites and other information dissemination channels are functional and regularly updated with the current features of products and services offered. | The Bank shall: 1. Provide documents to consumers that:  a. Are written in clear, simple English, minimum font size 10, and spacing 1.0.  b. Are not misleading or deceptive.  c. Are given in a durable format for future reference.  d. Clearly state the name and contact details of the bank.  e. Include the license type of the bank and contact details of its regulator. 2. Explain all technical terms clearly to ensure consumer understanding. 3. Disclose and use the agreed communication channel for all customer correspondence. 4. Display at all customer engagement points:  a. Lending rates (prime and max)  b. Deposit rates  c. Exchange rates where applicable  d. Complaint procedure and CBN escalation steps. 5. Ensure websites and all info channels are functional and regularly updated. | - Inadequate or misleading disclosures can result in:  - Regulatory sanctions or fines  - Loss of customer trust  - Legal action from misled consumers  - Customer churn or reputational damage | High | High | - Product Managers - Compliance & Legal Team - Corporate Communications - Customer Experience Unit - IT/Web Team | - All product documents reviewed by Legal before public release. - Content template standardization for disclosures. - Pre-launch checklists for regulatory and consumer protection compliance. - Quarterly audits of all product-related content online and in-branch. - Centralized update control for websites and marketing content. | Medium | Medium | - Real-time update approval protocol for rates and service information. - Staff training on disclosure standards and technical terms. - Language accessibility review for all disclosure materials. - Chatbot/FAQs integrated with updated disclosure items. | - Immediately for all new products. - Quarterly content and format audit. - Ongoing updates to websites and customer materials as product features change. | - Head, Legal & Compliance - Product Team Leads - Marketing & Communications Head - Customer Service Manager - Website Administrator |
|  |  |  | 5.2 | DISCLOSURE OF TERMS AND CONDITIONS | FSPs shall comply with the following minimum standards during the lifecycle of contractual relationship with consumers:  5.2.1 Disclose in writing, all terms and conditions of a product or service on offer, as well as the features, risks, benefits, fees, and other associated charges.  5.2.2 Provide oral explanation on contractual agreements:  a. At customer’s request; or  b. If it is obvious that the customer is vulnerable or cannot understand the agreement.  5.2.3 The phrase “Terms and Conditions Apply” or any other phrase conveying a similar meaning shall not be used, except where such terms have been disclosed in the contract. Where terms and conditions are disclosed in other medium accessible to consumers, the consumers attention shall be drawn.  5.2.4 Make opt-out option available for customers to unsubscribe from digital services at the time of establishing the contractual relationship.  5.2.5 Provide information on cancellation or switching procedures, including when products and services are delivered through agents or digital channels.  5.2.6 Disclose in contracts, the possibility of variations in interest or foreign exchange rates due to changes in market conditions.  5.2.7 Allow consumers a minimum of two (2) working days from date of receipt, to review draft contract before execution except where they waive this in writing.  5.2.8 Give consumers a cooling-off period of three (3) working days after the execution of a credit contract, within which they may cancel without having to pay any penalty or charges. However, the consumer may waive the option with written notification.  5.2.9 Embed a pre-read or pause function before any purchase decision or transaction via digital channels, to enable brief time to review transaction and key terms and conditions before authorization or consent.  5.2.10 Provide information on product usage and how to obtain support services when the need arises.  5.2.11 Credit contracts shall contain the following:  a. Name and contact details of customer.  b. Type, purpose of credit, tenor of the contract, amount or credit limit, and moratorium (where applicable).  c. Applicable interest rate, details of lending fees including late payment/default (where applicable), variable rate information (where applicable) and total cost of the credit.  d. Key features and risks, conditions precedent to drawdown, insurance requirements (where applicable), early liquidation terms.  e. Applicable Annual Percentage Rate (APR) to be calculated using the formula stated in Annexures B and C.  f. Repayment schedule for term loans, collateral pledged and its estimated value.  5.2.12 Provide consumers, a Key Facts Statement (KFS) in the format attached as Annexure A stating a summary of key information on consumer loans.  5.2.13 State the rights and responsibilities of consumers, including the conditions that may lead to termination or cancellation of contract.  5.2.14 State how disputes can be resolved and the contact information of the established internal complaints handling units as well as the details of the external complaints’ resolution unit.  5.2.15 Implement disclosures that are commensurate to targeted consumer segments. | The Bank must: 1. Disclose in writing all terms, conditions, features, risks, benefits, fees, and charges of a product/service. 2. Provide oral explanation of contracts if requested or if the customer is vulnerable or lacks understanding. 3. Use “Terms and Conditions Apply” only if the terms are fully disclosed and accessible; draw consumer’s attention to external media if used. 4. Provide an opt-out option from digital services at the start of contract. 5. Disclose cancellation/switching procedures (including for agents and digital channels). 6. Disclose in contracts the possibility of rate variations due to market changes. 7. Allow 2 working days review period before contract execution (unless waived). 8. Allow 3 working days cooling-off period after executing a credit contract (unless waived). 9. Implement a pre-read or pause function before digital purchases or approvals. 10. Provide product usage info and support contact details. 11. Credit contracts must contain:  a. Customer name/contact  b. Credit type, amount, tenor, purpose, moratorium  c. Interest rate, all charges, late/default terms  d. Key risks, drawdown conditions, insurance if applicable  e. APR and how it's calculated (Annex B & C)  f. Repayment schedule, collateral, estimated value 12. Provide a Key Facts Statement (KFS) (Annex A). 13. State consumer rights/responsibilities including termination terms. 14. Provide complaints resolution process (internal & external contacts). 15. Tailor disclosures to targeted consumer segments. | - Non-disclosure or inadequate disclosure can lead to:  - Consumer complaints or lawsuits  - Contract disputes  - Regulatory sanctions for unfair consumer treatment  - Loss of consumer trust and reputational damage | High | High | - Legal & Compliance Department - Product Managers - Risk Management - IT/Digital Channels Unit - Customer Service & Relationship Officers | - Use standard contract templates vetted by legal/compliance. - Implement digital contract platforms with embedded pause/pre-read functions. - Pre-launch legal and consumer protection review of all new products. - Training of front-line staff on disclosure obligations. - System-enforced delay (2-day review period) and cooling-off period for credit contracts. - Built-in APR calculator tool and KFS generator. - Standard cancellation/opt-out procedures on all platforms. | Medium | Medium | - Internal audit review of executed contracts against disclosure checklist. - Consumer testing of contract language readability. - Embedded alerts and disclaimers for digital credit products. - Real-time chat or call-back options during onboarding for clarification. | - At product onboarding and prior to execution of any contract. - Ongoing updates whenever product features or fees change. - Ensure KFS and oral/written explanations are available during every new contract cycle. | - Head, Legal & Compliance - Product Development Manager - Customer Experience Lead - Digital Channels/UX Manager - Internal Audit |
|  |  |  | 5.3 | NOTIFICATION OF CHANGES IN RATES, TERMS AND CONDITIONS | FSPs shall comply with the following minimum standards to promote transparency in dealing with customers:  5.3.1 Not vary terms and conditions, without the consent of customers. However, this does not apply to interest rate variations.  5.3.2 Notify customers of possible variations in interest rates and other terms and conditions, through the agreed channel of communication. In the case of interest rates, the notice shall state:  a. Reason for the variation.  b. Commencement date.  c. Revised repayment schedule (where necessary).  d. Alternatives available such as concession, restructuring, re- negotiation, opt-out or termination of the contract.  5.3.3 Notify consumers in default of credit repayment within 3 working days from the day of default, that a default charge would be applied after 7 working days in the case of Deposit Money Banks (DMBs), and 3 working days for Other Financial Institutions (OFIs). | The Bank shall:  1. Not vary the terms and conditions of contracts without the customer’s consent, except for interest rate changes. 2. Provide advance notice of possible variations in interest rates or terms using the agreed communication channel. 3. In case of interest rate changes, notify customers with details of:  a. The reason for the change  b. The start date of the new rate  c. The updated repayment schedule, if applicable  d. Available alternatives such as concessions, restructuring, renegotiation, opting out, or terminating the contract 4. If a customer defaults on repayment, the bank shall:  a. Notify the customer of the default within 3 working days  b. Inform them that a default charge will apply after:   - 7 working days for Deposit Money Banks (DMBs)   - 3 working days for Other Financial Institutions (OFIs) | - Lack of timely and proper communication regarding changes can result in:  - Regulatory non-compliance  - Customer disputes and dissatisfaction  - Financial penalties and reputational damage | High | High | - Legal & Compliance Unit- Customer Service Department- Product/Loan Management Team- IT/CRM Team | - Integrate system triggers to auto-generate notifications for changes and defaults - Use standardized templates with all required elements (reason, effective date, alternatives) - Include rate variation provisions in contracts and disclose clearly - Maintain audit trail of all customer notifications and confirmations - Align CRM systems with regulatory timing for default communications | Medium | Medium | - Implement dashboard monitoring to track all rate change notices sent - Train staff on timelines and consequences of non-compliance - Periodic system audit of communication logs | - Before any change in interest or terms and conditions- Within 3 working days of default (initial notice)- 7 working days after default before applying penalty (DMBs)- 3 working days after default before applying penalty (OFIs) | - Head of Compliance- Chief Risk Officer- Head of Customer Service- ICT Manager |
|  |  |  | 5.4 | ACCOUNT STATEMENT | FSPs shall comply with the following minimum standards to promote disclosure of financial transactions:  5.4.1 Provide monthly statements (confirmation/investment advice as the case may be) for all products and account types, at no cost.  5.4.2 Make account balances and statements available on customers’ request.  5.4.3 Notify consumers of transactions on their account immediately it occurs. At a minimum, the notification shall include date, currency, amount, payer, transaction reference, channel, and the cleared account balance.  5.4.4 Notify consumers when their accounts have become inactive or dormant, and the related consequences.  5.4.5 Ensure clarity in descriptions on account statements. At a minimum, it shall include, transaction reference, payer transaction channel, location, and account balance.  5.4.6 Disclose default charges in account statements separate from the interest charge.  5.4.7 Provide consumers with a closing statement when a contract is terminated or concluded. | The Bank shall: 1. Send monthly account statements or investment advice for all account types free of charge. 2. Make account balances and statements available upon customer request. 3. Immediately notify customers of every account transaction with key details: date, currency, amount, payer, transaction reference, channel, and cleared balance. 4. Alert customers when accounts become inactive or dormant, stating the implications. 5. Ensure clear descriptions in statements with transaction details including reference, channel, location, and balance. 6. Clearly separate default charges from interest in statements. 7. Issue a closing statement when a product or contract ends. | Failure to comply with these provisions can result in poor transparency, regulatory penalties, loss of customer trust, disputes, or miscommunication over charges and balances. | Medium | High | - Operations Department- Customer Service Team- IT / Core Banking System Admins- Compliance Department | - Automated monthly e-statements - Real-time transaction alerts (SMS/email) - Dormancy alert systems - Core banking integration for real-time balances - Statement description format templates | Low | Medium | - Periodic review of statement formats for clarity - Internal audits of transaction alert accuracy - Dormancy alert trigger review and escalation process - Ensure final statement generation is part of account closure process - System flags for correct tagging of default charges vs. interest | Immediately or within 90 days of final regulation issuance | Head of Operations, Chief Compliance Officer, Head of Customer Service, IT Systems Manager |
|  |  |  | 6 | PROTECTION OF CONSUMER ASSETS AND PRIVACY | To ensure adequate protection of consumer assets and privacy, FSPs shall comply with the following minimum standards:  6.1 DATA PROTECTION 6.1.1 Protect the privacy and confidentiality of consumer information and assets against unauthorized access and be accountable for acts or omissions in respect thereof.  6.1.2 Embed personal data protection in the design of products or systems.  6.1.3 Obtain written consent of consumers to collect and process their personal data for specific purposes and provide them with the option to withdraw the consent at any time.  6.1.4 Not share personal data of consumers to a third party without their express consent and provide details of information to be shared.  6.1.5 Design clear and simple “Opt-in” and “Opt-Out” options for data sharing with 3rd parties.  6.1.6 Review data processing and privacy procedures to ensure that consumers’ data are accurate and used only for the purposes for which it was initially obtained.  6.2 FRAUD PREVENTION 6.2.1 Protect customers’ assets against fraud or misuse at all times and be liable for losses arising from breach of required controls.  6.2.2 Test product suitability with consumers and make necessary modifications to reduce the incidence of fraud or transaction errors.  6.2.3 Implement the following measures across transaction channels:  a. Multi-variant customer identification and multifactor authentication mechanisms for transactions consummated.  b. Automated transaction monitoring, alert functions and behavioral monitoring to detect and prevent fraud.  6.2.4 Sensitize customers on fraud threats or scams.  6.2.5 State and periodically communicate procedures for reporting suspicious, unauthorized, fraud, lost or stolen payment instruments and/or authentication information to consumers.  6.2.6 Provide secure and simple user interfaces for digital financial services that will minimize the risk of mistake or double transactions. | The Bank shall ensure the protection of consumer data and assets by doing the following:  Data Protection 1. Safeguard consumer personal information and financial data from unauthorized access. 2. Build data protection into the design of systems and financial products. 3. Get written permission from consumers before collecting/using their data and allow them to withdraw that consent at any time. 4. Only share consumer data with third parties when the consumer agrees in writing and is informed of what data will be shared. 5. Design easy-to-use opt-in/opt-out features for data sharing.6. Regularly review data practices to ensure data is correct and used only for its original purpose.  Fraud Prevention 1. Keep customers’ money safe from fraud and take responsibility if systems fail. 2. Test products with consumers to fix issues that might lead to fraud. 3. Deploy the following controls:   - Strong customer ID and multifactor authentication   - Automated systems to monitor and flag suspicious transactions 4. Educate customers about fraud risks and scams. 5. Provide clear instructions for reporting fraud, stolen cards, or unauthorized activity. 6. Design secure and user-friendly digital platforms to reduce errors or duplicate transactions. | - Breaches of personal data and privacy due to poor access control or data sharing without consent. - Financial loss due to fraud, phishing, identity theft, or inadequate digital platform design. - Regulatory sanctions and reputational damage due to non-compliance with data and fraud requirements. | High | High | - Data Protection Officer (DPO) - Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) - Head, Digital Banking - IT Security/Infrastructure Team - Customer Education Team - Compliance Department | - Data Protection Policy (aligned with NDPA) - Data Sharing Agreements - Consent forms and opt-in/out options - Multifactor authentication - Fraud monitoring software - Cybersecurity awareness campaigns | Medium | Medium | - Conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA)  - Schedule periodic privacy audits  - Simplify and test UI/UX for digital platforms  - Real-time fraud simulation testing  - Set SLAs for consumer fraud complaint response  - Maintain updated customer communication on fraud trends | Within 90 days of regulation finalization | Chief Risk Officer, Chief Information Security Officer, Head of Compliance, Product Managers, DPO |
|  |  |  | 7 | FINANCIAL LITERACY AND AWARENESS | To enhance financial literacy and awareness, FSPs shall comply with the following minimum standards:  7.1 Design and implement consumer education programs for various segments, to:  a. Build skills, knowledge, understanding and confidence in the use of financial products and services.  b. Safeguard account and confidential information.  7.2 Disseminate consumer education and awareness programs through diverse channels that are appropriate for various consumer segments.  7.3 Disseminate fraud prevention tips in English or local languages (where applicable) to all customer segments through appropriate channels.  7.4 Provide information that will enable consumers differentiate digital financial services from conventional banking products.  7.5 Render quarterly returns on financial literacy programs conducted.  7.6 Provide user education at product sign-up stage.  7.7 Ensure access to information on all product offerings to enable consumers make informed decisions.  7.8 Contribute resources towards industry-wide implementation of financial literacy and capability programs. | The Bank shall: 1. Create and implement education programs tailored to different consumer segments to build knowledge, skills, and confidence in using financial products. 2. Educate consumers on protecting their account and confidential information. 3. Disseminate financial literacy programs through various suitable channels for different consumer segments. 4. Share fraud prevention tips in English and relevant local languages via appropriate channels. 5. Explain differences between digital and traditional financial services to consumers. 6. Report quarterly on all financial literacy initiatives conducted. 7. Provide product education at the point of signing up new consumers. 8. Ensure product information is easily accessible to support informed decision-making. 9. Support industry-wide financial literacy programs by contributing resources. | - Inadequate consumer education may lead to: ▪ Increased cases of fraud and cybercrime ▪ Low customer trust and satisfaction ▪ Regulatory sanctions for non-compliance ▪ Poor usage of digital platforms or financial products | Medium | High | - Head of Compliance- Corporate Communications- Financial Inclusion/CSR Team- Product Managers- IT/Digital Channels Team | - Develop a financial literacy strategy with measurable goals and timelines - Use multi-lingual content and diverse media (SMS, email, radio, social media, webinars) - Track and report quarterly to regulators - Integrate product awareness modules during onboarding - Maintain content approval and review processes for accuracy and relevance | Low | Medium | - Partner with schools, community leaders, and fintech platforms for grassroots education - Launch online/mobile financial literacy portals and chatbots - Conduct periodic consumer surveys to assess awareness levels and adjust strategy accordingly | - Quarterly returns on financial literacy activities - Ongoing for product onboarding education, fraud tips, and media content dissemination | - Chief Compliance Officer - Head, Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) - Head of Digital Channels - Marketing & Communication Unit - Product Development Team |
|  |  |  | 8.1 | INTERNAL COMPLAINT RESOLUTION | Complaints shall first be lodged with the FSP for timely resolution. For effective resolution of complaints, FSPs shall:  8.1.1 Provide access to efficient and free complaint resolution mechanisms.  8.1.2 Develop policies and processes on complaints handling that will guarantee fairness, transparency, responsiveness, and independence of the complaint handling mechanism.  8.1.3 Allocate adequate resources and structure for complaints handling under the oversight of an Executive Compliance Officer or its equivalent in Other Financial Institutions.  8.1.4 Designate a function for complaints handling independent of other business functions taking into consideration, the nature and complexity of their business.  8.1.5 Provide information on how to lodge a complaint, including the type of information to be provided by the complainant.  8.1.6 Disclose contact details, channels for lodging complaints, timelines for resolution and options for escalation at all customer engagement points. Where it is not practicable to comply with this, refer customers to where the information required could be obtained.  8.1.7 Make available a range of channels (such as walk-in, telephone, email, call center, portals, website, and social media) for submitting complaints appropriate to the type of consumers served.  8.1.8 Upon receipt of a complaint (inclusive of oral submission), communicate to the consumer immediately an acknowledgment containing:  a. A unique identification or tracking number,  b. Contact details of the complaints desk,  c. Expected resolution timeline,  d. Escalation options; and  e. An assurance that the complaint is being addressed.  8.1.9 Ensure that staff responsible for handling complaints declare any conflict of interest that may affect their objectivity.  8.1.10 Integrate all complaints collection channels to the enterprise complaints management platform.  8.1.11 Provide toll-free telephone lines for customers to make enquiries and lodge complaints.  8.1.12 Continuously engage customers until complaints are fully resolved.  8.1.13 Use the unique identification or tracking number in all correspondence with the complainant.  8.1.14 Keep records of all complaints, including transcripts of verbal complaint for a minimum of 6 years.  8.1.15 Provide emergency channels for reporting time-sensitive issues especially fraud-related complaints at all times.  8.1.16 Reconstruct customers’ accounts to establish underpayment or excess charges, where applicable.  8.1.17 Refund identified excess charges, non-payment, under-payment of interest on deposits or unauthorized debits to the customer’s account along with interest as provided in the extant Monetary, Credit, Foreign Trade and Exchange Policy Guidelines or any regulation issued by the CBN.  8.1.18 Resolve complaints received within the time specified in the Timelines for Complaints Resolution by Institutions.  8.1.19 Provide a Summary Resolution Communication (SRC) for resolved complaints to the complainant within 24 hours after resolution. The summary shall convey at a minimum:  a. The basis of the decision(s).  b. The right of appeal available to the complainant for a second level review by the entity.  c. The right of escalation to the CBN, or other Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) where the complainant is dissatisfied.  8.1.20 Where a complainant is dissatisfied with a decision of an FSP, the complainant shall, within 30 days from the date of the receipt of the SRC, request in writing for a second level review.  8.1.21 A complaint shall be considered resolved where the complainant has indicated acceptance of the resolution in writing within 30 days after the receipt of the SRC, otherwise the complaint shall be deemed resolved or closed in the records of the FSP.  8.1.22 Upon receipt of a request for a second level review, the FSP shall review and communicate decision(s) within the timelines for complaints resolution for second level review.  8.1.23 Submit a Root Cause Analysis Report (RCAR) on quarterly basis to capture recurring complaint types, category and code, number of occurrences, root cause(s), planned remedial actions and implementation timelines. The report should be submitted to the Director, Consumer Protection Department, CBN on or before the 5th day of January, April, July, and October respectively.  8.1.24 Report complaints statistics in annual reports and the abridged Financial Statement in line with the approved format provided in Annexure D or any other format as may be prescribed by the CBN from time to time. | The Bank shall have fair and easy ways for customers to complain when things go wrong. These complaints should be handled by a well-trained, independent team with enough resources. Customers must be told how to complain, where to do it, and how long it will take. Institutions must allow complaints through many channels like walk-ins, phone, email, and social media.  Once a complaint is received, it should be acknowledged immediately with a tracking number and contact information. The bank must stay in touch with the customer until the complaint is resolved. Staff handling complaints should be honest and declare any conflicts of interest.  All complaints (even verbal ones) should be recorded and kept for six years. Customers must be refunded with interest if they were overcharged. Emergency channels must be available for fraud-related complaints. A summary of the resolution must be given within 24 hours, and customers must be informed of their rights to appeal or escalate.  The bank must also send quarterly reports to the CBN about complaint trends and how they’re being addressed, and include complaint statistics in their annual reports. | - Regulatory penalties for delayed, unfair, or untracked complaint handling. - Poor customer trust and reputational damage from unresolved or mishandled complaints. - Risk of litigation due to non-compliance with redress timelines and transparency obligations. - System inefficiencies if complaints are not tracked, resolved, or addressed at root cause level. | High | High | - Executive Compliance Officer - Complaints Management Unit - Customer Service Team - Legal/Compliance Department - IT/System Integration Team - Internal Audit | - Complaints Management Policy - Consumer redress workflow with timelines - Dedicated complaints team with oversight - Toll-free numbers and online channels - Customer communication scripts and FAQs - Tracking systems for SRC and RCAR submission | Medium | Medium | - Automate tracking and resolution alerts for complaint handlers - Integrate fraud complaints reporting with security incident management - Train staff on conflict of interest declaration - Establish clear SLA for second-level reviews - Audit complaints database quarterly for closure and escalation accuracy - Ensure quarterly RCAR submissions are signed off by senior management before CBN submission | Within 3 months of regulation finalization | Executive Compliance Officer, Head of Customer Experience, Risk and Compliance Leads, Internal Audit |

| 2 |  | CBN Consumer Protection Framework | 2.2 | Responsible Business Conduct | Financial Institutions shall observe high ethical standards and professionalism in their business transactions with consumers. They are required to assess the financial capabilities of consumers and offer only suitable products/services based on their needs and capability. In addition, they shall provide channels for consumers to make enquiries and complaints. The following specific areas will be addressed under Responsible Business Conduct:  Communication: All requests for information must be responded to timely and with clarity.  Provision of financial advice: FIs shall provide consumers with objective advice to enable them make informed decisions.  Responsible lending: FIs shall carry out proper credit worthiness assessment on consumers before granting credit to avoid reckless lending.  Debt collection: financial institutions shall adopt debt recovery processes that are courteous and fair to consumers. Consumers must be proactively engaged and given early notice of outstanding obligations prior to the commencement of debt collection efforts.  Sales promotion: marketing of products and services using incentives should be carried out in an ethical and professional manner. | The Bank shall:  1. Observe high ethical standards and professionalism in all business transactions with consumers. 2. Assess consumers’ financial capabilities and offer only products or services that are suitable to their needs and financial situation. 3. Provide channels for consumers to make enquiries and complaints. 4. Respond to all requests for information from consumers in a timely and clear manner. 5. Provide consumers with objective financial advice to support informed decision-making. 6. Carry out proper creditworthiness assessments before granting credit, to avoid reckless lending. 7. Ensure that debt recovery processes are fair and courteous, giving consumers early notice and proactive engagement before starting debt collection actions. 8. Conduct sales promotions and marketing using incentives in an ethical and professional manner. | Reputational damage, consumer complaints, regulatory sanctions, mis-selling, credit defaults, unfair practices | High | High | All Departments: Compliance, Risk, Sales, Advisory, Customer Service, Collections, Marketing | Code of Conduct, Ethics Training, Suitability and Credit Assessment Tools, Complaint Channels, SLA for Response, Marketing Approval Process | Medium | Medium | Mystery Shopping, Complaint Reviews, Agent Monitoring, Ethical Audits | Ongoing | Compliance (with Business Unit Leads) |

Remuneration and incentives structure in the industry shall encourage ethics and integrity.  3. Customer shall be notified when an activity threatens to violate the terms of contract. | The Bank shall: 1. |  |  |  | 2.2.2 | Provision of Financial Advice | 1. Financial Institutions shall act in the best interest of consumers in the provision of advice and execution of transactions. For consumers to make informed decisions in choosing financial products and services, they must be acquainted with the features, costs, risks, penalties, terms and conditions. Thus, before consumers sign up for any financial products, FIs shall: a) Give clear information on the features of the services and products; b) Assess whether the products or services of interest suit the consumers’ needs. Where a product requested does not meet the needs of the customer, the FI is obliged to advise or caution the customer in writing before granting such; and c) Assess the consumers’ ability to fulfill the terms and conditions associated with the financial products and services;  2. Financial institutions shall provide appropriate financial advice to consumers before the sale of any financial product or service. For financial products or services that are complex or potentially risky to consumers, financial institutions shall document pre-contractual and subsequent deliberations with consumers. In addition, records of meetings must be acknowledged by the consumer.  3. The CBN shall use appropriate mechanisms (such as examining FIs’ records of pre-contractual deliberations with customers (see Section 2.2.2.(2)), mystery shopping amongst others) to monitor financial institutions and ensure that they properly engage customers prior to the sale of financial products or services. | The Bank shall: 1. Provide financial advice that is in the best interest of consumers. 2. Before offering financial products/services, FIs must:     a) Disclose clear product/service features, costs, risks, and terms.     b) Assess if the product fits the consumer’s needs; if not, caution the consumer in writing.     c) Evaluate the consumer’s ability to meet product terms. 3. Keep documented records of advice sessions and have them acknowledged by the consumer for complex or risky products. 4. Allow the CBN access to such records for supervision (e.g., mystery shopping). | - Failure to offer appropriate financial advice and document advisory interactions can result in: ▪ Breach of regulatory expectations ▪ Customer disputes or litigation ▪ Fines or sanctions by the CBN ▪ Damage to consumer trust and institutional reputation | Medium | High | - Head of Product Management - Executive Compliance Officer - Customer Relationship Managers - Advisory Team | - Implement Customer Suitability & Risk Profiling tools - Provide product fact sheets and risk disclosures for each offering - Require documented customer acknowledgments of advisory sessions - Introduce a compliance checklist for high-risk or complex products - Maintain audit trails for all advisory engagements | Low | Medium | - Regular compliance spot-checks and mystery shopping simulations - Periodic CBN regulatory audit readiness reviews - Automated flagging of complex/risky product sales requiring enhanced advisory protocol | - Ongoing, with documentation before each product/service sale | - Executive Management - Compliance & Risk Units - Internal Audit - Legal & Regulatory Affairs Department |

Make consumers’ statements of financial position available at all times. 5.
